BOARD OF TRADE. SESSION 1910.
RUNCORN AND WESTON ELECTRIC LIGHTING.
PROVISIONAL ORDER.

(Supply of Electrical Energy for all purposes within the Urban District of Runcorn and the town- ship and parish of Weston within the Rural District of Runcorn in the County of Chester to acquire lands by agreement—to break up streets, etc., and lay down and erect Electric lines, wires, posts and apparatus— rates and charges—lncorporation of Acts and other provisions).

NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that the Castner Kellner Alkali Company, Limited whose works are at Weston Point, Runcorn aforesaid and whose registered offices are at 13 Abchurch Lane in the City of London (hereinafter called " the Company ") intend to apply to the Board of Trade on or before the 21st day of December next for a Provisional Order (herein- after called "the Order") under the Electric Lighting Acts ISS2 and 1888 for all or some of the following amongst other purposes (that is to say) :- 1. TO authorise the Company to generate store and simply electric energy for lighting heating power and all other purposes public and private as defined by the Electric Lighting Acts within the Urbt.n District of Runcorn ard the township and parish of We:3ton within the Rural District of Runcorn in the County of Chester (herein referred to as "the area of Supply.") 2. TO enable the Company to acquire by agreement or take on lease and hold lands and property or interests or easements in or over lands and to appropriate for the purposes of the Order any lands belonging to or held by them and to construct and maintain upon such lands and property, stations and works for the genera- tion and supply of electricity for lighting power and other purposes together with all buildings, engines, apparatus works and appliances which the Company may consider necessary for the purposes aforesaid and to empower the Company to sell or dispose of any lands not required for the purposes of the undertaking. 3. THE names of the streets in which it is proposed that Electric lines *shall be laid down within a period to be specified by the Order are as follows :—Within the township and parish of Weston—South Road, Weston Point and Sandy Lane—Within the Urban Dis- trict of Runcorn—Weston Road (being the main road from Runcorn to Weston) from Sandy Lane to High- lands Road, Highlands Road, Greenway Road, Sandy Lane—High Street from Waterloo Road to the Junction of High Street with Church Street—Church Street and Waterloo Road. 4. TO authorise the Company to break up cross or interfere with the following streets, roads, canals, bridges, railways and tramways not repairable by the public at large, viz : (a) STREETS—Norman Road from its junction with Cawley Street to Heath Road and the following bridges and railways, namely : The Bridge known as Delph Bridge carrying Bridge Street over the Duke of Bridgewater's Canal. The Bridge known as Doctors Bridge carrying Greenway Road over the Duke of Bridgewater's Canal. The Bridge known as Waterloo Bridge carrying Waterloo Road over the Duke of Bridgewater's Canal. The Bridge carrying Greenway Road over the London and North-Western Railway. The Bridge carrying Heath Road over the said Railway. Sandy Lane. The Bridge known as Victoria Bridge carrying Victoria Road over the Duke of Bridgewater's Canal at the entrance to the Big Pool. The Bridge called Bates Bridge which carries Sea Lane over the Duke of Bridgewater's Canal. The footbridge which crosses the Duke of Bridge- water's Canal at the top of Ellesmere Street into the Manchester Ship Canal Works, known as the " Sprinch Yard."

_ _ The footbridge which crosses the Duke of Bridge- 'water's Canal from Halton Road (near to the bottom of Stonehills Lane) to Canal Street. The footbridge which carries the footpath from Balfour Street across the London and North-Western Railway to Picow Street. Westfleld Road (otherwise Cock and Hen Lane).
The continuation of Percival Lane to its junction

wiiii"-w.estfield Road (otherwise Cock and Hen Lane) by the road which runs in a south-westerly direction from the-said continuation under the bridge, carrying the Dock Branch of the London and North-Western Railway. The Towpath of the River Weaver Canal. The Manchester Ship Canal. (b) RAILWAYS—The Dock Branch Railway Line of the London and North-Western Railway Company in the Urban District of Runcorn. The Dock Branch Railway Line of the Manchester Ship Canal Company in the Urban District of Runcorn,and the extension of that line in a southerly direction to join the siding or tramway of the Com- pany. _ (C) TRAMWAys.—The private tramway of the

Runcorn and Helsby Red Sandstone Comptiny. 5. TO authorise the Company to take, collect and recover rents rates and charges for the supply of electricity for lighting power or other purposes, and the use of any machines, lamps, meters, fittings or apparatus connected therewith, and to prescribe and limit the price to be charged therefor. 6. TO confer upon the Company all or some of the powers of the Electric Lighting Acts, 1882 and 1888, and any enactments incorporated therewith, and to alter vary or extinguish all rights and privileges which would or might interfere with any of the objects of the Order, and to confer all other rights and. privileges necessary for carrying Ku& objects into effect. , 7. TO incorporate with the Order such of the pro- visions contained in the Schedule to the Electric Lighting (Clauses) Act, 1899, and in any Act amending or extend- ing the same as are applicable to cases in which the Undertakers are not the local authority, and to apply such provisions to the undertaking to be authorised by the order subject to such variations and exceptions as may be contained therein. 8. TO make special provisions with respect to the rights and obligations of the Company to afford a supply of electricity to premises having a separate supply, and the terms and conditions on which such supply will be afforded, and if and so far as is necessary to modify or exempt the Company from the pbligations in reference thereto imposed, upon undertakers by the Electric Lighting Act, 1882, and the Acts amending or extending the same. 9. TO provide that the Company may refuse to supply electrical energy to any persons whose payments for the supply of such energy may be in arrenr, and to require that the consumers of electrical energy shall give notice to the Company, before quitting any premises supplied with such energy by the Company, and to provide for the liabilities of such consumers when the requisite notice is not given. 10. TO empower the Company within a limited period after the commencement of the Order and with the consent of the Board of Trade, to transfer the undertsking authorised by the Order to a Company to be named in the Order on such terms and conditions as may be approved by the Board of Trade. AND NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that the draft of the Order will be deposited at the offices of the Board of Trade on or before the 21st day of December next and printed copies of the draft Order when deposited and of the Order when made may be obtained (at the price of one shilling for each copy), at the Counting House at the Works of the Company at Weston Point Runcorn and at the offices of the under-mentioned Solicitors and Parliamentary Agents. AND NOTICE IS HEREBY FURTHER GIVEN that a map shewine the boundaries of the area of supply and the streets in which it is proposed that electric lines shall be laid down within a specified time and a copy of the advertisement as published in the London Gazette will be deposited on or before the 30th day of November, 1909, for public inspection with the Clerk of the Peace for the County of Chester at his office at Chester, at the office of the Clerk to the Runcorn Urban District Council at Runcorn, and at the office of the Clerk of the Runcorn Rural District Council at Runcorn and at the office of the Board of Trade, Whitehall, London.

AND NOTICE Is HEREBY FURTHER GIVEN that every local or other authority, company or person desirous of bringing before the Board of Trade any objection respecting the application must do so by letter addressed to the Board of Trade marked on the outside of the cover enclosing it "Electric Lighting Acts" on or before the 15th day of January 1910 and a copy of such objection must also be forwarded to the ucder-mentioned Solicitors or Parliamentary Agents. DATED this 16th day of November 1909, BAKER, BLAKER & HAWES, 117, Cannon Street, London, Solicitors. LEWIN GREGORY & ANDERSON, 6,The Sanctuary, Westminster, Parliamentary Agents.

IN PARLIAMENT. SESSION 1910. WARRINGTON CORPORATION. (Conferring further Powers on the Corporation of Warrington ; New Bridge to replace present War- rington Bridge ; Construction of New Bridges over River Mersey; River Walls; Widening and Improve- ment of Streets and Roads ; Purchase of Garven House Property ; Purchase of Lands by Compulsion or Agreement ' • Extension of Public Baths and Technical School ; Sale of Howley Recreation Ground ; Power to deal with proceeds of Sale ; Extension of Town Hall ; Further Provisions as to the Gas, Water and Electricity Undertakings of the Corporation ; Free Wiring ; Supply of Electricity in bulk; Motor Omnibuses; Licensing of Drovers, &c.; Ice-Cream Provisions : Advertising Vehicles; Common Lodging-Houses; New Streets and Build- ings; Sewers and Drains ; Infectious Disease and Sanitary Provisions ; Subscriptions ; Borrowing Powers; Rates; Police Provisions; Incorporation, Amendment, and Repeal of Acts). NOTICE is hereby given that application is intended to Fe made to Parliaratnt in the ensuing Session, by the Mayor, Aldermen and Burgesses of the county borough of Warrington (in this :Notice called "the Corporation ") for leave to bring in a Bill for all or some of the following purposes (namely) :- 1. To empower the Corporation to make and main- tain, wholly in the county borough of Warrington, and the County Palatine of Lancaster, the following works or some of them, or some part or parts thereof (that is to say ) : Work No. I,—A Bridge to replace the present Warrington Bridge crossing the River Mersey between Bridge Street and Knutsford Road and occupying as nearly as may be the site of the existing bridge. Work No. 2.—A training wall on the northern bank of the River Mersey commencing at a point 70 yards measured in a south-westerly direction from the south-east corner of Bridge Foot House and extending in a north-easterly direction for a distance of 120 yards or thereabouts and terminating at the westerly end of the Packet stage. Work No. 3.—A training wall on the southern bank of the River Mersey commencing at a point 33 yards or thereabouts measured in a north-westerly direction from the south-west corner of the Bridge Jun and extending in a north-easterly direction for a distance of 75 yards or thereabouts andlerminating at a point 47 yards or thereabouts measured in a north-westerly direction from the south-west corner of Water Street. Work No. 4.—A widening of Knutsford Road com- mencing on the southern bank of the River Mersey at the south-east end of Work No. 1 and extending in a south-easterly direction for a distance of 103 yards or thereabouts and terminating on the east side of the premises now occupied by Mr. John Lunt. Work No. 5.—A widening of the western side of the southern approach of Warrington Bridge from a point on the southern bank of the River Mersey at the termination of Work No. 1 and extending in a southerly direction for a distance of 50 yards or thereabouts to Wilderspool Causeway. Work No. 6.—A widening of Chester Road on the south-east side from its Junction with River Road to its junction with Stag Bridge. Work No. 7.—A bridge crossing the River Mersey at Howley commencing on the western Lank at a point 87 yards or thereabouts measured in a southerly direction from the south corner of the warehouse of the Bridgwater undertaking of the Manchester Ship Canal Company and terminating on the eastern bank at a point 70 yards or thereabouts drawn in an easterly direction from the point of commencement. Work No. B.—An approach road on the western side of the said bridge and commencing by a junction with the said bridge at its commencement and terminating by a junction with Parr Street, at a point 90 yards or thereabouts, measured in a westerly direction from the point of commencement of this work. Work No. 9.—An approach road on the western side of the said bridge commencing by a junction with the said bridge at its commencement and terminating by a junction with Navigation Street and Egerton Street, at a point 134 yards or there- abouts measured in a northerly direction from the commencement of this work. Work No. 10.—An approach road on the eastern side of the said bridge, commencing by a junction with tbe said bridge at its termination and terminat- ing by a junction with Knutsford Road, at the entrance to Victoria Park, Work No. 11.—A river wall along the south side of the River Mersey and a widening of the north side of Knutsford Road commencing at a point 120 yards measured in a westerly direction from the entrance to Victoria Park, and extending in a westerly direc- tion for a distance of 210 yards and terminating at a point 57 yards or thereabouts measured in a north- easterly direction, from the centre of the north end of Grove Street. The whole of the above works will be situate in the County Borough of Warrington. - 2. To enable the Corporation in connection with the above-mentioned works to construct all necessary and proper foundations, embankments training walls, arches, girders, piers, supports, anchorages. piles, plat- forms, jettys, landing stages, wharves, sluices, engines, dynamos, weighing-machines, sheds, offices, approaches, buildings, lifts, stairs, apparatus, machinery, appliances, and works counected therewith. 3. To provide for the carrying of tramways mains and pipes and electrical conductors, wires and apparatus on or along the intended bridges, and to authorise agreements with companies and persons in respect thereof. 4. To empower the Corporation to place piers and supports for the intended bridges in and upon streets and roads, and in the foreshore or bed of the River Mersey, and in other respects to alter or interfere with the bed, banks or foreshore of the said river. 5. To make such provisions as may have been or may be agreed upon, or as may be thought proper by Parlia- ment to be prescribed or authorized by the Bill for the protection of any Commissioners or other body having jurisdiction over any part of the River Mersey, or for the protection and benefit of landowners and other bodies and persons whose property, rights and interests will or may be affected by the intended works, and to authorize, confirm or give effect to any agyee- ments or arrangements which may be entered into between the Corporation and such landowners, bodies or persons, or some or any of them, and to empower the Corporation to execute any works necessary for the purpose. 6. To authorize the Corporation to remove, sour, take, and carry away all rock, beds of gravel and sand and other impediments, and execute all other works necessary or convenient for making or maintaining and repairing the intended works and approaches thereto. 7. To empower the Corporation to. deviate laterally and vertically from the lines and levels of the intended bridges, street works, river walls and other works shown on the deposited plans hereinafter mentioned to the extent to be shown on the said plans, or to be defined in the intended Act, and in either case beyond the limits of lateral and vertical deviation prescribed by the Railways Clauses Consolidation Act, 1845. 8. To authorize the Corporation, for the purposes of tbe intended Act, to break up, cross, alter the level of and otherwise alter, widen, narrow, divert, stop up and interfere with (either temporarily or permanently) streets, roads, highways, footpaths, rivers, streams, navigations, watercourses, sewers, drains, pavements, mains, pipes, tramways, telegraphs, telephones, electric wires and conductors, and apparatus, to raise, sink or alter steps areas, cellars, windows, spouts and pipes, and to under-pin or otherwise strengthen (either tempo- rarily or permanently) houses or other premises. 9. To make special provisions as to the accommoda- tion of persons of the labouring class displaced by the execution of any of the works authorized by the Bill. 10. To empower the Corporation to purchase or acquire by compulsion or agreement or to take on lease lands, houses and buildings, and rights or easements therein. 1L To make special provisions with respect to the compensation to be paid in respect to the taking of lands or the execution of works under the powers of the Bill, and with respect to the method of ascertainment of such compensation, the payment of costs, the delivery of claims, and other matters of procedure connected therewith, and to provide that the benefits accruing to any person from any street improvement or other work shall be set off against the purchase price or compensa- tion payable by the Corporation. 12. To exempt the Corporation from the operation of section 92 of the Lands Clauses Consolidation Act, 1845, so as to enable them to purchase compulsorily part only of certain properties. 13. To make provision for the correction of errors in the plans, sections and books of reference to be deposited in connection with the Bill as hereinafter mentioned. 14. To empower the Corporation to bold lease and dispose of any lands acquired or to be acquired for the purposes of the Bill and not required for those purposes. 15. To authorise the Corporation to appropriate and use for the purposes for which they were acquired, or for any purposes specified in the Bill, certain lands and properties now held by the Corporation, and to empower the Corporation to borrow moneys for the purchase of lands and properties. 16. To prohibit the anchoring or mooring of vessels under or near the intended bridges or either of them, and to authorize the Corporation to make, place, and main- tain beacons, lights, buoys, mooring-posts, works, and conveniences under or near to or in connection with
the bridges, and to authorise and enforce bye-laws and regulations in regard to the navigation of the said river in the neighbourhood of the intended bridges or ether of them.

• 17. To sanction and confirm the purchase by the Corporation of No. 78, Sankey Street and the lands adjacent thereto, end to empower the Corporation to the same for the extension of the public baths, or for such other purposes as the Corporation may deem expedient. 18. To authorize the Corporation on lands already acquired or to be acquired by them to alter, extend, improve or enlarge the existing Town Hall buildings and public baths and technical school. 19. To empower the Corporation to sell, lease, or dispose of the lands known as the Howley Recreazion Ground, in the borough, and to make provision for the application of the proceeds of such sale.

.120. To authorize the Corporation to grant licences to diovers, slaughtermen and others, and V) prohibit under penalty unlicensed persons from holding them- selves out as holding licences, and to empower the Corporation to make provision for the licensing of hackney carriages, including the grant of occisional licences.

21. To provide that enactments Mating to hackney carriages and other public vehicles shr.ll apply to vehicles conveying passengers to and from railway stations within the Borough. 22. To empower the Corporation to lay out, improve, furnish and equip for the purposes of public' recreation and enjoyment the lands known as Victoria Park and to authorize the Corporation to purchase part of St. Elphin's Park and to lay out and improve the same. 23. To make further provision for improving the water supply of the Corporation. 21. To make farther provision with regard to the -anufacture and supply of gas and particularly to pro- vide for the increase of discounts on gas accounts and the use of anti-fluctuators for gas engines, the giving of notices of removal and discontinuance of supply and the method of dealing with erroneous registration by gas meters, to require any person who has a private installation of gas for power or other purposes to pay a minimum charge for gas supplied by the Corporation and to impose other terms and conditions in connection with such supply, to prescribe a minimum charge for gas laid on to premises having a supply of electricity, and to regulate the construction and repair of pipes and apparattis between the mains of the Corporation and the meters on the premises of consumers. 25. ro amend the provisions of the Warrington Cor- poration Gas Act, 1877, as to charges for gas in and beyond the borough, and in particular to provide for a lower minimum additional charge or for an increased discount to consumers outside the borough. 28. To amend section 107 of the Warrington Corpora- tion Act, 1899, and to empower the Corporation to make byelaws with respect to the nature materials, work- manship and strength, and the mode of connection, disconnection, alteration and repair of gaspipes, meters, taps, fittings and apparatus, and with respect to the giving of notice to the Corporation by persons requir- ing a supply of gas or intending to construct or alter their gas-fittings, or other apparatus. 27. To authorize the Corporation to supply, fix, repair, and remove motors and electrical fittings of all kindaand all materials and work necessary in connec- tion nierewith, and to take such remuneration and make such terms and conditions as they may think lit in relation thereto, and to provide that the same shall not be liable to distress for rent or to execution.

28. To require any person who has a separate supply of electricity from any installation other than that of the Corporation to pay a minimum charge for any supply he may require from the Corporation, and to enable the Corporation to impose other terms and conditions in connection with such supply. 29. To require electric lighting consumers to give notice to the Corporation before removing from any premises supplied with electric current by the Corpora- tion to provide that the Corporation may refuse to supply electric energy to persons owing money to the Corporation, and to authorize the Corporation to allow discounts or rebates on electric lighting and power accounts. $O. To enable the Corporation to enter into and fulfil agreements for the supply of electric energy in bulk or otherwise to the local authorities, companies oc rnrsonl: outside the district, and particularly to empower flu_ Corporation to supply energy to any consumer whose premises are within 200 yards (or such other distance as the Bill may prescribe) of any electric main or cable of the Corporation, and to empower the Corporation to supply electric energy for traction purposes to be used either within or beyond the borough, and to authorize the purchase of electric energy in bulk by the Corporation. 31. To empower the Corporation to lay mains, pipes, wires and other apparatus for electric supply in streets and other places not dedicated to public use. 32. To empower the Corporation to provide and run motor omnibuses either within or outside the borough and to take fares and charges for conveyance therein, and in connection therewith to acquire and provide land, buildings, plant, apparatus and other things, and to make bye-laws and regulations for regulating the travelling in and use of such omnibuses and for prevent- ing nuisances and injury. 33. To confer further powers upon the Corporation in reference to the laying out of new streets, the erec- tion of new buildings, and the construction of sewers. 34. To authorize the removal of dilapidated build- ings, to prescribe the area of habitable rooms, to prevent water flowing on footpaths, and soil and sand from being washed into streets. 35. To amend section 70 of the Warrington Corpora- tion Act, 1899, and to make provision with respect to the removal or alteration of any door, shutter, trap, platform, sign or other projection, apparatus, or thing against or in front of any building and causing or likely to cause danger or obstruction to the use of any St reet.

36. To require that all communications with sewers of the Corporation be made by the Corporation at the expense of the owner or occupier of the premises con- cerned, to amend and extend the provisions of section' 19 of the Public Health Acts Amendment Act, 1890, to provide that watercourses may not be covered up except in accordance with an approved plan. 37. To make further provision for improving the sanitary condition of the Borough and particularly to impose penalties for the improper construction or repair of water closets or drains, to enforce the pro- vision of sanitary dustbins, and to authorize the Corporation to provide street orderly bins, to require a certificate to be given in the case of a person dying of infectious disease, and to prohibit the blowing or inflation of carcases, and to make provision with regard to the manufacture and sale of ice creams and other similar commodities and the inspection of premises in connection therewith, and the use of vehicles and stands by ice-cream dealers. 38. To make further provision for the regulation and control of common lodging-houses, and to empower the Corporation to close or obtain orders for the closing of common lodging-houses infected with infectious disease.

39. To enable the Corporation to pay compensat ion to persons who may for the purpose of stopping the spread of infectious disease cease their employment, and to prescribe and enforce penalties on persons with- holding information from the Medical Officer of Health and to make other provisions for preventing the spread of infectious disease.

40. To prohibit and prevent. street cries and other noises, and to prohibit any person having the care of more than one cart when passing through the streets. 41. To make such provision as the Corporation may consider necessary or the Bill may prescribe for the protection of their gas and water mains against electro- lytic action or interference by the laying of telegraphic or telephonic cables wires or other apparatus. 42. To require that dairies and milkshops within the Borough shall be registered and to make such provision in reference thereto as may he considered desirable. 43. To make provision for the regulation of the trade of hairdressers, barbers and fried fish dealers, and to amend the provisions of the Public Heslp Acts with respect to any such trades. 44. To authorise the Corporation to deal with persons found in unlawful possession of stolen goods the owners of hich cannot be found and to mak% further provisions iu reference thereto. 45. To enable the Corporation to borrow moneys for the construction of the intended bridges street works and other works, and for the widening of ?'Market Gate and Buttermarket Street, and for any of the pur- poses of the Bill or of the water undertaking of the Corporation upon the security of any of the revenues and properties of the Corporation or the borough fund and borough rate or improvement fund and improve- ment rate, and to provide for the repayment of such moneys and the suspension of the sinking fund or instal- ments of principal with other usual provisions in con- nection therewith, and also to authorize the borrowing of money to repay expenditure incurred in connection with the widening of Bridge Street and in connection with the water undertaking of the Corporation, and for other purposes to be specified in the Bill. 46. To enable the Corporation to collect all rates upon one basis of assessment and to consolidate all the rates levied in the Borough, and to provide for the same being collected upon one demand note and to alter the existing mode of assessing the rates levied in the Borough. 47. To enable the Corporation to use one form of mortgage for all purposes, and to secure all loans indifferently upon the properties or revenues of the Corporation, to use sinking funds instead of borrowing,

BOARD OF AGRICULTURE AND FISHERIES. SMALL HOLDINGS AND ALLOTMENTS ACT, 1908. COUNTY OF LANCASTER. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that FREDERIC IMPEY, Esq., the Commissioner appointed by the Board, will hold an INQUIRY (1) As to the extent to which there is a demand for SMALL HOLDINGS in or near the township of Culcheth, or would be a demand if suitable land were available; and (2) as to the extent to which it is reasonably practicable, having regard to the provision of the Act to satisfy any such demalld. The COMMISSIONER will attend at the Newchurch Church of England School, Culchetb, on Thursday, the 2nd day of December, at the hour of 7 p.m., when be will be prepared to see any persons who desire to buy or lease Holdings exceeding one acre and not exceed- ing 50 acres which they are prepared themselves to cultivate.
Signed T. H. ELLIOTT (Secretary)

COUNTY BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON TO PAINTERS AND DECORATORS. The Baths Committee and Health Committee of the Council of the County Borough of Warrington are prepared to receive TENDERS for the Internal PAINTING of the IkIEN'S IST CLASS PLUNGE BATH and the ADMINISTRATIVE BLOCK, Aikin- street Hospital. Specifications ac., may be seen and forms of tender and all further information obtained at the office of the Borough Surveyor, Town Hall, on and after Saturday next. the 27th November, at which place tenders must be delivered on or before Five o'clock p.m. on Tuesday the 30th day of November. The lowest or any tender not necessarily accepted. THOS. LONGDIN, Borough Engineer and Survvyor. Borough Engineer and Surveyor's Office. 25th November, 1909.

To enable the Corporation to subscribe towards hospitals, infirmaries, nursing institutions, charities and other benevolent objects not excpeding such sums as may be prescribed by the Bill, and to pay other expenses reasonably incurred in the administration of local affair&

49. To provide for the payment of the expenses of carrying into effect the purposes of the Bill, and to permit the application of any funds, revenues, and rates of the Corporation for that object. 50, To make further provision with regard to the evidence of appointments of officers of the Corporation, the confirmation of bye-laws, the recovery of demands and penalties, the right of appeal and other matters of procedure, the authentication and service of notices, the application of penalties, the indemnification of persons acting under the powers of the Bill, the saving for indictments and that justices shall not be dis- qualified.

- 51. To provide that in executing works in default of an owner or occupier the-Corporation shall .not be liable save in case of negligence. 52. The Bill will, so far as it may be decried necessary or expedient, vary and extend or repeal, alter, and consolidate, and amend all or any of the provisions of tbe Warrington Improvement and Market Act, 1854, the Warrington Corporation Gas Act, 1877, and the Warrington Corporation Act, 1899, and all other Acts or Orders relating to the Corporation, and will or may incorporate in extorts() or by reference and with or without alteration the provisions or some of the provisions of the Lands Clauses Acts, the Railways Clauses Consolidation Act, 1845, the Harbours, Docks, and Piers Clauses Act, 1847, the Electric Lighting Acts of 1882 and 1888, and any Act amending the same respectively, and the Bill will vary or extinguish all rights and privileees which would interfere with any of its objects and confer other rights and privileges. And notice is hereby given, that plans and sections of the intended works showing the lines and levels thereof, the plans also showing the lands and other Roperty intended to be taken compulsorily under the powers of the Bill, together with a book of reference to the plans, and a copy of this Notice as published in the London Gazette, will, on or before the 30th day of Novem,,er instant, he deposited for public inspection with the Clerk of the Peace tor the county of Lancaster at his office at Preston, and also with the Town Clerk of the county borough of Warrington at his office at the Town Hall, Warrington. Printed copies of the proposed Bill will be deposited in the Private Bill Office of the House of Commons on or before the 17th day of December next. Dated this 17th day of November' 1909. J. ,-AN INSURANCE CLAIM. Interesting Casa. At the Borough Police Court, on Tuesday' Resannah Lister, oriAlarket-street, sued the National Life Aseur- once Company, whose headquarters are at 149, Leaden- hall-street,Loadon, E C. for £l3 12s. insurance money, which she said should ha:ve been paid on the death of her sister-in-law, Mary Adams, whom complainant had. insured. She was represented by Mr. A. Browne and Mr. W. H. Cranston, of Leigh, appeared for the ;astir- ance Company.—Mr. Browne said that the case was brought forward under a clause of the Industrial Assur- ance Act of 1896. Mrs. Lister was the wife of Thomas. Lister, who kept a shop in Market-street. She was the idatighter of Mrs. Broughton. %Vim) had insured her sister- in-law (Mrs. Adams) in the British National Premium Association. In 1907 this company was transferred to; the Progressive Insurance Company, and in January , last that company was arnidgamated with the National Standard Assurance Co. Ltd. Under the old company Mrs. Lester was entitled to £l6 16-s„ bat the superin- tendent of the new c3mpany visited her and told her the amount was £l3 125., and thereupon Mr. Heywood,, who was their agept, filled up a proposal form, which was to state the relationsiiip between the proposer arid proeosed, and on this form Mrs. Adams was referred to as Mrs. Lister's mother. Answering this proposal an agent came down and told Mrs. Lister that she caule have full benefit if she continued payin.<, 8d per week, and she did so until tbe death of Mrs. Adams on October Bth. The only contention that the company could bring forward was that there was no insurable interest, but fortunately , there was a very strong insurable interest in this ease. Mrs. Lister had many times helped Mrs. Adams with food and raomey.—Mr. Btowne's statements were corroborated by complainant, her husband, and Mr. Heywood, thillate agent to the company. Mr. Creston said that there Ult 9 no blood relations between Airs. Lister and Mrs.Adiims. The proposal form was incorrectly filled in by the agent. That -was a distinct untruth which was known to the agent at the time, also to Mrs. Lester. Policies were only issued on the truth of statements made and he submitted that the complainant could have no legal claim on that point. He thought they were perfectly justified in contesting that case, as such practices did the business of the Company hsrm. After consultation tbe chairman (Mr. H. Roberts) said it was the unanimous opinion of the bench that there we some insureble interest which they assessed at £5. They did not, think there was any wilful mis- -representation. It was a n.v.tter of common knowledee that the poorer people of the country were totally ignorant of their true legal position as policy holders,. He did not cast any reflectiun upon their Company at £3 3s. costs were also allowed to Mr. 13rocvLe.

div.head: REV. F. B. MEYER.
div.p: REV. F. B. MEYER.
HIS VIEWS ON THE CONSTITUTIONAL CRISIS. Addresses to Free Churchmen.

Warrington had the honour of a visit on Monday from the Rev. F. • B. Meyer, one of the most widely respected leaders of the Free Churches, Who came to address A series of meetings in the Parr Hall under the auspices of the Warrington Free Church Council. Mr. Meyer is rne of the most striking and winnina personalities in, the religions world of to-day. His activities are bv•no means limited to his own denomin- ation, in fact his services are so freely given for the benefit of Nonconformity in general that he is by common consent regarded as the "bishop "of the Free Churches. Kindliness and sympathy are depicted in his countenance and his speeches are so frank and outspoken, so thoroughly human and practical, that he always commands Close attention. He can crack a joke with the utmost relish, and his criticisms, though never lacking in paint and directness, are so playfully put that no-one would be so ungracious as to resent them. But when protest- ing against some great evil, or pointing his hearers to a lofty ideal and noble effort,t here is a manly, straight- forward ling in his appeal which denotes the fire and earnestness of conviction. Mr. Meyer's visit to Warrington had been looked forward to with great interest and pleasure by all who had had the privilege of hearing him on previous occasions; and there were large and appreciative gatherings.

IDEALS IN NATIONAL LIFE. In the afternoon Mr. Meyer preached from Exodus iii., 14v. The sermon was mainly Biblical but he alluded to social questions just for a minute or two. He said that there was nothing needed in this country to-day more than that the aristocracy should recognise their brotherhood to the democracy,that those who were in high positions should recognise their brothers who were in need and sorrowful and the one thing he dreaded ,this week more than enot her in this great Constitutional struggle was that it would drag class against class. He said that when Moses slew the Egyptian it was the act of a man who thought he was going to reform the world by his own right arm. No man ever would he able to reconstruct society by brute force or even by intellectual force. They, could not when they were face to face with enormous wrongs which were hurting an entire people. No-one had an arm strong enongh or or voice loud enough or big enough to emancipate a people. Everything had to be done with the help of God. A Divine power was needed to fit people for the highest ideals of national life. Referring to the French Revolution, he :laid that they demolished royalty by brute force. But Pe Robespierre and what t iwasnth their oeraecseulatn?d for '[hey years st ;h streets of Parisi ran with noble blood. 'What was it that saved England from a French Revolution? What was it that was working in the hearts of our countrymen at the time of the Chartist Riots? Meat Britain was raved by the outbreak of the great Methodist Revival. It was because of Wesley and Whitfield and many other ministers who preached the gospel to crowds of people. In all parts the fire of the Holy Ghost broke out and the tire of the Holy Ghost sated England from revolution and the work that was done by the Gospel in those days prepared the people for the mighty work that was done by Earl Shaftesbury and all those great reforms that wete associated with his name. Continuing he said he knew that a great deal could he raid for the Socialists—a great deal for certain reforms which men were advocating. He knew there was a great deal of thought now twine exercised by men forsocial construc- tion but he more and more felt in his heart that they were never going tn meke those schemes possible, even if they were desirable, nuless they began by overthrowing the drink triffic and immorality. They must get at the root of things. It was no use having a reform on paper. They must rave the people and if they saved a people they made a referl Cmed and reconstructed society CIVDUTY.
After the service tea was partaken of and then a con- fermee was held.

Mr.PArtxxit presided and extended a hearty vveloome to Mr. Meyer. The secretary (Mr. E. Wynne :fortes) informed Mr. MAver that there were 19 churches in the Warrington • tend District Free Church Council. Mr.llleyer congratulated them on the number affiliated. He said that the Council ought not to judge party politics. They ought never to make it hard for a Tory or a Radical as such to enter a public body. They were tbe custodians of the public morals of the town and whenever its morals were being traversed they were bound as a community to insist upon it that the.morals of the town were kept clean and pure. He said that the Council would never do its proper work in the world until it cleared out of the town all that was immoral and hese. The temperance people ought never to allow a Brea ster S.ssions to come or go without making a protest against the issue of new licences and demanding the withdrawal of old ones. (Applause).

div.head: PUBLIC! MEETING
div.p: PUBLIC! MEETING

MR. MEYER AND THE POLITICAL CRISIS. In the evening a public meeting was held, tbe hall being crowded. Mr. C. B. Parker presided and amongst those present on the platform were :—Revs. F. B. Meyer, J. Vonge, E. B. Keeling, J. S. Flughes, H. Wall, and W. Reid. Messrs. George Clarke, E. Wynne Jones, A. Monnflold, J. C. Holland, E. England, and T. Dale. The CHAIRMAN explained that the meeting had no connect:on with Mr. Clarke's visit, as both events were separately arranged about the same time. The mission was mainly under the auspices of the V.ll.C.A.‘and all the connection the Free Church Council had with it was one of sympathy and help. The ,nresent meeting was distinctly under the an.pices of the Free Church Council and they were indebted to Nlr. Clarke for standing aside and allowing them to hold it. They trusted and believed that a meeting of that character and a man like Mr. Meyer would not make any awk- ward break in the conduct of the mission but rather that it might help it forward. Mr. Parker proceeded to urge the claims of the Civic League of Help. remarking that similar organizations had done wonderfully good work not only in Germany but in many towns in this country. He would like to ask for the interest and sym- pathy of the Free Churchmen of Warrington for the League. He did not ask it of them as Free Churchmen, because happily the League was on a.somewhat broader basis. Mile it was purely a citizens' organization, he was confident Witt the inspiration, love, sympathy and help which would be imparted through it, would come in the main from the teaching of the Lord Jesus Christ in the different Churches. Every one who had been engaged in charitable work must have felt the great difficulty there was in giving charity or help

div.head: SCHOOL FEES.
div.p: SCHOOL FEES.
MOTION FOR ABOLITION DEFEATED.
The Working Classes and Football.

The most important business at the monthly meeting of the Warrington Education Committee on Monday was the adjourned debate on the motion brought forward by Mr. A. J. Jolley "That on and after January 1:4,1910, the local authority no longer aanction the charging of tees in any of the public Elementary schools within the Borough." The DIRECTOR read the following letter he had received : "Friars Green House, November 17th. Dear sir,-1 am instructed by the Warrington Branch of the Independent Latour Party to send you the following resolution for your committee's consideration That having regard to the burden placed on poor parents by lhenharging of school fees,aud to the unnecessary dis- tinction which is thereby occasioned, this branch is of opinion that such fees should be abolished and hopes that you will see your way to take this step, ard.thus bring Warrington into line other to,,vn, Will you kindly lay the resolution before the next IL t ei ing of the Education Committee? Thanking you in anticipation. yours truly, R. PIERCE W'JtL.uS for the branch. The Rev. Canon STEVENSON, 'oho re opened the dis- cussion, said he felt sure that the motion had been brought forward by Mr. Jolley ,ighest and test intentions. Mr. Jolley was a rn3a with an extremely logical mind and tho moVon was extremelv logical, and if they were to regard it merely iror, point of view they could not advance an 3 thing it. it was said that the English Decn
with • the
thnl ninEt ;dora

governed by logic. There we-se other thins, • 'Fe con- , sidered outside the logical point of vie- elesped the Committee would pause before ' -toed to , the motion. One bad every sYmpatt:‘, s sss, fenny poor parent such as those Ia sshorn tau been made in the letter which haff been read. S•s-cses;.. the town wanted to press hardls on t boss) A° wore -table to hear the liuraen or who had even at diffscui,s in bearing the burden, and there were ~tines and seasons in the life of the town, such as the ci,al stritte, when the managers of the schools reruitted all the fees for some months until the strike was .-)ver. (liar, hear). He contended that there should be a eullicient number of free places where those who could not 'llford to pay should have ample opportunity ef placing their children: On the other hand there was a large number of working men in Warringter who wished to pay the fees, and it was not a burden to them to do so. They could afford the money and they had that Lancashire independence which made them think they would rather pay than have their children educated lor nothing. If they abolished the fees the children would not be better taught, and the rates of the town would he increased, and they would not like to add an additional burden even though it might not be a large one to the rates of the town. Mr. PLINSTuN . aid that at the last meeting of the committee, an absolutely untrue statement was made about himself and several other members. It was to the effect that they desired to give a stab below the belt. Their only intention in Atoesting the special meeting was that there should be an opportunity of having a full night's debate on this all-important matter, and also that opportunity should he given to test the feeling of the town in the municipal elections. If the electors were appealed to there would be a majority in favour of exemption. Education was com- pulsory, and therefore it ought to be free. It would be. free if the people of the town chose to demand the free places which they had a right to claim. They should not be compelled to pay fees against their will. The Roman Catholic schools and the majority of the infants' departments were already free. He thought if they looked at this matter from the point of view of the parents, who had a right to demand free education, and also considered the loss of grant involved in collecting the school fees on many occasions, they would come to the conclusion that the time had come when the fees, 'which once amounted to over£2,ooo but which had gradu- ally gone down to much less should be abolished. He ventured to say that if the resolution were defeated, within a short period there would be A still further substantial decrease and they would be compelled to abolish the fees—a procednre which only meant lid. on - the rates. Dealing with the argument that the Church schools would he placed in a bad position by the aboli- tion of fees, Mr. Pliuston asked if the religious teach- ing was not worth the £2O, £3O, or £4O, which the fees represented in some eases? Mr. R. T. FAITICLOUGH said heobjected to the aboli- tion of school fees because they would he pauperizing people. At the present time certain children received free education as well as free meals and clogs, and the only difference between those scholars and the work- house children was that the latter had 'free clothing ae well. It would be a serious thing if parental control ; were lost and the Committee had to stand in the place of the parents. A parent might deeite to send his children to a certain school, not simply on account of , the education given, hut on account of the class of children who attended. There were two class of parents —the undesirable and desirable. The former did not • talso relay pride in their chilclrensand non-payment of school tees could be made an excuse forneglecting to send the children to school. A desirable parent would willingly pay for his child, and they ought not to deprire him of Iris -control. He could now send his child to any school he wished,but if the fees were taken away there would only be one class, if the committee were short of free places they should build schools for free scholars. The speaker also • contended that the abolition of fees would pro} ably lead to unpleasantness , between the school managers and the committee, as the ' amount at the managers' disposal to carry out the ' recommendations of the authority with regard to insprevements would be reduced. • ; The Rev. Canon STEVENSON pointed out that the • school fees did not gotowards the-prevision of religious , instruction, but to the upkeep of the buildings. Councillor WILKINSON said he had chsnged his atti- tude since the last meeting. The total amount received In school fee*: per annum was .£1,600. Mr. BURGESS: £2,200 is the total, £1,600 is what the authority gets. , Councillor WILKINSON continuing, said between £4OO

an1..£500 was returned to the managers. One school which stood in a uniqnq position, where fees of from 2d. to Bd. were paid, received out of that £4OO or £5OO theta= of £l5O. That left for the other twenty schools on an avProse £l2 10s. each. He waated to know whether they ought to consider that from a finAncial _ _

point a vieW: fle walk not going to be led away by the Ictetement that pnrental control was lost if they took sway the fee 4. The parents of the children attend- ing the Benmont and Bolton schools did not think they had been deprived of control. It would be a greater blessing for a household with only lbs. a week coming in to have the fees then that the school managers

should Itave £l2 10s. a year. Mr. UNswouTH said there were only eleven schools in the town where fees were received, so that they received about £35 each—not £l2 10s. The abolition of fees would be taking ay indivilual liberty. If a parent WAR willing to pay for his child he could not uuderstand why he sbould not he allowed t do so Those who wanted free places conid have them if they applied. He deprecated the throwing away of £1,500 or £1,600 a year. which now went towards the rates. Mr. UPSoN said that in the schools where fees were charged there sere a number of free places available for parents to apply for. Rarely did they bear of a parent being refused. As to the alleged loss of attend- ances caused by children being s.nt home for fees, he found that taking the returns for May, August, Septem- ber end October. the attendance in the fee-paying schools was slightly higher than ant in the free schools. In Manchester and Liverpool there were non-provided schools and Courcil schools charging fees, and if Manchester and Liverpool could not afford at the present time to abolish fees, neither could Warrington. Councillor ROBERTS said he had pleasure in listening to

the traespa,ently honest but absolntely unsophisticaied speech of Nr. It. T. Fairclnugh. Its honesty was only equallei by its utter illogicality. He did not think for a moment that he would snegest seriously

that the retention of parental regpon%ibility was to he obtained by the payment of id. 2d. or 31. a week. 'What the comntittee were overlooking was the fact, whether they liked it or not, that the Board of vdnert- tion had created a condition of things in Warrington that was grossly anomalous ' • in insisting that provided schools should be free they had created a condition of thinga they were bound to take notice of. The position Unsworth suggested was to his (the speaker's) mind absolutely contrary to fact. It was not a qnes- tion of the parents wishing to be allowed to pay the fees. The question was Should those parents who are not fortunate enough to send their children to pro- vided schools be compelled to pay the school fees ?" (Hear, bear). Mr. UsswoßTH : They are not compelled. Councillor ROBERTS: Excti.e me, they are. Where do you cot the £1,600 a year from ? Mr. UNswoRTH : From the voluntary payments of the parents, _

Councillor RonrcQTs : The £1 ,600 a year is raised by compulsion, and by no other method. Continuing. he said the fact that the statutory numl er of free places had not been provided, was one of the few blots on the administration of education in the town. They were waiting for those ignorant peonle, who did not know their legal paition. to compel them to do a duty they ought to have voluntarily as•umed years ago. They had been trading mules false pretences. The resolution if insisted upon minht cause financial inconvenience to certain schools. They must* not forget that the managers of those schools had special privileges and they should consider how much those privileges were worth.

say so. It slid that if the Church .of England schools were closed, and the Education Committee bad to provide tt e schoola in tlts same district, to replace these schools would cost something liko £200,000. In order to replace the schools ttey would have to get the land for the buildings and playgrounds. &c., and the cot might he a great deal more. As a financier 111 r. .Tolley had fallen in his (the sreaker's) estimation. He used to tiu.t him when be brought in his Budget every year, but for the future he should receive it with a certain amount of hesitation. (Laughter.) The rev. gentleiran pointed out that out of every 2s. spent on education in Warrington, ld. was provided by fees, 9d. by tTe rates and is. 2d. by the Government. Alderman I'm:mos said the only objection he had to Mr. Jolley's motion was that it was rather inopportune.

As an Eftlisliman also he enroised his very 'treat regret that the Constitu- tional question was likely to arise or that by their action they might set class against class or raise a passion of feeling which he thought would he very detrimental to the best interests of the country. It was alsolutely certain that the will of the people must stand. (Applause). It was absolutely certain—and he was not speaking as a party politician but as a student of history and of that great movement which was spreading through the world to-day in which the people were coming to their own—that if there WAS a collision letween the two Houses, the popularly-elected House, which represented the people, would have the ultimate decision. (Applause). It must be so. It' was in the genius of the English people and it was in line with
that remarkable - all through the
pss-chiCal movement world people_ were
in which claiming

their right. At the same time he deeply deplored that there should be such a collision. He thought it would hurt the State. It would certainly hurt the Church and it might .ultimately almost afT ct the Monarchy itself. He could only hope that wiser counsels would prevail. that these hot bloods might get cooled, and that Lord Lansdowne might be able by wise statesmanship to evade that conflict which

which- was certainly going to hurt the House of Lords more than the House of Commons. (Applause.) \Then he spoke as he had done about the MOVEMENT OF THE PEOPLE they must remember that he had just come beck from a world tour. He was in Constantinople in *larch and April and he found the mighty -uprising of tne young Turk party to shatter the despotism of the Sultan end to liberate the great Turkish people. He travelled across the Indian Ocean and through Singapore to Chine, and all through that vast Empire he ford again and again the people asserting themselves end demand- ing Constitutional Government which, so far as the cities were concereed, was being granted. In his judg- ment, before many years were passed those great nations of Turkey and China would be governed, AR indeed Turkey was governed to some extent, by a Constitu- tionally-elected Parliament. He crossed Russia, and there also he found the people demanding their rights, though they found it hard to assert them. Now he came back to our own land and saw this great people's movement which reminded him of those 'mighty words uttered by one of the greatest men of the last century, when upon the field of Gettisbnrg . Abraham Lincoln said that from that moment and onward government of the people, by the people and for the people would 'be the recognized standard of civilization. "(Applause.) If it were true that the people of this country and of the Empire were more and more taking their rights and holding the supreme 'power, it became more than 'ever necessary that they should be penetrated by the spirit of true religion. He would rather have godless aristocrats than godless democrats. He would rather. if he must chose, that the upper classes gave themselves to irreligion and Sabbath breaking than have the masses of the people drenched in strong drink and regardless of the restrictions of God's day. (Applause.) He did not feel, thank God, that be had to make that choice and he did not see why either class should become irreligious or pleasure seeking, and forgetful of the Almighty. For his part his lot was cast amonest the great mass of people and especially in cnnnection with the movement for which he stood upon that plat- form and that kindred movement—the brotherhood movement which was marvellously, influencing the workingclasses of our time. For those two there was a mielity work to he done to lay hold upon the mass of the people and penetrate them with the Gospel of Christ. He would say to his brother ministers and to all present that be desired more and more to see the restrictions that many of their churches put to the free entrance of people, broken down. He Loped to live to see the time when the pew rent system would be abolished—(applause) —end when the church doors would be as free for the entrance of the whole mass of the people as tte
house doors or the doors of any ofber public building. The speaker in urglpg the duty of church members to support their ministers remarked that they ought not . . _ _

_ to have to depend upon bazaars and fancy fairs and their attendant evils. The minister should not have to depend upon a certain individual taking a pew,to have to stand right with the man who paid a big sum of money

_ Loan who pelt., . for a big pew, and to be careful lest he trod on his toes or hurt his feelings by what he might say. There was also need in some churches to alto, their method of procedure. They were not going to get the • BRAINY MEN OF THE GREAT TOWNS in Lancashire unless they gave them something worth coming for. They would not come to hear a number of Sunday school girls sing. They would not come for imperfect and untrained' choir singing.

He did' not think for a single moment that they could over-value the services of their choirs, but they must take care not to exaggerate that sort of thing. ' They must see to it that the worship of God was not done for the people by the choir, hut by the people for themselves. They must go back upon the good, strong, old-fashioned hymn tunes. Their prayers must be shOrter. A man ought not to pray more than about four minutes; if he prayed longer it appeared to show that he was making no in public for what he missed in private. (Laughter.) They wanted short prayers, the reading of the Word of God as if God were speekine through it— their ministers needed to learn elocution but how could they learn it unless they paid them a bigger salary ?—(laughter)—sermons straight from the shoulder and dealing with those 'great subjects which were exercising the minds of men. He loved to take a big text even though he could only preach a small sermon—a big text, a far horizon, the expanse of God's own sky—the Old Book was full of themes like that. An hour and a quarter's service .at night, with a man putting his whole soul into it, with strong sing- ing, with a few good voices here and there to say "Amen," and the Gospel had not lost its power. Jesus Christ was still the friend and lover and the beloved of men. The people of this country hal their faults but he did not think they had drifted away from rever- ence or cievotion to Christ. He wanted Christian people to open their churches, to give more facilities for entrance, to let: the services be brainy, strong, vigorouit and intense. Alluding to recent criticisms of Warringten, the speaker said that if ell the salt in that meeting-were scattered through Warrington the place could not be going to putrefaction—unless they kept it in the salt cellars. (Laughter). He was not there to pronounce on the STATE OF MORALS IN WARRINGTON. He only knew that evil was always present and that it was always trying to surmount the good, that the tides of black ink were always washing against the white marble quays. If they wanted to keep up the character of the town he prayed the young men present to prepare themselves for municipal and public life, for he held that such work ought not to get into the hands of the publicans or their nominees. (Applause). He was not going to say unkind words about publicans, because SOMA of them were greatly to be pitied—and men who were put into tied houses. But when men put their nominees upon public bodies not for the public interest but to serve their own trade or private interest, they at once had the cloven hoof. If abed men put up for election the Free Churchmen should put tip good men in npposition.lt was better to lose an election than not to fight and make it difficult for unsuitable candidates to get elected. The longer he lived the more sure he was that while a lot of sin came from the cussed- neve; of the human beart,a great deal of it came from the evnditions under which the people lived, and that if they wanted to make the world radically better, side by side with their preaching of the Gospel they ought to remove the stumbling blocks out of the -fa ay of their weaker brothers and sisters. closely packed together that decency was impossible, that there were drinkshops at every street corner for workingmen to pass, that immoral women were allowed to frequent public thoroughfares, none gainsaying them, that there were in penny-in-the-slot machines horrid and dirty pictures which were demoralizing young life ; supposing there was anything acted on the boards—he thanked God it was not as it used to be--of the theatre or music hall that was de inciralizing to the youth Of Warrington, he said that in all such cazes they as Free Churchmen and as Christians were bound to stand up and Ray "This thing shall come to an end." (Applause.) The speaker appealed to young people to study the Bible; it was those who had not read it who did not believe it. They might ask "Are there not some things in the books of Judges and Joshua that you would not read to children ?" Yes of course* but how did they come there? The book was telling the story of the way in which God had dealt with humanity. Were they going to find fault because it held up the looking-glass before the heart of man rind reflected it ? They would never have known what the Gospel had done for men unless, those books had been put in the Bible ; they would never have realised the difference between our civilisa- tion and that. Those things happened when men were living in the twilight ; they had never heard of Christ or the Sermon on the Mount, and they could not be judged as we who were living in the noon-tide. Mr. Meyer proceeded to commend the splendid work which the Free Church Council had done in the direc- tion of unity and he emphasised the fact that one denomination would not flourish because another wag going down. They all did better when everybody else was doing better. He was dead in earnest about this question. He believed ministers were breaking their hearts, and chapels were empty and the dry rot was there because of the cursed jealously with which a inan said" That. man who has come to that pulpit is going to hurt me," and began to depreciate him in his heart They could not depreciate another man tenfold without depreciating their own souls 100-fold. Oh that to-d5l we might dig a big grave and consign to q jealousy and bigotry and the constant chafing "'- one denomination against another, and might there* never be a resurrection. (Applause.) They would aggrandise their own individual church when they lived for the welfare of all the churches. Dealing with modern church methods, i fr. Meyer said that if Church could only hold its people by theatricals an" raise its funds by BRIDGE AND WHIST DRIVES, if it could not keep its Sunday school teachers except by " Kiss in the ring," the sooner it shut up shop the better. (Applause.) To allow that kind of thing oft church premises was clean against the .purity of the Church of Christ. They could not work with Christ and keep in with the world. The Cross of Christ stood between them, as His risen members, and the things that the world cared for. He hoped—and he said it lovingly—that Mr. Clarke's mission would bring such a new influence upon this town that they might lose the taste for those things aud that the young people might say " Give us something solid. Give us the Bible, the circle, and Christian work." Mr. Meyer concluded by urging his hearers to give themselves to God. He spoke to them as a man, as a citizen, as a" Englishman who loved his country. (Applause.) Mr. GEORGE CLARKE delivered a short address. He said he did not believe that Warrington was all bad but when he looked at fhe large number of public-houses which men and women had to pass, and thought there were perhaps many heavr hearts and a great deal of sin in the town, he believed that if he could get all the ministers and clergy of the' town,all the churchwardens, elders,deacons and Christian Church members to come together, to stop criticising each other, and to unite in the great task that lar before them, they might sweep Warrington for Goa. He did not know much about politics; he was sick to death of them. Once be was a politician, and he learnt that the party that was in did its best to stick in, titnl that the party that was out did its best to get (Laughter.) He had come to Warrington for one thing only, end that was that he wanted Jesus Christ to reig" in the heart.; of the people, and the name of Christ to be uplifted in the town. (Applause). A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the Rev. r. B. Meyer, on the proposition of the Rev.J. S. Huoult'?* seconded by the Rev. E. B. KEELING.

Stuntz has arrived, and will turn out w:th tho "A" team to-day at Wilderspool against Cadishead. The Australian tbreequarter reached Warrington on Mon- day evening at 623 hiving come through from Plymouth with Messrs. T. Davies and T. Barnes, the deputation from the Warrington Club. TheAn gentle- men met the "Suevic " when she came in late on Sunday evening, and soon found their man, who was delighted to meet his n9iv friends in a strange country—for England is strange to Stnntz. On the journey up he marvelled at the small fields, the green- ness of the country, and the apace. Like most Colonials he had got the idea that England was a very crowded place and that people were jostling each other allover the surface of the island. It was a dis- tinct pleasure to him to find that there is plenty of room to play football and other sports as well.

At Warrington (Bank Quay) a crowd of something like 800 poople had assembled to greet the new arrival, and he -had the heartiest of Lancashire welcomes on emerging from the station. The people aeon recognised the biouzed face of the Colonial t.nd cheered heartily. He is a smart well-set-up young fellow, ab lit sft. lOinches tall, and weighing llstones Gibs. His age is 23, though like most of the men from sunny Australia he looks older..

div.head: JOHN STUNTZ
div.p: JOHN STUNTZ

It is not easy to get Stuntz to talk of his exploits "down under," but we all knom that he has won fame as a sprinter with few supericrs. His best time is 12secs. for 120yds.—a fine performance and a bit better than what we recogni,e as even time here. He has won a large number of handicaps at this distance. On the football field, too, he has earned renown not only as a runner but as a clever player. In inter- national matches he has done well, and this last season in Sydney scored three tries in one match before a crowd of 50,000 people. He speaks highly of the N.U.game and says it is mailing great progress in Australia.

Stantz commenced his football in 1904 with the Womerah Club, in whose blazer he appears in the above photograph. After two years with this club, he joined the Eastern Suburbs Club, Sydney, where he benefited much by the coaching and skill of Messenger. In 1907 he represented New South Wales against Queensland, and subsequently played in nearly all dm international matches as wing three- quarter. The reason he did not join the touring party, last season was that he was training for a big handicap at the time.

I hope the Warrington crowd will not expect miracles from the new man—at least not for a match or two until he has got his football legs. Six weeks or so on board steamer is not the best training, and Stuntz will not be able to do even time yet awhile. In fact we cannot expect him to touch such figures at all on the football field. But I fancy he will soon prove himself the speediest footballer in the Northern Union. Here's luck to him! Warrington fairly staggered the League leaders, Runcorn, on Monday, and a defeat of 27 points to nil took all the chirp out of the Linnets. How they come to have attained such an exalted position is a mystery, for they gave no indications of being a class side at Wilderspool, and the heavy defeats on the Oldham and Warrington grounds require a lot of explaining away. I don't imagine for a moment that Runcorn played up to form on Monday, but they should certainly have been capable of better things. Lack of physique seemed their greatest weakness, and in the scrummages the dark green forwards were swept away like chaff by the burly and speedy War- rington six. The backs had the fault of lying too close up, with the result that they were often caught out of position when the Warrington men combined effectively, Scarcely any of them played up to their reputations, and on the day's play only Butterworth, 'who worked really hard, and Richardson who was safe and plucky, were worth their places in a first class side.
Warrington gave their most Lrceful display of the season, and rather curiously it was in the nature of an anniversary. On the 23rd of November last rear Warrington in a Monday match defeated Old-.

To-day's match at Wakefield recalls recollections o the very unpleasant game there last season. On ap wound as hard as E,t/ine the Trinity players indulged in some very rough tackling, and the best of Warring- ton's backs were knocked out early on, or the home team would not have won by a try to nil. This season also they have gained an unenviable reputation for roughness, and have had several men sent off the field. Warrington are in for a hard game, but with proper refereeing they should win.

The same team exactly that did so well against Runcorn, has been selected for the match to-day. I am glad the committee have stuck to Frawley, who is coming on fast and should be a valuable threequarter ere long. The side is : Tilley, full back; Fish, Dickenson, Taylor and Frawley, three quarters; Jenkins and Brooks, bait- backs; Boardman, Shugars, O'Neill, Thomas, Belton and O'Malley, forwards.

be should go so many times round the. track; that he should skip, and take his baths regu- larly? Every football club should have a coach besides a trainer—a man who can teach foot- ball. If this is not done soon I do not see how we are to expect players to take the places of those whose career is drawing to a close. A Nursery for Young Players.

If I were asked I should say -that the veterans almost without exception can still make the majority of the youngsters blush. Let me men- tion only one of the old school—Grenville Mor- ris, of Notts Forest. I should not care to say how long this Welshman has been playing big football—if I did so I should perhaps convey the idea that he was impossibly old—yet one reads every week that he has few suipenors. Morris, in many ways, is quite by himself. He has not yielded to the craze of "pass-the-ball"; he plays, as he has always done, the game of the individualist, always colouring his football, Whether he be successful or not, he stands out above his fellows. He says that the gams would be all the better—it would assuredly not be-the wooden thing it is to-day—if more attention were paid to dribbling. One calls Association football "the dribbling code," but how many men know how to dribble? Precious few. It is enough for most forwards to run, to pass, and to shoot. They fight shy of beating the half- back by sheer cleverness of footwork. This idea of a creche for the development of young 'players is no fanciful idea; I put it forward as a sound business proposition. Kent rear more of. their own cricketers than any other county simply because they have a well-organised nur- sery, a school in. which cricket is taught and by means of which cricketers are made. Money is not Everything.
Woolwich Arsenal introduced a young man named Buckenham, who first came into prominence as an Arany player. He did sufficiently well to
Woolwich Arsenal have a Soldier Centre Forward.

convince those wh+3 saw him play against Bristol City that there was much football in him. But will the most be made of his latent talent? Want of encouragement, or, rather, lack of teaching of the little-known football, is the whole secret of preee.nt-day mediocrity. It is true that we have still some teams who play with wonderful cleverness, and do not suffer when compared with the best sides we ever had; but we have no guarantee that when the cleverest of our footballers Pass out of the game there will be men worthy 01 tilting their places. It seems to be assumed that -a big. purse will buy the best team; money, I know, counts for much when one sets out to build a team, but it i 1 not everything.

Widnes were the visitors to St. Helens on Saturday, the match being witnessed by 8,000 spectatirs. Aspey s•arted for Wiines, who early on got dangerous, Turtill saving a cc' tam try from a mistake by Helsby. Widnes again forged ahead, and from a clearance Jones got bold and dropped a goal. St. Helens asssorted themselves, and Flanagan was ordered back after crossing. After quick end-to-end play, Jimmy Greenwood crossed from a round of passing. Daintith followed with one for Widnes Jones failing from an easy position. Then followed the try of the day. "Matt' Creevey stole away, and later gave to his brother Charley. who scored a grand try at the corner. Barton improved. Lambert, the Widnes centre three-quarter, bad several ribs staved in and had 'to retire. St. Helens held Widnes well in hand at this part of the game, and from combination between Flanagan and J. Greenwood, the latter scored, and Turtill improved. After a spell of pressure at the home end, St. Helens again sot aggressive, Flanagan cross-kicking to J. Greenwood, who again scored, the place-kick failing. Half-time score :--St. Helens 2 goals 4 tries (16 points), Widnes 1 try (5 points). Widnes livened .up, and after Lally and Inca failed to cross, George Aspey eluded Turtill and planted the leather under the posts. Aspey failed from an easy position. The remaining play was all in the "Saints' "favour, who penned Widnes in close quarters. Near the close Charley Creevey crossed twice, and Briers added to the St. Helens score, Tort ill and Creevey again contributing with good goals from diffi- cult positions.
