div.head: Warrington Overwhelm Runcorn.
div.p: Warrington Overwhelm Runcorn.

Runcorn held the distinctive position of League Leaders when they came to Warrington on Monday to fulfil a postponed fixture, but at the end of the game they had been rudely deposed. Warrington were in good form and trounced the Linnets by the big score of 27 points to nil. Runcorn were somewhit weakened by the absence of Padbury, their best forward, but otherwise the side was representative, while the homesters could be considered at full strength. The Runcorn match is always an attractive fixture t.t War- rington, and the spectators rolled up in goodly numbers, fully 5,000 contributing to a gate of .£96. Fine dry weather prevailed, and some capital football was witnessed. It was a sowewbat reezarkaide thing that none of the officials appointed for the match turned up. Mr. C. Platt, of Swinton, was persuaded to take the referee's whistle, and the touch jedges were Mr. F. Turner, Warrington, and Mr. Cawley, Runcorn. Teams :

Warrington: Tilley, hack ; Fish, Dickenson, Taylor and Frawley, three-quarter hacks ; Brooks and Jenkins, half backs; Neill, Shugars, Belton, Boardman and Thomas, forwards. Runcorn : Richardson, back; Hughes, Butterworth, Moran,. and Unsworth, three-quarter backs; White and Watton, half backs ; Walker, Kennedy, Langley, Smith, Peacock and Williams, forwards. Warrington started the game and were soon on the aggressive, but smart passing by White, Watton, Butter- worth and Hughes drove them back. Play settled at centre where the home vanguard -made light of the Runcorn scrummagers and rushed them off the ball. Runcorn were driven back and some fine work by the home back division took play to near the line. Here Brooks got hold and throw to Dickenson, who doubled_ in and made a dash for the posts, Richardson grassing him by the legs only a foot from the line. Watton temporarily relieved, but Fish ran down on the left and the Runcorn defence was again troubled. There was some hot forward work and the ball coming loose, Shugars picked up and literally forced himself over the line with the Runcorn full back clinging desperately to him. It was a fine effort, and the cheering was great when Fish improved with a smart goal. Runcorn were by no means daunted at this reverse and clever work by Moran and Butterworth in turn was checked by Brooks and Dickenson, but the Cestrians showed rare tenacity and clean passing gave them a footing well inside the Warrington quarters. Here Hughes was just a shade lacking in speed to complete a good passing movement, whilst a clever series of exchanges between White and Watton were badly supported at a most critical time. Walker showed his side a great example when he made a fine dash for the line; his pass went astray and Butterworth knocked on with a clear course. By easy stages Warrington drove the opposition out and when O'Malley led the way with a rush the Runcorn defence showed signs of giving way; Riclittrdson, however, stood his ground manfully though Jenkins tackled Watton near the line. A shot at goal by Thomas missed the mark and then O'Malley was unluckly in not scoring, after he had beaten the Runcorn centres. Then came a brilliant piece of combination between Fish and Brooks, and the three-quarter was in full sail for the line when he was whistled back for a forward transfer, and Runcorn escaped. Watton and Kennedy changed the venue and momentarily Runcorn had the better of the duel. The effort was not sus- tained, despite some clever work by Walker and Langley, and after the Warrington forwards had raced clear, with Shugars, Belton, and Neill in co-operation, Richardson saved splendidly. From the scrimmage which followed Jenkins worked adroitly round a pack and kicking high and wide of Richardson; the ball went over the line and Richardson failing to gather, Dicken- son raced up and scored. Moran tried a shot at goal without success, and near half-time Warrington swept down in a body on the Runcorn citadel, but this time the defence held out, and at the interval Warrington led by two goals two tries (ten points) to Runcorn nil. Runcorn resumed without Unsworth, who was badly shaken in a collision with Tilley which sent him over the touch line. Warrington completely overplayed the opposition once the ball was in motion again, and a smart bit of work by Frawley took play to the me. Brooks received from the scrum and dashed over with the third try, Fish missing an easy goal. Runcorn could hardly clear their line for more than a few minutes, and after a fine run by Dickenson, Fish received the ball near tho corner and easily beat the tackler, Thomas failing at goal. Langley, Walker and Kennedy made a burst for Runcorn and crossed the centre line, but Taylor picked up and by a fine dodgy run cleared all but the-full back. When challenged he threw wide to O'Neill who scored cleverly at the corner. Warring- ton monopolised the play and nothing but generous penalty awards in favour of Runcorn gave them any relief. At half way Fish got the ball and completely baffled the opposition by a brilliant run down touch which he finished up behind the posts, and also kicked a goal. Before the end Warrington again got near the line, and Brooks scored the seventh try with a typical dash from the scrummage. Shugars had a fruitless shot at goal, and the game ended with the score: Warrington 3 goals, 7 tries (27 points) ; Rnncorn nil.

div.head: FOOTBALL GOSSIP.
div.p: FOOTBALL GOSSIP.
BY B. BENNISON.
ILLUSTRATED BY JACK DODWORTTI.

It is such an unusual circumstance to find Notts County winning by as many as three goals to one at St. James's Park—and I am bound to say that I have long regarded the County as nothing more than a serviceable side —that one wonders whether it is not a fact that Newcastle's greatness has been seriously im- paired.- The League champions went off with a bang; there wore times in September when they left absolutely no room to doubt their greatness, but it has been plain in recent snatches that there are obvious weaknesses in the side. I shall always be.lieve that Andy Aitken Was allowed to leave Newcastle long before his best football days wore over; and since David Gardner,. one of the most unlucky players when International honours were being distributed, had the cruel misfortune to break his leg, the United have been uncertain at half-back, and the teams that are given to wobbling in the intermediate divi- sion must expects trouble. Weak Half-Backs. Without exception, moderate half-back play is the secret of inconsistency, if not really downright bad play. .Take Chelsea as an 'r•L
Notts County Defeated Newcast'

example. Hero is Bon Warren, as fit at over he was for practical purposes, corn- panionless, and in trying to patch up weak- nesses is not like the great man we know him to be when he is fighting for his country. Warren is wasted, because he cannot help, fret- ting and fuming. One could give a strikingly big illustration of the want of success that comes from moderate half-back play. You will have noted that Everton are falling from their high estate. They are clearly not so good as they we twelve months ago. I have a shrewd sus- pition that the practical disappearance of old Jock Taylor is telling heavily against Everton. Taylor held the side together as only a great centre-half can do. It did not matter in the least that he was old; when John Bell, who also learnt his early football lessons with Dumbar- ton when the "Sons of the Rock" had a name to conjure with, dropped out, Taylor, I think, was left as the oldest footballer in the _English League. It may be that Everton will hit upon a worthy successor to the veteran Scot; until they do, one is afraid that one of the top posi- tions is not for them. Perhaps it is saying little too much to write down the rather disap- pointing performances as being wholly due to the absence of Taylor, for the leaving out of John Sharp suggests that the forwards have gone wrong. I have not seen much of Coleman this season, but I can hardly believe that he deserves to be dropped. After all, Ido not think Everton can improve rpon Sharp and Coleman.

Inexperienced Footballers. Going back to Chelsea, you can swell under- stand 1.114 t the mighty crowds that turn up cheer- fully week after week at Stamford Bridge are wondering whether the sort of football they see is worth their most liberal patronage. Frankly, Chelsea are the most disappointing team we have. People are shouting aloud for recruits, and there can be no doubt that new men are badly wanted; but where are the players to come from? Few of the new men I have seen this season meet the requirements of the First League, which, 4o uphold tradition, must produce the highest and the most exacting pro- fessional football. And the reason, to my think- ing, is this: they have not been allowed to re- main as probationers long enough; they are not developed as they should be. I seriously doubt whether sufficient importance is attached to the training of the youngster who signs on for a, big club. Rather is he allowed to go his own way. We hear a. great deal about "special training." div.head: CERTIFICATED CLASS TEACHERS.
div.p: CERTIFICATED CLASS TEACHERS.
The Religious Difficulty.

The Warrington Certificated Class Teachers' Associa- tion held its annual meeting in the Wycliffe Memorial Buildings on Friday evening, Mr. E. Yates presiding. Mr. G. NEWBURN, secretary, read his report which stated that the past year had been a successful one so far as class teachers were concerned. The membership was steadily increasing, the total number being 187. Mr. YATES introduced the incoming president for the ensuing year, Mr. SAM PRICE, who said that up to the present they had had little to complain of in local educational affairs, but there are signs of trouble in the fixture, and it would be well for teachers to keep strongly united. (Applause.) Referring to the religious question Mr. Price said there were those who preferred secular training or some colourless moral instruction for their 'children, and they were placed in a position of privilege— schools being built for them-at the public cost. Those people however, who regarded definite religious instruction as a fundamental part of education were called upon to provide at their own expense sites and buildings in order that their children might receive the education which as a matter of conscience they required for them. The upholders of definite religious teaching were penalized on account of their con- scientious belief, and until the privileged position accorded to secularists by the educational legislation begun tn 1870, was swept away, there could be no permanent settlement of this question. The voluntary schools bad struggled for years and attained results beyond all expectations, but they were not competing on equal terms with schools backed by the public purse. But such advantages should be the heritage of all children, and it was unjust that anyone should be debarred on account of conscientious beliefs. An equit- able solution might be found not in ignoring but in recognizing in the full the religious differences of the country. (Applause.) In areas where only one school could be maintained teachers should be appointed in proportion to the children. A hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Price was accorded, on the proposition of Mr. A. RICHARDSON, seconded by Mr. A. MALCOLM. The following appointments were made :—President, Mr. S. Price; vice-president, Mr. A. Knowles; secre- tary, Mr. G. Newburn ; treasurer, Mr. T. Edden ; committee, Messrs. Longshaw, Wilcockson, Glover, Turner, Armstrong and the Misses. Bolton, Ewart and Jewkes.

div.head: CHESHIRE M.P's EXPERIMENT.
div.p: CHESHIRE M.P's EXPERIMENT.
TURNING WASTE LAND INTO PROFITABLE AGRICULTTRAL HOLDINGS.

Mr. James Tomkinson, M.P., who is touring the Crewe Division, states that the report in a Tory news- paper that be had had a difference with the Govern- ment on the land taxation proposals is absolutely inaccurate. The Budget, he says, hits him very hard, but believing it to be a fair, just and equitable scheme, he is enthusiastically in favour of it, as it puts taxation on the tacks of those best able to bear it. He has coal and stone under some of his properties, and he holds that the Chancellor of the Exchequer's proposals are reasonable and equitable. With regard to land taxation, the Budget proposals will not increase the burdens on agricultural land at all. In the discussion in the House of Commons on the increase of land values, he drew Mr. Lloyd George's attention to cases where agricultural land had been greatly improved by the thrift and industry of the tenants. He knew land which had been so neglected that it was almost valueless and nearly waste; but in the bands of careful, persevering tenants it had increased in value for agricultural purposes by from 50 to 100 per cent, In an interview with the Chancellor of the Uxchequer he cited some of these cases, and Mr. Lloyd Ceorge said he did not intend t 9 place any additional tax on purely agricultural land unless it became necessary to be utilised for building purposes. Mr. Tomkinson refers to an experiment he, in conjunction with Sir John Brunner, made in Surrey. Sir John Brunner and him- self and others acquired 360 acres of land which was little better than waste at .£l2 an acre for the purpose of the creation of small holdings. They had 4300 applicants for those small holdings. That land was now covered with thirty or forty little homes, managed by industrious, thriving holders, many having gardens, orchards, with hives of bees and other sources of income. That was an example of how a waste might be turned into a fertile area if only the people hsd access to the land.

div.head: "FATHER" OD THE STAFFORD COUNCIL
div.p: "FATHER" OD THE STAFFORD COUNCIL

Mr. Alderman Great Re; J.P:, solicitor, • Stafford, "father" of the Town Council, has just died at the age of seventy-five. Mr. Great Rex had been twice mayor of the borongh, and a member of the corpora- tion for over forty years. He was actively associated with the volunteer movement in 1863, and held a com- mission in the local corps. He was vice-chairman of the Stafford Board of Guardians, and in many other ways was identified with public work.

div.head: FROM WARRINGTON TO WIEN AND BACK.
div.p: FROM WARRINGTON TO WIEN AND BACK.
ARTICLE VI.

We were up betimes on Friday and spent another absolutely golden day in visiting the sights of Munich. First we drove to one of the great public baths provided for the city through the generosity of a certain citizen named Mueller, who had given, I understood, a sum of one and a half million marks for this and other purposes. I have described the noble church-like building, with its tower and • avenue; its sprays, descending from the roof in rainbow beauty; its simple, but effective, mode of teaching people how to swim; its sumptuous range of Turkish and of other special baths in my Report to the Town Council, as well as the beautiful Open Air Bath to which we subsequently drove through leafy roads, and by the side of murmuring cascades, and shining reaches of that bright green water, born in Alpine glaciers far away. The ldtter is 300 metres long, and is continually replenished by the river Isar, and overshadowed by majestic chestnut trees. Immediately beyond it is a sandy open-air Gymnasium, and a Ladies' Bath has also, been pro- vided somewhat further on. On leavingOthese, we visited a great Mixed School, with 1,600 children, and, eFcorted by a bonnie, brown-eyed lass who spoke French charmingly, w ith one or two familiar friends,l wandered slowly through its spacious rooms, and saw its happy " babies, ' seated mund small tables practically in the open air ; its rosy girls, engr,ged in learning such domestic arts as cookery and sewing ; its sturdy boys,some busy at the bench and lathe. Then, driving back, we saw a line of childien happily pro- ceeding to the neighbouring church, and, riding by tho dazzling booths which filled the Mf adow just below the Glory Hall," we paid another visit to the Exhibition, and, whilst my comrades gazed
WITH SOME IMPRESSIONS BY THE WAY. (SPECIALLY WRITTEN FOR "-THE EXAMINER" BY ALDERMAN BENNETT).
the citizens of Munich seem to take it as a matter of course.

.Returning, we walked roune the open colonnade of the impressive " Glory Hall," adorned with busts of many of Bavaria's greatest men, and afterwards climbed up into the hollow vast interior of the giant statue of Bavatia, which, with fine imagination and consummate skill, has been erected right in front of this Valhalla, and .looks out with a majestic calm across the long flat Meadow, with its glittering booths, to ail the splendours of the noble city just beyond. So huge the statue is that by a spiral stair we ascended to the very top, and stood erect within the figure's mighty head. Our handsome black, bare-headed friend, the Rev. Stephen Walsh, handsome, left us in the afternoon, and had to journey 'night and day ;n order to get back to "Bennie Dundee"- in time ta preach upon the Sunday morning; and Alderman Thompson, Mr. Shawcross, Professor Adshead, Miss Gurney and others were leaving us the following (14y, including a vivacious little lady called Miss Scatcherd, who was intimately acquainted with Mr. W. T. Stead and keenly interested in "Julia." Two or three of the party had been invited to cline with Profes3or Valendas at his ccuntry mansion. The rest of us dined together at the Hotel, and afterwards we made a presentation of two travelling bags to our good secretary, " guide, phil- osopher, and friend," Mr. Fleury R. Aldridge. It was accompanied by the warmest pos.ible expressions of our gratitude and regard. And seldom was a little gift se well deserved. Every member of the party was continually indebted to Mr. Aldridge at' every stage of the journey, and perhap3 the brightest memory, in all the _Tour is that of the unfailing

div.head: TOWN HALL AND MARKET PLACE, MUNICH.
div.p: TOWN HALL AND MARKET PLACE, MUNICH.

once more at the absorbing plans and models in the Town Enlargement Hall, I had just time to glance inside the huge pavilion dedicated to the staple trade of the 1 cabty, the bt ewing of good German beer. And then we webt to the palatial New Rat haus, and again expel ienced the delights of civic hospitality in the datk and church-like civic restaurant. And here a satisfying glass of lager beer led up to all the usual lavish list of local and of other wines which had been generously provided for our entertainment. The Oberburgomaster (Dr. W. von Borscht) was a sturdy fellow with a business-like black beard, and was accompanied by his daughter. As usual, other local notables were of the company, and very pleasant folks they were. In the course of the inter-dinner speeches (formn Get many, as I have said before, I think, they sandwich the main toasts in between the courses), our Chairman, Mclennan Thompson, felicitously alluded to the fact that, at his lovely private dwellinghouse our hest had " turned a wilderness into a garden," adding very aptly that this was what we were all seeking to do. Judging from the portraits of the place which we were privileged to see as we sat the table, Mr. Thompson's words did not exaggerate the actual facts. It was evident that Dr. von Borscht's home and its surround- ings were a special source of pride t) him, and I shall never forget the light of gratified appreciation which came into his face and lit the soft eyes of his comely daughter as this pretty compliment was paid. His speech, like all the speeches we had heard, WEIS notable for its warm sympathy with all the objects which we had at heart. He generously pointed out that, in the Housing Problem, they (the German people) were "both givers and takers ; ' that England and Germany could assist each other in promoting its solution; and, after intimating his regret that it was not possible for us to see his home in the beautiful valley of the Isar for ourselves, informed us that it had been consttucted to his own designs after 30,000, building plans had passed through his official hands. And then another notable housing reformer arose to propose another toast. It was, I think, our good friend Professor Berlepsch Valendas. And a happier toast could not have been suggested. It was "England and Genkany against the slums," and we drank it with a strane light in our faces and a new throb at our hearts. And somehow, then, and many a time upon my journey, a voice rang, like a bell, within my brain : "Were half the power that fills the world with terror, Were half the wealth bestowed on camps and courts, Given to redeem the human mind from error, There were no need of arsenals nor forts." But the good time is not yet, alas! and Oberburgo- masters, Aldermen and Councillors may drink each other's health in every wine upon God's lovely earth and fraternize like veritable brothers, and within the breasts of the great toiling multitudes goodwill may hold unquestioned sway, but kings and kaisers and ambitious statesmen may at any moment bring their aspirations to a bloody end, and lock two friendly nations in most deadly fued. And, therefore, we must be prepared, as Captain Crosfield and Lord Roberts say. But the hideous pity of it all! "It must be," said one of our companions of the afternoon, with a sad shrug of the shoulders; "but I for myself can be without an army. I like peace." How many of us have said that in our time, and yet how help- less we still seem to stem the tide of national misunderstandings, selfish quarrels, and insensate struggles for the things which really do- -not matter. "England and Germany against the slums !" Yes, let us fight for that; and then, perhaps, We shall not want to fight for any baser cause. • There was not any stated programme for the after- noon, and so I drove out with my good friends, Councillor Walker, of Walsall, and Councillor Wortley, of Don caster, to visit the great Municipal Sale Yards and Slaughter Houses, cur German com- rade of the morning very kindly joining us. These Slaughter Houses were a sight worth all the journey, and I wish the Health Committee of my native town could see them tco. Afterwards we visited the " Cemetery in the Woods," which Professor Valendas had especially commended to our attention, and it was, in some respects, more interesting still. I have described both places in my Report, and I will only „a_dd that, if I cordially approve of Munich's method of disposing of its sheep and oxen, I am not prepared, as yet, to acquiesce in Munich'k,method of disposing of its dead. For they are taken to the Cemetery and exposed to the, gaping public in great glass Morgue-like cases, and, passing through the central ball, where the religious rites are said, and entering the apartment just beyond it, we came suddenly upon six poor dead faces (are they really poor, I wonder?) lying peacefully behind the glass and almost covered up with flowers—a little child, three women, one with a face of alabaster calm, and two worn out and weary, yet majestic men. For Death has always something in his mien of majesty. Another portion of the building was reserved for cataleptic or other doubtful cases, and, if the seeming corpse should rise from that strange sleep i which s sometimes mistaken for:" Sleep's brother Death," by means of an electrical arrangement just above the prostrate form, a swift alarm was given to the attendants, and those deemed dead might go forth to the wondering world again. The whole arrange- ment seemed to me to be distinctly gruesome, but on sanitary grounds it may be plausibly defended, and
courtesy, the tireless tact, the constint fore Eight, and the quite illimitable patience and good humour of the man who organized it to the smdlest detail,aud never seemed to make a single mistake.

The party who were— leaving numbered, perhaps a dozen, and the remainder were to still t at 7.15 'upon the following morning for Passau, and thence to sail down the Danube ta. Linz. But the Kaiser was to visit Munich the sirne day, and I naturally desired to see him in the midst of his own people. Mid so I talked the matter over with Mr. Aldridge, and, with ready courtesy, he looked out all the trains for me, and I found that, by leaving Munich at a quarter past one, I could intercept the party at Linz the same evening; and so, • iir spite of some good-natured efforts to dissuade me, I promptly fixed the matter up. In the meantime, some of my -Mends had gone out, under the guidance of a German comrade of the afternoon, to visit another interesting Munich institu- tion, the famous Lowenhrau-Keller, with its terraced gardens and gigantic concert room. I followed with two other friends a little later, hoping to join them there. But I paused upon the way to gaze up through a great street telescope at Saturn, with his mystic rings, a planet which had shone upon us nightly with surpassing radiance ever since we started on our journey. Very beautiful the great world lookel with its bright starry girdle, floating there vo calmly in the depths of the space, a world to which our own poor planet seems diminutive ; but, as I gazed at it through that gigantic telescope, I felt as though I wished to steal it and attach it as a gleaming pendant to my watch chain. My comrades evidently did not share nay astronomical yearnings, and had left me to it in disgust. I hailed a passing tram and rode on to the Lowenbrau and found the ."Keller," but I did not find my friends. Moreover, both the concert room and the big terraced gardens were, for some mysterious reason, shrouded in darkness, and the great main entrance closed. In vain I sought to find an explanation, and returned, intending to once more enjoy the glories of the flofbi auhaus, not dcubt- ing that I should discover my lost comrades there. But I could not find it, and for once I wished that I had learnt the German language. . Not that I like it. It is almost as guttural as the Welsh, and I can understand the story of Mrs. Langtry, in her recent book, about the lady who had married a German, and, after a month of misery, applied for'a separation order, on the plea that her husband was always swearing at her. . At last, however, after perhaps a dozen futile enquiries, I met a pleasant fellow who spoke English fluently, and he was go Azl enough to guide me to the place I. wanted. But I hid done my boon companicns an injustice. They might have been there—no doubt had ; but I could not find them now. And so my new-found friend and I enjoyed a quiet smoke together, and, as we talked, he told me of an interesting institution which he called "the Simpli- cissimus." It was,l understood, an Artists' All Night Cafe similar to some of those which are described so cleverly in" Bohemian Life in Paris," and my curiosity was instantly aroused. It was already very late, and I was very tired, and so I hired a cab, and we rolled on swiftly through the dark and silent streets together, talking freely of Munich,and of Germany; of England and of many things besides. I had previously dis- covered that the friend on whom I had so strangely lighted out of all the thousands in this busy city was no other than the "lift man" at the Bayeriseher Hof, but we had not chanced to meet befoie,and only made each others acquaintance at midnight accidentally in the great Maximilian Strasse. Anyhow, he was a singularly pleasant and intelligent cempanion. At last we reached the Cafe. There were other vehicles about the door, and, as we went inside, we came across a picturesque apartment, dimly lit with shaded lamps and partly filled with visitors. But all the walla were covered with amazing pictures, beautiful, fanciful, weird, grotesque, poetic—piciures of every soit and kind, and all of them the work of one or other of the patrons of the place. Some of the artists who had frequented the Cafe had, my comrade told me, won a European fame, and I could well believe him. In a narrower room, almost every inch of which was oocUpied, we managed with some difficulty to obtain a seat among as strange and picturesque a company as I have ever met. Long haired artists, long haired poets, some with a smile of far-off meaning in their eyes, some jolly and rotund and obviously very human, crowded round the tables with their lady fi lends some artists, and some models probably—and sipped the red wine of the country, or its tawny beer, or heartily,

partook of the good fare paovided, and talked and laughed and joked amid a halo of tobacco smoke and an abounding atmosphere of camaraderie and boon companionship, whilst ever and anon some member of the strange Bohemian—or shall I say Bavarian—com- pany would rise from his place amid the crowd, proceed to the middle of the room, and either beauti- fully improvise on the piano, or declaim some original poem, or sing, with quite contagious spirit, some , delightful song. A very pleasant and intelligent Swiss lady, who spoke English perfectly, happened to be sitting by my side. She had, I gathered, come, like me, to see "the Simplicissimus " from curiosity, but she discoursed on that and other things with much intelligence and zest. I gazed upon the spectacle with unabated interest for above an hour, and my complaisant comrade seemed disp sed to stop until my interest was exhausted, That might have been at breakfast-time perhaps, but I suddenly remembered that the Kaiser was to arrive at his Bavarian capital at eight o'cleck—they live " the strenuous Mfe in Germany—and that it was already close on three ; and, reflecting that, if German artists and poets could sit up all night with impunity, weary English travellers were scarcely equal to the task, I grudgingly prepared to go. But, ere we left, some kind habitue—possibly the author—distributed a printed sheet with the p rtrait of the lady of the house upon the top, and a poem in her honour under- neath it ; and then one of the singers of the place stood up and sang a verse with admirable skill and much t ivacity, and all the rest joined in the chorus ; and, long before they reached the end cf the poem, I caught the knack of it, and, though I did not under- s'aud a word, I found myself and my companion—the genial " lift-man "—chiming in as though we had been artists and 13obeinians all our lives, And then we tore ourselves away, and walked back through the silent streets, and by the plashing fountains, and the shadowy trees, and underneath the shadow of the strarrge old buildings, through a sleeping city, which, however, was already hovering on the verge of day— the Kaiser's day !, I snatched three hours repose or so, deferred my breakfast, and soon after half past seven, I found myself close by a noble fountain, almost like a waterfall, the name of which I do not recollect. There was a singular absence of excitement yet ; no barriers, practically no decorations, and scarcely any people; but almost as sooa as I had taken up my place, I observed a sudden influx of the loyal Alunchenites, and presently they lined up in two rows al( ng each side of the broad street down which I gazed uninterruptedly from my pisition by the fountain. Then Caws at the window opp)site began to thicken. And then tall German officers, in bright blue uniforms, began to canter by; and one or two of my companions of the previous day rode past in carriage, all obviously going to receive the Kaiser at the Station. Presently I saw the popular Prince Regent pas an elder!y and somewhat undis irguisled-looking fellow with a short white beard, and, I rhink, a short moustache. his was the man who had so long controlled the destinies of Bavaria in the place of the "Mad King," Louis, who lived, our comrade of the previous afternoon informed us, at a castle somewhere out beyond " the Cemetery in the Woo .8." A few more soldiers, passed, and suddenly I caught a distant shout of "loch ! hoch ! hoch "! it sounded more,like "Ho ! Ho ! Ho !" -

and then perhaps half-a-dozen cartiages rolled slowly by, and in the first of these, so far as I can recollect, here sat the great war lord of Europe, side by side with the grey-haired old Regent, driving quietly, with little outward pomp or show, and with no outward signs of wild excitement, to the Palace, erehe starter' on his arduous duties for the day. There was just a running stream of "Ho! Ho! Flo's ! " ; a strong, tall, lordly figure, with a striking light monstache, receiving these continuous salutations with conscions dignity and royal calm, and then the vision passed, the crowds dissolved, and I followed the retreating carriages to the Palace. I strolled about is precincts for awhile, and then walked back to the Hotel and breakfasted, to learn I orn Mr. Shari cross that one of our companions, a most agreeable young architect from Croydon, bad been taken ill, the previous day and was threatened with appendicitis, and that he was not able either to go to Paris, as he had intended, or to accompany the members of our party who had left that. day for home; that Mr. Aldridge and some twenty others who were _going on to Wien had left for Passau by the 7.15 train, as arranged; that Professor Adshead, Mr. Shawcross himself and some other members of the party, thanks to the kindness of Professor Berler sch Valendas, bad been honoured with invitations to see the Kaiser at the &alums, were shortly going thither in full evening dress, and were not starting back for London till the afternoon. I gathered that due earn, was being taken of our friend, and then, less lucky than the favoured three, set off towards the Marien-Platz,(a sort of Albert Square immediately in front of the Town Hall) to try to get another glimpse of the most-talked7of King in Europe. I had seen him riding through the streets of London on the day of Queen Victoria's Funeral, and been much impressed by his appearance, and, in spite of his idiosyncrasies, I must confess that I have always had a sett of sneaking admiration for him. For the Kaiser is every inch a King, and, much as I have often disagreed with him, and much as tie has often irritated me and all my countrymen, and all his own, on many an unforgettable occasion, I honestly believe him to be entirely high-minded and patriotic. Moreover, be is greatly gifted, and the very power he sways endows him with a sort of curious fascination.

gut the crowdS-I%;e-rii-veri-de.;e---NVltiiin the Marien- Platz, and I had not a little difficulty. in working my way up a side street, and round the end of the great square, to the thronged pavement opposite the central door, and gazing at the outlines of the lovely building, pret ily bedecked with long ,green wreaths,as were the buildings opposite, and at the favoured company who filled its windows, not to mention all the other windows round the square; at those tall, broad, impressive warriors of the German army who were ranged around the footpaths, and at the German banner floating high above the heads of that great Munich crowd. I stood just by a fine old German soldier, who wore upon his gallant breast four decorations, one of which was not unlike our own Victoria Cross. Upon his bars I read the words " Weissenburg," " Worth," "Sedan " and " Paris," and I found that the old veteran had taken part in those great battles which when he was in the prime of youth, had humbled poor Franco to the dust, and laid the broad foundations of United Germany. I think it was upon one of his medals that I read the words "Gott mit uns, 1870," and I gathered that he had received the Cross, of which lie seemed partioularly proud, from the old Emperor himself. I tried to talk with him and shook him by the hand—l always like to take the hand of a hero —and chatted afterwards with an American lady and her son, who was studying at Karlsruhe ; and then, dissatisfied with my position, slowly worked my way towards the other end of the square, and stood amid still denser crowds just by the entrance to the quaint old Rathaus. And, almost as soon as I had reached this spot, I saw a moving line of carriages approaching through a quaint and narrow lane just opposite, and heard once more these cries of "loch! Hoch !Hoch!" which heralded the coming of the Emperor. I stood on tiptoe as they passed, but did not see much owing to the equal eagerness of all the swaying crowd. And then the glittering company dismounted and were lost within the ancient building. Here some skilled choir was greeting the great monarch with a song of welcome, for the sound of it came musically through the open windows and across the square. And then there was another lull ; another sudden stir ; another sudden outliurst of that "Hoch! Hoch ! Hoch !" and then I saw the Kaiser, once again, bare- headed in the midst of a a weet group of maidens clad in white, and wearing garlands, and with such escort Wilhelm slowly moved between the eyes of the adjoining multitude across the illaricn-Platz and by the Virgin's Column, and, to music's martial sound, walked slowly through the central door of the Town Hall, to be received with pomp befitting the occasion by the Oberburgomaster and the leading citizens of Munich.

But rime was getting short. My train was nearly due. And I desired to peep, before I left, inside the Frazten-Kirvlie, a great two-towered brick building which was close at band, and served as the Cathedral. I had but time to saunter slowly through it, arid then I hailed a cab and asked the driver to take me, as quickly as he could, to the Picture Gallery which the Kaiser was, I understood, presenting to the citizens of Munich later, in the day.. On every side we saw the people rapidly dispersing, -many of them bearing banners which had doubtless graced the great Reception in tbo Rathaus.
"Wave, Munich, all thy banners wave, And charge with all thy chivalry !"

How those old rhymes keep buzzing in my brain ! But Munich, after all, appeared to take the Kaiser's visit philosophically, and, apparently, was anxious to get back to work again. The decorations, save in the immediate precincts of the Mathaus, were astonish- ingly meagre ; and the city, as dwhole, was much less moved, at any rate, by outward loyalty than cities of

the same importance on this side the Channel when we hail the coming of the King. I heard, on two or three occasions, that the Emperor is not so popular in Southern Germany as he is in Prussia, and this may, perhaps, to acme extent, explain the fact. And, after all, there is a good deal to be said for English freedom !

My cabby managed t) conduct me to the Picture Gallery expeditiously. It stood in a side street just by the Isar. Baedeker spells it Isar, Campbell Iser. Which is right I cannot say. But the approaches were all guarded, and I could only peep at the big building and the green and rolling river once again, and then drive back to the Hotel. There were a hundred things in Munich which I had not seen, and I was loth to leave it., for a lovelier city I have seldom visited; bpt Wien lay cu before, Wiest and the mighty Danube ; an 1, if I did not catch the train •at 1.15, it was just possible that I might miss them both. I nearly booked for Lindati instead for Linz, and took a third class ticket in order to see what third class travelling in Germany is like. Ido not think the carriages ate as good asour owa,but the fares were very much cheaper, and that is something to the credit of the German system. Just ere we started, I observed two statues towering high above the platform of the great and busy station. I seemed to know their names instinctively. For one was Watt, the other Stephenson. And, sore at heart t ) find how much the Germans beat us ia s) many things ; distressed that brother Jonathan, and not John Bull, had found the Pole ; ashamed to feel that France had been the first among the rt alms of earth to navigate the air, I was relieved exceedingly to find these handsome statues in a German station. "At any rate," I said, "t was my native laud that made a servant of the filmy steam, and built the earliest lqcomotive ! " And, laying this proud unction to my soul, I left for Linz. I wieh that I could dwell upon the journey, but lack of space forbids. ,We changed at llosenbeim, from whence a line runs out to Innsbruck in the beautiful llo,enlicim is a thriving centre of the salt trap, and has a populatio i of 15,400. Be3ond the town, we cress the river Inn, and pr( sently we skirt a lake which bears the name of the Simrosee, and arrive at Prien, and then the great r Chiernsee, a broad, dim m'rror in the shadowy day, up in the right. And nearly al the way we catch vaAtto visions of the far blue hi.ls, and, once or twice, a pitch of whiteness which we take f.r snow ; and, as we pass through Tranntstein, a sweet pleasure place, arid getting nearer to thos) noble heights, reach. Salzburg, dominated by great mountain peaks and lovely build- ings, a new glory comes into landscape, ' and the toaris's at the station, and the peasants in their Tyrolean caps, and all the atmosphere of this delightful place suggest the Alps. I tramp off to the Customs Office's, for we have crossed the Austrian frontier now, and buy a spray of artificial edelweiss, and get int the train again with a dim longing to ascend those tall blue peaks, and reach the region of perpetual snow, or daily by the lovely, river in the lovely town and dream awhile. But it cannot be ; and so I pass the Austrian jotters, with my baggage duly chalked, end after a brief interval, glide out into anolier country. The uniforms are different; I notice instantly a difference in the Lees ; the coinage, too, has changed ; but the German language still prevails, and frontiers, after all, seem somewhat stupid and superfluous.

Long ere I get to Linz, the night descends, and after a six hours journey, I scramble from the train and get into a rattling omnibus, and, through still leafy streets, I ride into the town, and, pass'ng through a spacious square, with the inevitable monument, I see a bridge, and, turning sharply to the left, a great broad stream, and pull up suddenly at tne Flotel Krebs, the mighty Danube rolling swiftly as the Isar, in the darkness just across the way, the yellow lights of Linz reflected on its bosom, and a searchlight flashing from some distant/ building on the hids upon the o her s'de. I find my room, glance round the place, and hasten through the somewhat lonely square,aud peep at the big Ch Irch, and rind the Post Office, and ask if there are any letters, and return in time to greet my friends as they troop rff the river steamer which has brought them dolvn from Passau,and is something like an hoer behind the time. The scenery, they say, was lovely, but the afternoon was wet, and, in their hearts, I think that most of them were rather sorry that they had not stopped with me to see the Kaiser, Once more we meet, a company, around a well-filled table ; my comrade gets a litre of the native wine for something like a shilling and merrily comparing notes an hour slips pleasantly away. And then, at Mr. Aldridge's suggestion, we all ride off upon a crowded tram to see the great Linz Fair, a sort of Austrian , October Fest, a cross between an Earl's' Court Exhibition and a Stratford Mop ; and stroll roll about and listen to the music, interview a lion-headed man and sit out by the brightly-lighted tables till the rain --Zegins to fall. And then land my friend from far Australia bail a cab and drive back through the silent and deserted streets to our Hotel. it is absolutely pouring now,hut I am not content until I have trudged across the ugly iron bridge which spans the river Danube—as long,perhaps,as the great bridge at Westminster—and then, wet through and weary, I ascend some curious stairs, proceed along some rather dirty corridors, and, hanging up my dripping clothes' to dry, and opening my spacious window, gaze out, in the darkness, at the rolling river and the twinkling lights beyond. ( (To be concluded).

Lord Lansdowne at once assumes that the Lords have already made up their minds, and he speaks as the muter of the legions round him. He does not trouble to discuss the right of the Lords to reject the Budget. He calmly takes it for granted. He declares that the right of rejection is "indispensably to us to-day." _ _ _ _ _

He puts the claims of the Lords at their highest and he complains that the House of Commons, by grouping all their taxes in a single Finance Bill, has driven the Lords back upon rejection. He admits that the Lords cannot amend a Money Bill, but he asserts that they have a perfect right to reject it. Then he paints black the picture of the Commons. If they could graft licensing and land valuation on the Budget, what is there to prevent them from grafting on it a Home Rule Bill? Then the apologetic was heard and the organiser of Revolution began to coo and coax in tones of seducive blandish- ment. They did not propose to kill the Budget. They merely wanted to refer it to the people.

THE CONSEQUENCES OF REJECTION. But the consequences of rejection? "We are ready to face them," said Lord Lans- downe. Deadlock? "How long will.it last? You hold the key in your own hands. Why blame us? Is your Budget so perishable that it will not keep for six weeks?" This struck the crowded benches as a good joke. The Peers roared at it. The note of levity fitted their reckless mood.

But whatever happens, the struggle had got to come. Let the Lords who doubt the wisdom of rejection consider whether they will stand worse or stand better if they shirk et their responsibility. "The people will think worse of us and not better if we have not the courage of our opinions." And finally Lord Lansdowne watned the Lords against the danger of failirig those who look to them—a delicately veiled alllusion to the " Trade " which the Pears heard in guilty silence. The end of a speech notable chiefly for the way it skated over thin ice and avoided the main issues was a hypocritical assurance that by rejecting the Budget the Lords would not pronounce a final verdict, and would not refuse the grant of aids and supplies to the Crown.

permanent and overwhelming majority in the House of Lords. No opposition to Tory Governments: nothing but opposition to Liberal Governments. He pinned the peers down to the choice between adherence to tradition and violent unconstitutional revolution.
Published by fhe Free TraJe Union, Lcrndon! TARIFF REFORM MEANS TRUST

admonitions, uttered with all the arts of a Conslammate orator,. would do so. But.it was obvious that he knew he Was speaking to deaf ears. Yet he continued to pile warning: upon warn- ing, telling the peers, that their.rash policy would weaken their power of resistance.

Lord Rosebery's speech sounds the death-knell of the feudal Revolution. It is the death-rattleof the hereditary Chamber. He at least is not defucie)d and deceived. He knows that the-peers are marching to their doom. DEATH OR DAMNATION.

div.head: LORDS' ADVENTURE. LANSDOWNE LEADS THE
div.p: THE LORDS' ADVENTURE. LANSDOWNE LEADS THE
ATTACK.
LOREBURN SCARES THE BACKWOODSMEN.
ROSEBERY DAMPS THE POWDER.
WHAT WILL THEY DO?

The pugnacious peers may after all turn out pusillanimous! They have not yet rejected the Finance Bill, or bludgeoned the Budget, and it is an Open question whether they will do anything so momentous and provoca- tive. Since Lord Lansdowne intro- duced his historic amendment on Mon- day there has been a constant stream Of rhetoric arid small talk in the Upper House, and the more they have demon- strated, the more the opinion has grown that they will not be as big as their words when the crucial trioment arrives. ' It was timed to arrive on Thursday, then Friday was Inentioned, and now we are told it will be Tuesday before the vote is taken. In. the meantime some forty more peers are to have their "go" at the Budget,and it is conceivable they may talk out Their majority. The "backwoods Men" are not convincing as political leaders, and even Lord Rosebery suggested that the House would be stronger by their absence. If they can only summon up sufficient interest to leave the moors, and the deer-forests, and the race-courses again on Tuesday they may bring about the crisis Which other people view with more We than their own leaders. we Progressives want the Lords to throw out the Budget. We want the democracy of the country to ,1?e wantonly flouted, and 'twill 9e a thousand pities if, after screw- iing up their courage so high, our Tlereditary legislators fail to do their hereditary duty. Should the lordly bomb fizzle out like a damp squib then there will still be only one alternative agreeable to the great mass (,)f the people of this country. The Lords may swallow the Budget, but they must be taught a, lesson whether they do so or not. The time has gone 1 y when such an anachronism as a ;louse of Lords veto on progressive !egislation can be tolerated. There must o.e a fresh place found in the Constitu- tion they treat so flippantly for the wearers of coronets and other °rnamental insignia of rank. And in our view that place has long been available for their reception. It only r,equires dusting, and its name is 121-1 E SHELF.

div.head: OPENING THE REVOLUTION.
div.p: OPENING THE REVOLUTION.

The scene was strange in the Gilded 'Fhamber on Monday. There were qundreds of peers assembled to guard their own interests and save their Drecious acres from paying a few Dounds per year to the community which creates the value. Most of them ,Were unfamiliar visitors, many did not Know their way in to the legislative Drecincts, and some few had to under- O the preliminaries attached to taking ", seat in the House for the first time. ut they were mostly of one mind and tntention, and they formed a solid uacking for Lord Lansdowne when that uncomfortable nobleman rose to '°Den the floodgates of revolution. The opening phases of the revolution 4re sensationally dramatic. Lord re\lre rises and moves the second reading of the Finance Bill without vouchsafing a word of explanation. He ts down so abruptly that even the veers are shocked, and a vague tremor 2f astonishment is felt rather than 4leard in the strained and tense atmos- Vlere of expectant emotion. The first ovv has been struck at the usurping I.lobles—a blow all the deadlier because lt is 'struck by the weapon of ironical

As Lord Lansdowne rises he is obvi- %sly ill at ease, and he opens on a tlyerulous note, acidly girding at the !llence of Lord Crewe. Silence, he :a37s, is sometimes more eloquent than :Deech ; and a double meeting lights v`v.ith a grim smile Lord Morley 's keenly 11R1lant countenance. The silence of Crewe has gone home.

div.head: igi
div.p: igi
THE LORD CHANCELLOR'S GRIM REJOINDER.

The Lord 'Chancellor followed with a grim rejoinder from the Government side. He spoke with an iron dignity and pitiless force which manifestly awed the listening Peers. He imposed upon them the spell of his masterful personality. As he developed his great constitutional argument he grew more and more predominant, until he seemed to tower over the rebellious nobles like an embodiment of the very spirit of the Constitution.

He begari by noting the fact that Lord Lansdowne had shirked the real issue, and slurred and blurred the extreme gravity of the unconstitutional steps which he advised the Lords•to take. Unprecedented, subver- sive, impossible—these were the epithets he applied to the Lansdowne motion. Step by step he built up the case against the Lords. He showed that the doctrine of " tacking " assumes the limitation of the powers of the Lor,ds. He turned Lord Lans- downe's defence of tacking inside out, asking if the Government were precluded from altering existing taxes merely because the Lords had rejected the Licensing Bill. With biting lucidity, he expounded the ancient and famous balance of power known to our Constitution,the envy of other nations. This the Lords are invited to destroy. What will follow? The House of Lords will hold the House of Commons and the Government in the hollow of its hand. "No wise man," said the Lord Chancellor, in menacing tones, "would desire that this House should possess such authority as that ; and no man of spirit would submit to it." The defiance rang out, and there was no answering defiance. The Peers took their castigation like school-boys under the birch. ,

After discussing the social needs for which the Budget provides, Lord Loreburn reviewed the destruction of the Education Bill and the Licensing Bill. " The Licensing Bill," said he in icy accents of ironic scorn, "was not alive when it came here. It perished by the stiletto in Berkeley-square. Now the Lords are about to destroy the Finance Bill, and to refuse supplies." A FATEFUL DECLARATION.

Reading 'slowly from a paper which he held in his hand, the Lord Chancellor made the fateful declaration of the debate. "It is impossible that any Liberal Government should ever again bear its heavy burden unless it is secured against the repetition of treatment such as our measures have had to undergo during the past four years. If we fail in the coming election, it will only be the beginning of a contest which can end only in one way. If we succeed I hope we shall not flinch in what will follow. "We have not provoked this contest (here a storm of jeering ' Ohs ' burst forth from the angry , peers). We have not provoked it, nor at any time desired it, but we are not afraid of it, and I hope that none of us will fail to do our duty in preserving the Constitu- tion of our country." There the Lords got the answer of the Government. . It is a final answer.

div.head: I NO COMPROMISE.
div.p: I NO COMPROMISE.
LORD PENTLAND VOUCHES FOR THE GOVERNMENT'S FIRMNESS.

The debate proceeded on Tuesday without many notable features. Lord Cromer's speech was an elaborate weighing of chances. He admitted that the rich man ought to pay more than the poor man, and in spite of his objections to the Budget he declared that he could not vote against it. Why? Because the Lords could not reject it without incurring other risks of an even more formidable character.

Then came the speech of the day from Lord Pentland, the Secretary for Scotland, better known of old as Capt. Sinclair. He opened with a plain declaration that the GOvernment will consider no compromise to relieve the situation created by the Peers. He warned them that things could never be again what they once were. They were destroying the executive control of the Commons. They , were paralysing the executive. They were creating a deadlock from which there was no escape except by revolutionary change. The same plea might be urged ' every session about every Bill until for government by representation had been substituted government by plebiscite. Lord Pentland went on to tell the peers that they did not realise the position of Liberal Governments confronted with a

div.head: LORD BALFOUR'S BLUNT WARNING;
div.p: LORD BALFOUR'S BLUNT WARNING;

Thursday, the Fourth, Day of the Revolution was a black-letter day for the usurpationists. Lord Balfour of Burleigh (a member of a former Tory Government) delivered a speech which produced a far more profound impres- sion even than Lord Rosebery's. Its crushing force was due to its fierce sincerity, its passionate honesty, its, indignant independence, and it made the peers shiver unmistakably in their shoes.
Lord Balfour said" Take it how you like,, if you pass this resolutio.n, if you. make it
cost me
rower 1
rod for thee own bacit when thou voted for Protection. tide Is the shop. the ONLY shoo. You can Wilsey btu

a precedent—l care not with what safe- guards you accompany it, whether you say it is only to be done on extreme occasions or by any other safeguard—you have made a, change in the practice and in the Constitu- tion which will prevent things going on as they have gone on up to the present time. My Lords, if you win, the victory can at most be a temporary one. If you lose you have altered and prejudiced the position, the power, the prestige, the usefulness, of this House."

This is one of the four smashing blows from men of their own rank which has taken all the heart out of the Lords. They are hardly likely to assemble in such numbers and such high spirits on the resumption of the debate next week, as they did for the introduction of Lord Lansdowne's fatal amendment. On Tuesday they learnt that there would be no Bill of Indemnity upon which they had always calculated. They also were warned by Lord Cromer that Foreign Powers would be likely to take advantage of constitutional and financial 'chaos —which is one of the things that present a real terror to the Backwoodsmen. Thirdly came Lord Rosebery's cruel allegation that of this House. which numbers 600 Peers, nOt more than 150 are qualified by age, experience, and position to vote in the forthcoming division. Lasf comes the emphatic declaration by Lord Balfour of Burleigh that under rio circumstances can the House of Lords hope tb win the battle upon which they have entered. All these candid advisers believe in a Second Chamber. None of them enjoy the Budget. By their abilities and careers they completely overshadow in the public mind the 9ther Peers on the Opposition benches, and they have declared against rejection! Well might Lord Balfour tell the revolu- tionists that they were between Death and Damnation!

div.head: AN ELUTION CONSIDERED CERTAIN.
div.p: AN ELUTION CONSIDERED CERTAIN.
THE PTZEIVIIER'S EXPECTED ANNOUNCEMENT.
The following notice was despatched on ThursdaY. morning from the Liberal Whips' office to, the supporters of the Government .

"Owing to the' prolongation of the :debate in the House of Lords on the .Finance Bill, the House of Commons ,will not meet on Monday and Tuesday. Your presence is urgently required on :Thursday, December 2nd." It is expected that Mr. Asquith will ;ann6unce on Thursday that the IGovernment will advise a dissolution of. Parliament at the earliest practic- able moment. This is understood to ' .nre'art that the writs will not be issued :.until the first week irt January, and several Liberal members', in reply to inquiries, have received assurances to that effect.

div.head: PEOPLE MUST BE MASTERS,
div.p: THE PEOPLE MUST BE MASTERS,
MR. SEDDON, M.P., ON THE COMING
STRUGGLE.

Mr. QT. A. Seddon, M.P., for the Newton division, ancldressed a meeting at Ci-ank, near gt. Helens on Saturday night. He said that if they rightly understood the present situa- tion they could only come to one conclusion, and that was this : that we were on the eve of a revolution in this country, a revolution which had been created by a class of people who were non-representative. If the workers had understood their original position they would have been ni‘ asters in their own house long ago.—(Cheers). The cause of the Lords' opposition to the Budget was not quite evident upon the surface. Lord Lansdowne said the other day that they were going to refuse to pass the bill until the people of this country had passed their opinion upon it. This was a right assumed by the Lords that the King himself would not dare to put into operation, because every Budget was only for a year, and when that year had expired then the representative or majority Government could .alter or destroy. How was it that the House of Lords was attempting to do some- thing that had not been attempted for 300 years, for they must remember that when this was last attempted it was attempted by a king, and he lost his head through it. If they were going to permit the House of Lords to have more power than a king, then they were unworthy of their sires, and they not -worthy of representative govern- ment. (Cheers).

div.head: MR. A. J. KING, M.P. GIVES
div.p: MR. A. J. KING, M.P. GIVES
A Warning to Cheshire Squires and Parsons.

Mr. Alfred J. King, M.P. for the Knuts- ford division of Cheshire, met a large number of his friends and constituents on Saturday evening in the Drill Hall, Wilms- low. Mr. Alderman Royle was in the chair.

Mr. King, M.P., who had a cordial recep- tion, said it had been the tradition and experience of this country for hundreds of years for the Prime Minister to dissolve Parliament on one of two grounds only— either because the natural term had ended or that the Government of the day had lost the confidence of the House of Commons.—(Hear, hear.) " Neither of those positions obtains to-day, and it is perfectly certain that if we had a Tory Government in power, no matter how unpopular it might be, and no matter how many by-elections it had lost, there would have been no attack from the Lards. The reason for all this is that' we have a second, a hereditary chamber, which has for the first time in our history taken upon itself to interfere with questions of finance. The Peers are trying in this way to get the power to dictate what Government shall be in power and when an appeal to the country shall be made. Well' if the people take that lying down' it will not be worth while for them to take part in any further general elections.—(Cheers.) If the, Government are forced to go to the country and appeal to you, and you don't send them back with such a majority of public opinion behind them that they can do away for ever with the obstruction of the House of Lords, I say that for the ordinary voter there will be very little interest in any future general election."

div.head: STAY TO REVOLUTION.
div.p: A STAY TO REVOLUTION.

• "There is growing up a feeling of unrest and discontent. We may by wise legislation divert this stream into useful channels, for useful irrigating purposes, and grow there- from a crop of social ameliorations for poor men, women, and children in our country. We may on the other hand, by means of the temporary power of the House of "lords dam up -this stream; but the waters will go on accumulating, and when the flood comes it will carry away other things besides the power of the House of Lords—it will carry away other institutions which we have been accustomed to venerate and reverence. (Cheers.) Therefore I say to those people who are so frightened of Socialism, as I say to Cheshire squires and parsons who tell me we are leading this country to revolution : If you are so frightened of revolution you ought to thank God for the Liberal Government and

div.head: DUKE OF DEVONSHIRE'S WARNING.
div.p: DUKE OF DEVONSHIRE'S WARNING.

A CONTEST WHICH IS UN-EQUAL. The contest between the House of Lords and the House of Commons is not an equal contest. House of C'ommons, strong in its representative capacity, strong in the sup- port of Ole great masses of the people, and strong in the undivided and indisputable control it passesses over the resources of the country, is more than a match for its opponents hi the contest.—The Duke of Devonshire in 1884.

div.head: "EVERY PICTURE TELLS A STORY." Read the Truth AlAut the Loaf.
div.p: "EVERY PICTURE TELLS A STORY." Read the Truth AlAut the Loaf.

There are pictures on the walls to-day- which tell a story,. politeness alone forbids us calling it a "calculated lie: The Tariff Reformer is peculiarly fond of declaring that the price of food has risen' in the United Kingdom under a Free Tracte Government, and suggesting that this is due to Free Trade :and would not have occurred' had the desires ;of the Tariff Reformers been realized. Their particular instance is always the four-pound loaf. What are the facts ?• The Blue-book issued on Saturday by the Board of Trade shows that, whatever riee -there may have been in the price of the- four-pound loaf in the United Kingdom a greater, rise has taken place in the price in protectvd Germany. Here are the figures comparing the price in London and Berlin in 1900 and°l9oB : Price expressed in pence per 41b. 1900 1008 London (wheaten bread) ... s:2di Berlin (rye bread) s.ld, In Berlin the standard Toat'of rye bread— not wheaten—is fifty pfennigat. The consumer always pays the same, but: the weight varies. Thus, in 1900 a loaf weighing 2.02 kilogrammes was sold for frfty.pfennigs. In 1908 the weight had fallen to 1.57 kilo- grammes. In other words,. the • German workman received nearly as quarter less bread for his money. It is not in bread alone, however, that Protected Germany has suffered more than Free Trade England from the rise in prices. Here is a comparison of a number of articles of daily consumption which have risen in. price since 1900. The price in 1900 is shown by the index number 100. As compared with this, the prices in 1908 in London and Berlin were :
London. Berlin. Beef Mutton Pork Bacon . 113 Butter Eggs 107 Potatoes In only one instance where a comparison is given—that of sugar—was the rise in price in Berlin less than in London.

div.head: LORD ROSEBERY'S COLD DOUCHE.
div.p: LORD ROSEBERY'S COLD DOUCHE.
AGAINST THE BUDGET BUT AFRAID OF REVOLUTION.

On Wednesday, Lord koseber stepped into the limelight with charac- teristic opportunism. Nobody knew whether he would join the revolu- tionists or not, so skilfully had he sus- tained his role as the man of mystery. Bur if the noble iconoclasts had counted on his support, they were bitterly disappointed. The Glasgow speech proved to be a broken reed. _ _ _ _ _ _

I mint confess," said he, "that I do apprehend the result of the appeal to the country on an unreformed hereditary Second Chamber mixed up with the promises of the Budget. I doubt if you are choosing the best battlefield on which to risk your attri- butes and perhaps your existence." The peers listened to this prophecy of coming disaster with downcast faces. With cruel irony Lord Rosebery produced a comic parody of a deathbed repentance. Was it really too late to adopt some desper- ate device to give a semblance of decency to the revolution? "Some of us," said this Job's comforter," are very young. I wish we all were." Uneasy laughter applauded this sally. "Some of us have taken no part in public life. Their names will not greatly count in the division." The backwoodsmen manfully strove to stifle their blushes. But there was a remedy for this grotesque element in the revolution. "Let u's select 150 peers and depute to them the right of voting on the Budget. That will impress the country."
