div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 27TH, 1909.

The Lords have become THE LORDS fascinated by their own AND THEIR eloquence. Instead of LEADERS. concluding the debate on Lord LAXSDOWNE'S Tesolution on Thursday, they are to continue the discussion into next week. The conse- quence is that the arrangements of the Government and the House of Commons will be thrown into disorder. But, as Lord CAMPERDOWN said on Tuesday, consequences must be left to take care of themselves. The Peers are reckless about them in small, matters as in great. When the division actually comes about, it will probably be found to have been much influenced by the speech made by Lord ROSEBERY on Wednesday. There will be more absten- tions than had. been counted on. It must have been with some surprise that the House
siis

learned that the Episcopal Bench proposes to abstain from voting for the most part. The .A.RcHmsrioP OF CANTERBURY, who is under- stood to be in favour of the Budget, made the announcement. We cannot congratulate the Bishops and the Archbishops on their loyalty to their convictions. A great opportunity presents itself for doing something to obscure a bad record in cOnnection with progressive legislation, and they are to turn their backs upon it and walk away. This is a pitiable line 'of, conduct, and it is not excused by the ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY'S explanation that the vote will be of a party character. On how many occasions has the Ecclesiastical Bench abstained when the vote was between parties? The principal now adopted is new. We do not think their action means that the ARCHBISHOP and his colleagues have -not the courage to support the Government when the majority in the House of Lords is opposed to such a course. But it is open to that interpretation. The BISHOP OF HEREFORD is a notable exception

to the clerical band in the Upper House.. He stood up and supported the Budget in the sturdiest fashion in the course of Thursday's debate, twitted the Lords temporal about their subservience to the liquor traffic, and warned them that if they rejected the Finance Bill the answer would be: "Never again in this country shall the fundamental liberty of the people be endangered by any privileged. class."

Lord ROSEBERY seems to have addressed an audience almost unprecedented in that assembly. No finer compliment than such an attendance could have been paid to the vivid personality of one whom we may perhaps be allowed to call the most iri- descent of contemporary politicians. There is no man in public life at present who might, if he chose, exercise such a command- ing influence as Lord ROSEBERY. But his speech explained clearly enough why, instead of being at the head of one of the great parties in the State, he is left to plough a lonely furrow. He has developed into a political Ishmaelite. His hand is against every man. He denounces the Budget in terms of great extravagance, but he tells the Peers that if they vote against it it will be at their peril. He cannot be said to blow hot and blow cold. He is always perfervid, and his breath is a Sirocco, which scorches friend and foe. He seems to be going one way, and then takes a sudden turn the other. The Speech was a brilliant and surprising performance, but we regret to be compelled to observe that it was a performance only. Lord ROSEBERY becomes more histrionic with advancing years. The speech concluded with what must be considered to be a very remarkable suggestion. We all know that Lord ROSEBERY would like to weed out the House of Lords. He made proposals on that subject many years ago, and he revealed the fact on Wednesday that he is still disposed to make the weeding very drastic indeed. Why, he asked, should not the Opposition select 150 peers, specially qualified, and depute to them the right of voting on Lord LANSDOWNE'S amendment'? That is to say, why not send the " backs woodsmen " home again? Why not declare their unfitness to decide in so momentous a case? The• thing would no doubt be admirable if it could be done, but it cannot be done. It is the-" backwoodsmen" who have to decide everything. LORD LANSDOWNE i's leading them into a blind alley in the hope of stumbling on some way of compromise in a case where compromise I is impossible. But the " backwoodsmen " are his masters, and what is dorie ultimately will be done by them. Here is LORD ROSE- BERY telling them in effect that they are not qualified legislators, and that they ought to I go home and leave this business to those ' who are! The situation is not without its elements of comedy.

Warrington is not yet SCHOOL FEES. ripe for the entire aboli- tion of school fees and, perhaps fortunately, the Education Com- mittee holds this opinion. The motion to abolish fees in all the elementary schools on January Ist. was fully debated, and rejected by eleven votes to eight at the meeting on. Monday evening. The balance of 'argument was, on the whole, on the side of the motion. Theoretically, school fees should be abolished, but expediency for the time being dictates a more conservative policy. The cost to the rates has to be considered, together with the capital expenditure on new schools, and due weight must be given to the fact that there is already free accommodation equal to the demand. There are other arguments, too, which bear on the question and offer justifica- tion for differentiating between certain schools and certain scholars. But the chief consideration is that there is no public demand for the abolition of fees, and more- over the town cannot afford the luxury of Sacrificing on principle some £2,000 which is very willingly paid by parents who agree that they get value for the money.

The Rev. F. B. Meyer REV. F. B. MEYER'S holds a warm place in VISIT. the hearts of Free churchmen and on Monday evening a crowded and enthusiastic audience accorded him a right royal welcome and listened with rapt attention to the vigorous, timely and bright address in which he handled a surprising range of topics in his own inimitable style. As was to be expected, Mr. Meyer touched with due gravity upon the ill-absorbing constitutional crisis and his unhesitating declaration that if a conflct were forced the will of the people as reflected in the House of Commons must prevail, obviously accorded with the feeling of the great meeting, Mr. Meyer put in a strong plea for purity in civic life and rightly called upon Free Churchmen to combat the menace of "the trade" on public bodies. Discussing some of the hindrances to religious activity he spared neither the pulpit nor the pew in his frank criticism, but all was spoken in' such a kindly and warm-hearted way that resentment was impossible. Mr. Meyer's visit should have the effect of stimulating the local churches to still greater efforts and of still further strengthening the bond of union between the various denominations which comprise the Free Church Council.

It has long seemed to THE GUARDIANS us a curious circum- AND stance that notwith- TEMPERANCE. standing the - close association they have with so many victims of drink, the Warring- ton Guardian's in the aggregate always view temperance questions and proposals with a levity which falls a limo-ei way short of seem- liness. Quite recently they scoffed at and refused the offer of lectures on the evils of alcohol to the children under their care at Padgate Schools. These young paupers, many of whom doubtless have hereditary tendencies fo indulgence in strong drink, are denied the common know- ledge of the effects of alcohol on the human body through the short-sightedness, ignor- ance, and prejudice of a majority of the Guardians—fill-named, one would think! Judging by the tone of the discussion in the Board meeting on that occasion, many of the members would have been more inclined to grant their young charges a glass of beer for dinner than an opportunity of learning all about the evil and temptation of strong drink with which they are certain, every one of them, to be assailed as they go through life. •Such a ftame of mind in a public administrative body is almost incredible in these days of

enlightenment, so called. But it is nothing exceptional for the Warrington Guardians. They take joy in supplying free beer for the Christmas feasting at the Workhouse every year, notwithstanding the protests of individual members who have , some appreciatidn of temperance and who see unwisdom in tempting the depraved palates of men and women who owe their downfall in life to dissipation. Only oh Wednesday last, the usual protest was made but it was treated as a joke, and by such a man too as Mr. A. J. Jolley,whom we should like to acquit of ignorance.lf intoxi- cating drink is tabooed anywhere it should be forbidden in Workhouses, but there will have to be a different method of electing Guardians, or Government prohibition, before such an obviously necessary reform can be achieved
NOTES AND NOTIONS.

A large circle of Warrington people— not, llpunded merely by the limits of the Einmtanuel Church congregation—will regret the departure from the town of the Rev. Frank Vaughan. He brought a breezy, vigorous personality into the ministerial ranks of Warrington, and is one of those who will be difficult ta replace. Good wishes follow him to the distant sphere of North London. * * *

While the balance of reason—as against theory—seems to be on the side of continuing the existing system of charging school fees in non-provided schools, it is a circumstance not without significance that the managers of such schools are almost to a man in favOur of retaining the fees. •Free education may be a popular cry, but school fees are a solid reality, and have their influence on the scales when the balance of argument is being decided.

Three individuals who seem to have made a good thing out of empty houses were com- mitted for lengthy .terms of imprisonment at the Borough Court on Tuesday. Their stock-in-trade seems to have been purloined lead pipes and even an occasional copper hot- water cylinder. One depredator had earned among -his fellows the significant title of "The Empty House King." Property owners should feel grateful to the police for having captured this ingenious gang. Their mode of earning a living was altogether too easy and ittractive to last in these days of com- petition. * * _ _ _

The House of Lords have done the deed. Like Macbeth; they have hesitated over it long, but now at last it is done, and the English' people enter into a period of changed relationship towards their aristocracy. * * *

For the Lords have now raised a question which will have to be settled in one way or another, and which cannot be left in its present position. It is not possible in a State, any more than in a household, for more than one authority to manage the purse. It is common ground in all human affairs that the purse cannot be in two hands at once, and that the hand.that holds the purse is the hand that also rules. . * * *

We do not propose to argue this matter over again on constitutional grounds. There the Liberal Party had achieved a complete victory. But put aside all constitutional authorities and look at the matter from the simplest point of view. What would happen if the House of Lords won in this fight ? *

The whole position of politics would be changed. For the last fifty years no vote of the, House of Lords has ever upset a British Ministry. But henceforward no British Gov'ettiment could rule for More than a year without possessing a majority in the House of Lords. 13 ut that would be only the firpt result. The second result would be that no Budget could be passed which was not pleasing to the House of Lords. No Government, indeed, would ever bring a Budget in unless they were certain that the House of Lords would pass it. The House f Lords Would practically dictate the Budget .

But. all that is of small importance com- pared with the greater matters. The real point to keep your eyes on is what would be the social and political results? But, in the first place, it would mean that all the vested interests represented in the Lords would be practically free from new taxation from that time forward. What are those vested interests? * * *

Well, the most important is land. The Derby Return, published in 1875, showed that 525 Peers held 15,300,000 acres of culti- vatedj land in the United Kingdom. This was exclusive of their possessions in forests and wbods, in roads and rivers, or in London. But it showed that those 525 Peers then held one-third of the cultivated land of the Unitecl Kingdom. * * *

But if we add 5,0-00,000 acres for their other possessions—forests and woods, roads and rivers, and the London area—then the landed possessions of those 525 Peers come up to 20,000,000 acres. And the average of each Peer's landed estate works out at 38,000 acres.

You have only to Consider those facts, and to realise that no new tax will be placed on land if once the Lords get control of our finances. All these unearned increments will still go rolling into their pockets, and local authorities will still have to pay the high prices which they pay at present for their land. Nothing will be changed. *

Take one fact. We have been told on good authority by one who knows them, that the Dukes of Great Britaix are "poor but honest." The phrase throws a new light on what bne means by honest poverty. For the Derby Return shows that the Dukes possessed in 1875 no less than 4,000,000 acres, with a rent roll of £2,350,000. That is the sort of ,honest poverty which a good many people would be willing to share. Reckoning the increase in these estates since 1875, it works out at something not much less than .ElOO,OOO a year each; though it must be remembered that, while several of these Dukes are very rich, others of them scarcely get their fair share. * * *

The only other class- that is lariely repre- sented in the House of Lords is the clase of the brewers. They have succeeded during the last fifty years in obtaining several big Peerages, thus forging an interesting link between the Beerage and the Peerage. We may be sure then, that, while the landlords would keep the people strenuously off the land, they would console them for thrusting them into the slums by encouraging them to drink the greatest possible amount of liquor. There would certainly be no more taxes on drink. The people of Great Britain, in the eyes of these great landlords, are to become a landless but intoxicated people,consoled for being driven off the earth by perpetual immersions in alcohol. That is a pretty vision of revived feudalism.

RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
LIBERAL CANDIDATE FOR WIDNES.

A meeting of the Executive Council of the Widnes Division Liberal Association was bold on Tuesday, when the selection of a candidate to oppose Colonel Hall Walker, M.P.' was the chief business. For the past twelve months Mr. Max 111uspratt has been looked upon as the Liberal candidate, but he has now accepted the invitation of the Liberals of the Exchange division, Liverpool. Several names were put forward, amongst them being that of Mr. W. C. G. Gladstone, and a sub- • committee was appointed to make the selection. Mr. John Williamson, Liberal agent in the Widnes division, has accepted a similar position in the Wands- worth division of London. . BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the above Board was bald at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Mr. T. Baxter presided and there were also present :—Messrs, J. Spruce, T. Wright, P. Booth, C. E. Lina.ker jun,. H. Talbot, NV. M. Morris, P. Collins, J. Hallows, J. Mynekyrne A. Greenway, S. Taylor, A. Norman, J. W. Davies, G. Piling, T. Antwiss, A. Broome, G. E. Warburton, J. L. Jones, C. Bretherton, E. Britch, with G. F. Ashton (clerk), W. E. Hough, (deputy clerk), C.F. Parsons (master) T. Cooke, W.R. De Prez, J.Pearson (relieving officers).

div.head: DEATH OF MR. F. HORTON.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. F. HORTON.

The Chairman said that before proceeding with the business of the Board it was his painful duty to report that since their last meeting they had lost one of the members of that Board—Mr. Samuel Horton. He had known him since he was a child and had always been a Personal frieni of his. He had not attended a great many meetings of the Board as it was rather awkward to get from Manley, for which district Mr. Horton was a member. When he did come he was always a useful man and everybody who knew him, thought he was a most genial and good-hearted friend—(bear, bear), They all felt with his wife and young family the loss they had sustained, by Mr. Horton being taken away while in the prime of life, ashe was only 50 years of age. He was sure the Board would join with him in asking the Clerk to write a letter of condolence to his wife and family. Mr. Wright !Aid that as chairman of the Rural Dis- trict Council he had great pleasure, and also great sorrow, in endorsing Mr. Baxter's remarks. It was very sad that a man who was in the best of health should be taken away so very suddenly. Mr. Horton was always an attentive member and the Board were always pleised to see him present. He was a useful man in everything be bad to do. They felt heartily sorry that he had been out off so suddenly. . . •
Mr. Davies Mac: associated himself with the vote of condolence and said that Mr. Horton was always wel- comed with a smile. (Hear, hear). The vote was passed in silence, all the members standing.

div.head: NUMBER OF INMATES.
div.p: NUMBER OF INMATES.

• Mr. .1. Spruce reported that the number of inmates in be House was 179 as compared with 174 the cones- onding period of last year. Seventy-four vagrants ad been relieved, as compared with 70 relieved in the ame time last year.

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.
Whist Drive at the Liberal Club.

There was a very en joyable social function at the Liberal Club on Thursday evening, when a whist dtive was promoted by the Women's Liberal Associa- tion. About one hundred ladies and gentlemen attended, and competed at whist for six prizes from 7.30 until nearly midnight, with the usual interval for refreshments. The prize-whiners were : Gentle- men : 1, Mr. W. Bibby; 2, Mr. W. Furness: hidden, Mr. J. Fargher ; booby, Mr. J. Eastwood. Ladies: 1, Mrs. P. Garnett; 2, Mrs. Reid ; hidden, Mrs. Turner; booby, Mrs. Joseph Howes, junr.—The arrangetnents for the whist drive were in the hands of Mesdames. Osborne, T.Locker, Pemberton and Lindley, and there was a general feeling of gratitude to these ladies for the exce'lent way in which they had per- formed the duties allotted to them. The proceedings were well managed and enjoyable from beginning to end. Fcstival at St. Clement's.

The Dedication Festival in connection with .St. Clement's Mission was held on Tuesday last. Holy Communion was celebrated at 7.30 and the preacher at the evening service was the Rev. A. S. Cameron, M.A. vicar of Atherton and at ope time curate-in- charge of the Mission who took his text from St. Matthew xviii. 20. and delivered an able sermon on the necessity of faith both in Christian life and in everyday life. The choir rendered the anthem "I will magnify Thy name 0 God my King," the solo part being taken by Miss Gladys Ross. Mr. Eugene Dell presided at' the organ. Collections were in aid of Mission expenses. After the service refreshments were providgd in the schoolroom and a musical even- ing was giv& by the members of the choir. A short address was given by Mr. Cameron and a pleasant evening was brought to a close by the singing of "Auld Lang Syne " and the National Anthem. The refreshments had been prepared by the lady members of the congregation. "In the Crow's Nest." This was the title of an entertaining and instructive lecture given in Cairo-street achoolroom on Monday evening, by the Rev. E. W. Lummis, M.A., formerly pastor of Cairo-street Chapel. On leaving Warring- ton, Mr. Lummis, acting on medical advice, went to the South of England, and afterwards to Switzerland where he held the pastorates of three village churches In introducing Mr. Lummis, the Rev. C. Harvey-Cook said they gave him a hearty welcome to Warrington again—(applause)—and were glad he was restored in health and strength and able to return to .his work.— Mr. Lummis said he started on his tour to Switzerland in August 1905,sailing from Folkstone and journeying through France and Germany. He excellently described all the towns and places he passed, especially in Switzerland, and had crisp little anecdotes of each. The lecture was illustrated with magnificent lantern slides, the original photographs of which Mr. Lummis took himself. Scenes of all the most popular sanatoria at the foot of the mighty Alps were shown; also of the sanatorium where Mr. Lummis himself stayed, accompanied by his wife. During his stay in Switzerland, he occupied the post of pastor in three small hamlets. He seems to have had a snug retreat right- in the heart of the mountains which are of the Matterhorn type, and covered with perpetual snow. While pastor at the small villages he took photographs of his " flock " and when the slides were thrown on the screen the lecturer created much amusement by reciting the names of the whole of the people which seemed very gutteral in the ears of those present. Before oonducting the services Mr. Lummis had to learn the German and Swiss languages. Almost every Swiss of the average inte/ligence was able to speak French and German as well as their own language, which is a mixture of both. Mr. Lurnmis returned after five years absence via Geneva and Ostend. On the motion of Mr. J. Rymer Young seconded by Mr. W. H. Woodcoek and supported by Mr. C. Madeley, the lecturer was thanked for his lecture, also Mr. F. W. Monks for the manipulation of the lantern. TABLE AND HANGING LAMPS, new now designs showing.—J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge at., Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: Election Expenses.
div.p: Election Expenses.

The following returns of expenses incurred la recent municipal contests have been received at the Town Clerk's office :—Town Hall Ward, Councillor Jenkins, £2O 35., Mr. J. Lord, £4 4s. 3d.; .Latchford, Councillor Wilson, £26 9s. 4d ; Whitecross, Councillor Bellian; X2l 10s. lid.; Orford, Mr. J. A. Rushworth. £2O 17s. Bd.; Howley, Councillor Sankey, £4 17s. 6d.; St. John's, Councillor Steel, £3B Gs. 6d.

• Church Society Lectures. The Warrington Church Society i has successfully begun its winter session, the opening lecture being 'delivered by the Rev. E. R. Tarbuck, vicar of St. George's, Altrincham, and formerly of St. Paul's, Warrington, who took for his subject "Why I am a Churchman." Next Friday evening the Rector (Rev. Canon Willis) will deliver a lecture in the Conservative Club Assembly Room on ." The history of the War- rington Parish Church." He has made use of all available information in his power and obtained some very beautiful photographs of the various objects of interest. The Boy Scouts.

We wo-uld call the attention of our readers to the advertisement in another column of an interesting display to be given in Crosfield's Dining Hall on Thursday evening next, with the object of bringing the boy scout movement more prominently before the public. There will be a practical illustration of camp life—" early morning to night "—various drills, and the short sketch "Sons of the Empire." Corporal B. J. Francklin, Ist Syston Troop, Leicester, holder of the silver wolf, awarded for proficiency in all depart- ments of boy scout work, will take part. Crosfield's orchestra will play selections

Ragged School. Mr. H. G. Brandwood (organising secretary of the Ragged School) asks us to allow him space for an appeal to the public generosity in aid of the scheme for the purchase of an adjoining building as a Labour Home. Some £3OO are still required, and the Ragged School may be considered to have done well in two years to raise the bulk of the capital sum. , A Labour Home would greatly increase the public usefulness of of the Institution, and fill a want which is often felt by members of the "submerged tenth" in Warring- ton. The Treasurer of the Finance Committee is Mr. James Dodds, to whom friends are requested to send their subscript ions.

Oddfellows' Social. The Admiral Nelson Lodge of the Independent Order of Oddfellows (Manchester Unity), held their annual social on Thursday night. ,The fact that Cairo-street Schoolroom was crowded points to the success that the social committee achieved. The artistes were Miss Silcock, Master and Miss Runcorn, Messrs. Walter Dennett, W. Webster, J. Willett. and the Harmonic Glee Party, who sang with their usual good taste. The humorous portion of the programme was in the capable habds of Mr. W. Sutton, who kept the audi- ence in roars of laughter. After refreshments had been served and games indulged in by the children, a dance was held.

• £5OO Orchid. At the meeting of the Royal Horticultural Society at the Horticultural Hall, St. Vincent-square, London, on Tuesday, Alderman Bolton, of Wilderspool, exhibited a wonderful orchid of the genius Cypripedum, and was awarded a first-class certificate. The plant is absolutely unique, and is a hybrid grown by Alderman Bolton in his orchid houses at Wilderspool. It has taken some years to produce, and is the product of two distinct varieties. The plant was much admired in London, and has caused a sensation amongst orchid lovers, who value it at F-500. Alder- man Bolton and his manager (Mr. NV. H. Cain) are to be complimented on their great success.

Photographic Society. The annual meeting of the Warrington Photographic Society was held at the Old Academy on Wednesday night. The Treasureri statement was considered satisfactory, there being a small balance in hand. The following officers were elected :—Hon. secretary,. Mr. H. Holloway. 57, Bewsey-street ; hon. treasurer, Mr. C. Wilcockson, 20, Fair- field-road;' lapternist and assistant, Messrs. Owen and Lloyd, Curator Mr. A. C. Smithson. The announcement of the arrangements for lectures and demonstrations for the winter session indicated that the members could look forward to a ;.profitable enjoyment of the pursuit of their hobby. An enjoyable social on Thursday took,the form of a "brown supper and potting night." The idea was evidently a new one to the members, and was entered into with zest. The earlier part was spent in games. W. Spittle' won a prize for a "Spelling Bee" on the word Snowdrop, and Mrs. W. J. Walker another for a Musical Competition. Everything at the supper was brown. Mrs. Dodds gave4he Snowdrop Talk on " Simple Goodness." Another 'item of the evening was the potting of the bulbs, with appropriate thoughts and sayings about a beautiful life. A good number was planted, and a goodly show is expected at the White Supper in February, when small prizes will be •given for the best pot of snowdrops grown as a result of Thursday's "potting." Warrington Lady's Daparture for Buenos Aires.

On Thursday the 18th inst., Miss Norah Tunstall, eldest daughter of Mrs. Thomas Tunstall, The Lindens, Grappenhall left Liverpool by the P. and 0. steamship Orrissa, en route for Buenos Aires, where she is to bemarried to Mr. Charles Gorse, second son of Mr_ William Gorse, Sankey Bridges. Mr. Gorse has been abroad for about six years, engaged in stock-breeding and cattle-brokering, and became engaged to Miss Tunstall before he left England. The wedding is expected to take place a few days before Christmas. Miss Tunstall was accompanied to the landing-stage by a large number of relatives and friends who all joined in heartily wishing her a pleasant voyage, and much happiness in her future home. " HERALD " KITCHE'S RANGES save 50 per _cent

of fuel.—Agent J. S. GARLAND, Ironmonier, 51 to 55 Bridge st., Warrington.—Advt. Mr. T. J. Garnett, Mr. T. J. Garnett, who recently resigned the position of senior relieving officer of the Warrington Union, after twenty-nine years conscientious service, was the recipient of a token of appreciation at the- meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians on Wednesday. The present, which had been subscribed for by members and officials of the Board, took the form of a gold watch, bearing the following inscription:—" Presented to Mr. Thomas J. Garnett by the Guardians and officers of the Warrington Union as a mark of their esteem and" regard on the occasion of his retirement from the position of relieving officer after 29 years' faithful services. October 2nd, 1999."—Mr. W. Houghton, as the senior Guardian, congratulated Mr. Garnett on that happy close of long and efficient official career, which had been marked by ability, tact and dis- crimination.—Numerous members and officers of the Board having added their tribute of praise, and a letter from Mr. J. C. Sutton bearing testimony to Mr. Garnett's sympathetic treatment of the poor having been read, the Chairman made the presentation.— Mr. Garnett. who was received with applause, feelingly acknowledged the gift.

div.head: EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
div.p: EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
The monthly meeting of the Education Committee was held on Monday evening in the Council Chamber.
REV. JOHN YONGE RESIGNS.

The DIRECTOR mid a letter from the Rev. John Yonge stating that it was with very great reluctance that he sent in his resignation of his membership of the committee. He found it had become a greater tax upon his strength than he could stand any longer. He thanked the members of the committee and the officials for their courtesy to him daring the time he had been a member of the authority. The Rev JAMES DAVIES expressed his deep regret at the resignation of Mr. Yonge. The CHAIRMAN said on behalf of the committee generally he would like to say how much they regretted the necessity for Mr. Yonge to resign. He had taken a very great interest in education and they as a com- mittee would certainly feel his loss. He hoped he would long be spared to enjoy his retirement. Canon STEVENSON on behalf of the School Management Committee said they would miss Mr. Yonge's ser vices, very much. Ht had been most regular in attendance he had taken a great interest in the work, and his courtesy and general manner endeared himself to theta all. He deeply regretted his resignation.

div.head: MRS. CANN RE-INSTATED.
div.p: MRS. CANN RE-INSTATED.

The Rev. J. DAVIES moved (a) " That, for the pr ere appointment of a superintendent of cookery instruc ti o the regulations which apply to married women teachers adopted by the Education Committee at a meeting on March 15th, 1909, be suspended." (b) "That Mrs. Langdon Isabel Cann be appointed superintendent of cookery instruction, at a s dary at the rate of £l2O per annum; her engagement to commencelon December 1 The resolution was carried/by 16 votes to 4. THEFT FROM SHOP FRONT.

At the Borough Police Court on Saturday Richard Jebb, of Battersby-lane was charged with stealing a roll of flannelette from the shop of James George Blakely of Winwick-road.—The Chief Constable said that about half-past six the previous night prisoner was seen by Inspector Smith crossing the railway metals at Lythgoes-lane bridge. He caught him up and found be had the property, the subject of the charge, in his possession. He said I am caught fairly, could you let me go." Smith brought him to ttre Police Station. The cloth was afterwards identified to be Mr. Blakely's. Prisoner was fined 20s. and costs or 14 days' imprisonment. Inspector Smith as thanked for his services.
THEFT FROM SIDING. MAN'S FOOLISH ACT.

At the Borough Police Court on Saturday, Richard Coulson, of 7 Chapel lane, Stockton Heath, was charged with !gelling three bottles of pale ale value is. 6d. from a siding of the L & /sl.-W Rail Any at Wilderspool the previous night. The Chief Constable stated that the Company had for some time past been missing goods from the siding. On Friday night, Detective Hewitt of the company's police kept observation and at five o'clock visited the van and found everything intact. As be was going away he saw prisoner leaving the van. He questioned him and be admitted having taken one bottle of ale. Afterwards three bottles were found in his possession. He was a man of previous good character and bad worked for the compeny for over 15 years. Having regard to those circumstances be suggested that prisoner be leniently dealt with. Mr. Longland who appeared for prisoner said his employers had no previous complaints of any description against him. He occupied the position of a checker of the goods which were con- signed at the Wilderspool Siding of the Railway Company. Last week instructiona were given to him ,1 to examine the inside of the vans. On Friday night 1 he did so and unfortunately be took the three b ittles of beer. There was no necessity for him to do that and he could give no explanation. He was a married man and bad a wife and six children, two being very young. He (Mr. Longland) knew that the Railway companies suffered from petty thefts of that descrip- tion but ho hoped the Bench would deal lediently with him. The Chairman (Mr. J. W. Hayward) said that taking prisoner's previons good character into consider- ation they were going to deal leniently with him and he would be bound over for 12 months in the sum of 10s. to come up for judgmedt if called upon.

div.head: AN ELECTRICIAN'S EMBEZZLEMENT.
div.p: AN ELECTRICIAN'S EMBEZZLEMENT.

At the Borough Police Court, on Thursday, Ernest Watkins, who was arrested in Leek, Staffordshire, was charged with embezzling the sum of 125., the money of Harry Rogers, on September 6th.—Mr. Rogers stated that prisoner was engaged by him in August last and worked until Septemi.er 11th. On that day he received his wages. He did not turn up on the following Monday, and on making inquiries witness ascertained that prisoner,bad been selling his lamps at different places in town. Witness went to Miss Smith's shop in Horse- market-street, and found that prisoner had sold three lamps for 125., receipted a bill in his (Mr. Rogers) name and kept the money.—Prisoner said he took the money because he wanted it for his apartments. —The Chief Constable said prisoner had a good character. He had written to his mother with a view to obtaining a couple of sovereigns in order to pay the fine if it could be met in that way. It was a case where be thought the man was deserving of some considers- tinn.—Prisoner was lined 20s. and costs or a month's imprisonment.

div.head: "EMPTY HOUSE RING." EXTENSIVE ROBBERIES.
div.p: "EMPTY HOUSE RING." EXTENSIVE ROBBERIES.

The Borough Police Court on Thursday presented the appearance of a marine dealers's shop, large quantities of horse hair, sacks and brass and lead piping, being strewn on the solicitor's benches. The magistrates. with Mr. John Fairclough presiding, were occupied for two hours, listening to the evidence on charges of stealing or receiving against John Burke, Barbauld-street,, Edward Bolton and James Bolton, father and son, 38, Hardy-street.—John Burke and Edward Bolton were charged with stealing from a yard in Barbauld-street during October and November, 701b5.• of horse hair value 355.. the property of Messrs. G. and J. Weaver. Edward Bolton and James Bolton were charged with receiving the same, knowing it to have been stolen. Burke pleaded guilty, and both the Boltons, (who were represented by Mr T. S. Steel), not guilty.—The Chief Constable said that Mr. G. Weaver left the premises secure, on the 13th November. In the yard there were 1501bs. of horse hair tied up in a sack. On returning to the premises he discovered that the sack bad been open and 25Ibs. stolen. The police were informed and inquiries made and it was discovered that Edward Bolton had disposed of some hair to Mr.Matthews,marine store dealer's,Lythgoes-lane. It transpired that other quantities of hair had been Isold,to Mr. Matthews by Burke and Edward Bolton. It was identified by Mr. Weaver as his property. With regard to James Bolton, it vi £IS ascertained that on the evening of the 26th October, he went to Mr. Matthews in Pump yard and sold him a quantity of hair, also some to a Mr. Smith in Aikin-street. Detectives Reddington and Metcalf took possession of the hair.— Elizabeth Matthews, wife of Joseph Matthews, said that on Monday evening, October 25th, James Bolton went to her house and offered 361bs. of hprse hair for sale. She told him it was rather late to do any business that night. Eventually he left the hair and said he would call round for the money the next morning. His son came and received the money. On Monday, the 16th November, two detective officers went to her premises and took the hair away.—Detective Metcalfe said on Monday, November 16th, he recovered Blbs of hair that bad been sold. to Mr. Toole in Allen-street by the prisoner Burke. On the following Wednesday morning be went to Matthews and recovered 181bs. which had been sold by the prisoner, Edward Bolton. Witness went to Edward Bolton's house and questioned him about the hair and ho said a man gave it to him in Priestley-street. He took prisoners to the Police Station and on being charged, Burke said "Yes, sir, I plead guilty." Witness visited James Bolton's house and on opening the door James said "Is that you. Mr. Metcalfe? Come in; I was quite expecting you." Witness took him to the Police Station.--Mr. Steel, in his speech for/ the defence, said there was not a tittle of evidence against James Bolton.—The magistrates discussed the matter privately and on their return the Chairman said that Burke and Edward Bolton were guilty. James Bolton they would give the benefit of the 'douht.—The second charge was then proceeded with. John Burke and Edward Bolton were charged with stealing from the unoccupied houses 15 and 17, Folly-lane, some time in October or November, about lowt. 2qrs. 221bs. of lead, and a copper hot water cylinder, all valued at £2. The prisoners Burke and Edward Bolton forced an entrance into the house, 15, Folly-lane, and stripped the piping connected with the hot water cistern. They also broke the copper cistern and took it away.—William Hill aged 20, said that on Saturday, November 6th, he went to Bolton's house in the afternoon. While in the yard be saw a handcart from whieh Burke took a cylinder and carried it into the house. He was about to take it upstairs when Mr. Bradshaw came to the door. Jares Bolton said "Hurry up and lock the door. We don't want him to see anything." Afterwards Edward Bolton got a pot and began to melt the lead down. He then poured it into a mould. He gave Burke 3s, and said That will be enough to-day, until we see how we go on." Burke on receiving the money called Bolton the "empty House King." (Laughter.) Detective Holland gave evidence of bearing a conversation between Burke and Edward Bolton in the cells with regard to the the theft, in which Burke threatened to tell the police where they had got the lead from. On being charged by Detective Metcalf Burke admitted the offence.—Burke was further charged with stealing from an unoccupied house in Wilderspool-road in November about 22 lea. of lead piping value 55. 6d. the property of William Benson, also with stealing from an unoccupied house in Robinson's-yard about 41 lbs of lead piping. ,Prisoner pleaded guilty to both charges. On behalf of the Boltons Mr. Steel pleaded for lgniency. Edward Bolton was the only support of b s father, James, who was 54 years of age. With regard to James, Mr. Steel contended that the only evidence there was about him was that he was in the house at the time when the stolen goods were brought in. Edward Bolton was only a young man and he hoped the Bench would treat him as lightly as the circumstances would allow.—After private discussion, the chairman said there had been a great deal Of destruction to property and the bench were determined to put a stop to it by meeting out the utmost punishment that could bo given. The sentence on Burke would be 12 months bard labour, Edward Bolton 6 months hard labour and James Bolton 3 months bard labour. The Chief Constable said that no less than .£5O damage bad been done in the three houses It was monstrous. They bad bad only those charges preferred but the police could have brought 20 cases against them.

div.head: Warrington Borough Court.
div.p: Warrington Borough Court.

SATURDAY.—Before Messrs. J. W. Harward (chairman H. T. Fairclough, Dr. Markel and T. Pemberton. FOR AN UNLAWFUL PURPOSE.—George Sixsmith, of Turner-street was charged with being on the enclosed prentlses at the rear of a lock-up shop in Sankey-street on Friday night.—The Chief Constable said that a con- stable made an inspection of the premises near the railway bridge °tithe corner of Parker-street, and found prigoner sitting on a box. He brought him to the Police Station and asked him what he wanted there, and he said he did not know. There were many work-. men's tools about that prisoner could have put in his pocket. Prisoner, who had been before the Court previously, was sentenced to a months' imprisonment.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. C. White (chairman) Alder- man Smethurst and J. W. Hayward. THEFTS OF CLOCK AND TOBACCO,—ThOUMS Hayes and Joseph Collins, living in Bank-street were charged with stealing from a shop in IVinwick-road a clock, 6 packets of Woodbine cigarettes and a packet of tobacco the property of ara Jan e Knight.—The Chief Constable in asking fora remand of a week said that there would probably be other charges preferred against the prisoners. The police had been unable to make enquiries owing to the short time prisoner had been in custody. The remand vias granted. THErr OF A BICYCLE.—John Fletcher of no settled abode, was remanded for a week on the charge of steal- ing a bicycle value .E 3 the property of Robert Lee. The Chief Constable stated teat the prisoner took the bicycle from outside the Corporation Hotel and rode away in the direction of Cadishead. On arriving there he lett the hicyle against the gate of a field. The Cadishead police were informed.--The prisoner was arrested and brought to town. He was a stranger to the town and he asked for a remand in order to obtain the prisoner's antecedents. It was found that he was of good character. He hoped that the bench would take that into consideration. It was a foolish thing for the man to do.

tiRSD AY. —Verore Messrs. John Fairclongh (chair - ruan), C, White, H. Thornton, J, Rymer Young. A .1. Jolley, E. Woods, W. T. William:, and Dr. Naden TH EFT FROM A P ÜBLIC.HOIj SE.—Charles Shaw, of Edward-street, was charged with stealing from the Unicorn Inn, Winwick-ro id, on Tuesday a half-pint glass and a metal crusher, value 3d. It appears that the prisoner went into the Unicorn Inn and had some drink, and after his departure the articles were missed. Prisoner was ordered to pay 10s, and costs or 14 days. FRlDAY.—Before Messrs. Hy. Thornton (Chairman) A. J. Jolley and NV. Furness. NOT SUFFICIENT EVIDENCE. —Thomas Henry Huskisson a well-dressed stranger was charged with stealing between Wednesday and Thursday of last week from the British Workmen's Cocoa Rooms, Horse- market-street, a suit of clothes and other articles value £l. 17s. Gd. the property of Alfred Waring.—Tbe Chief Constable said that the prosecutor lodged at the Cocoa Rooms. On Thursday morning of last week, prisoner went ta prosecutor's bedroom and asked him to get up as he wanted to have a rest. He got up and left his suit of clothes on the be. and prisoner afterwards slept in the room. When prisoner departed later the clothes were missed. The police were informed, and from inquiries by Detective Reddington and Clough prisoner was arrested. It bad since been ascertained that prisoner on leaving the house on tha above morning left, by the back door instead of the front. Information bad also come to their knowledge that prisoner had pledged a watch in town, which he afterwards redeemed. On being questioned about this, prisoner said a man gave it to him at St. Helens RR a keepsake.—ln answer to a query by Mr. Furness. Mr. Hampton, from the Cocoa Rooms, said that other persons slept in the same room as Waring.— Pisoner said he was absolutely- innocent of the charge preferred against him. He had no need to touch the poor man's clothes.—The Chairman after discussioo with his collegues said there was not sufficient evidence , against prisoner to find him guilty and he would be dismissed.

div.head: hurghtli
div.p: hurghtli

There were large congregations at this church on Sunday when the foreign missionary anniversary ser- ,vices were held. Tue preacher in the morning was the Rev. John Yonge, who strongly urged the claims of missionary work. A service was held in the school at 250, when thc Eev. G. Parker, from Travancore, India, delivered an interesting address. In the evening Mrs. Johnson, who has spent some time in Madagascar, gave a graphics account of the work there, and held the close attention of the congregation with a description of the people and places. The collections were in aid of the London Missionary Society, and realized a satisfactory amount.
Wycliffe Congregational Church.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

There was a good meeting Oa Sunday last, presided over by the 'Secretary. Mr. Thomas Dale gave the address upon the words of the leader, of Israel unto Joshua "All that Thou oommandest us we will do, and whithersoever thou sendest us we will go.'! He referred to the willingness for service, and pointed out that there was much that needed doing to-day. Men were indifferent ; some were low in sin. There were the evils of slum life, and the great curse of drunkenness. Men were wanted to work for the salvation of the people. Might there he willing minds and loving hearts to sly to Jesus "We go at Thy command. We will do as Thou desire." Master B. Farrar sang sweetly" What shall the htrvest be " and " Angels ever bright and fair." Mr. W. H. Payton, Mug. Bac., presided at the organ. The Chairman read the lesson and Mr. A. Healey led the prayer. Three new members received a very hearty welcome. The meeting closed with the rousing hymn "Work for the night is coming.;

div.head: Emmanuel Church. Farewell Sermon of Rey. F. Vaughan.
div.p: Emmanuel Church. Farewell Sermon of Rey. F. Vaughan.

The Rev. F. Vaughan, who has been incumbent of Emmanuel (Reformed Episcopal) Church for the last six years, has now laid down the reins of ministry here to take up the pastorate of Christ Church, Harlesden, North London. He preached his farewell sermon on Sunday night before a crowded congregation. Taking for his text Psalm xlviii., 12-13 v., " Walk about Zion and go round about her: tell the towers thereof; mark well her bulwarks: consider her palaces that ye may tell it to the generetion following.."—,the rev. gentleman said that that church was their Zion, and it was there in days gone by that their fathers worshipped. In that place their dearest relations repented of their sins and realised their pardon. It was there that they had been emboldened to resist the temptations which arose from without and within. It was also to that place they came in the holy days of matrimony. It was their spiritual home where they experienced the touch of God. There they had experienced moral and spiritual upheavals which bad given birth to new aspiratians, hopes and fears. Other churches might have been hospitable friendly or inspiring, but that house was their real home. He did not wish to toich upon the political and social points, which the text touched upon, for he
Who has gone to Christ Church. Harlesden, N. London, after six years ministry at Emmanuel Church, Warrington.

bad never used his pulpit for political purposes, but he wished to speak of the great dangers which beset their path on account, of the very liberties they enjoyed to-day. He bad no intention to speak of their parti- cular ecclesiastical position or the work which they were called upon to perform in this twentieth' century. Despite the terrible evils which beget their path they were determined to )(now nothing save Jesus Christ and Him crucified. There Was a growing love of pleasure in the life of God's people.. There was also another danger, which was the growing attitude of contempt for God's Day and God's House. Whatever their opinion might be about the Sabbath it was God's intention that one day in seven should be set apart for His service and for the sacred ministry of His House. Then there was the advance of Popery and growing love of ritual, the havoc made by the liquor trade —all those were difficulties which beset their path, and bad to be overthrown. These were, crippling the moral and spiritual forces of the Church laf God. Christ was at the head of the Church. They must have the power to know the presence of Christ and if the Church must succeed, Christ must be centralized. They were to create a moral and spiritual atmosphere in which the generations yet unborn might breath. He laid down the reins of his ministry that night and he wanted to ask them that question: Had they grown in mental, moral, and spiritual forcefulness? Were they likely to grow; was there any prospect of their growing? His heart was very full and it was with difficulty he undertook that task. Every brick in that building represented the sympathies and sacrifices of their
ancestors. Concluding be appealed to all present to consecrate their lives to the Lord.

Mr. Vaughan leaves Warrington, with the highest 'regard and best wishes not only of his own congrega- tion, but of a much wider circle of Christian workers. During his connection with the Reformed Church at Warrington considerable progress has been made. The building has been renovated and a new organ purchased, and the whole of the church work reconstructed. The Institute in School-street, Knutsford-road, has been purchased and opened, and good work of a social and temperance character amongst men has been conducted
THE REV. F. VAUGHAN,

div.head: 1 tta
div.p: 1 tta
LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
Imperial Defence Bill.

One of the youngest. members (Mr. S. S. Lloyd Secretary for Foreign Affairs) had charge of the intro- duction of a "to consolidate the Empire for the purpose of Imperial Defence "at the weekly meeting of the Parliamentary Debating Society on Tuesday evening. A fairly large House gave him an 'attentive hearing and members on both sides afterwards spoke in complimentary terms of his speech. The Bill provides that an Imperial Defence Committee be constituted, consisting of representatives from the United King- dom, the dominion of Canada, Dependency of India, British South Africa, the Commonwealth of Australia and New Zealand, that the aforesaid Imperial Defence Committee shall meet every two years or oftener if considered necessary or advisable by his Majesty's Government. In the event of Great Britain and Ireland or any British Colony declaring or entering upon war, or in the event of any act of war against, or armed attack upon Great Britain and Ireland or any Colony, the emergency sub-committee shall decide as to what portion, (if any) of the imperial forces shall be called upon to take part in the operations following upon such declaration of war or armed attack. In addition to the regular professional army, there is to be a Territorial force, provided for the oefence of the United Kingdom and the Colonies, service in which shall be obligatory on all able-bodied citizens, and the training of the force shall be on similar lines to that laid down by the National Service League. In the event of war the Colonies shall place their naval and military forces (except their Militia) entirely at the disposal of the Mother country for the purposes of Imperial Defence. Mr. LLOYD said the Bill was not intended as a party measure but as a practical and sensible way of dealing with the question of defence. It was the duty of all of them to do all in their power to safeguard effectually the sacred privileges which had been handed down by their forefathers at the sacrifice of precious and heroic lives. It was absolutely necessary to take advantage of the present breathing space to prepare for any attack which might be made upon the Empire in the future. No country had shown such a genius for governing native races as this country—civilization and Christian- ity had followed the Union Jack everywhere—but there was a danger of the vast Empire being shattered unless adequate preparations for defence were made. Explain- ing the Bill in detail, Mr. Lloyd said it was desirable that generals or admirals who would be in command in time of war should be in command in time of peace. (Hear, hear.) With regard to the territorial force, be was opposed to conscription, but he considered that all the young manhood of the country should have military training. Such training would make the people more alert, intelligent,and polite,than they other- wise would be, in addition to making them better physically. The Bill 'would make the Colonies self- sunnorting in the matter of defence. (Applause.) Mr. F. A. JENKINS (Postmaster-General) seconded. Mr. W. NIGHTINGALE (NOrMaRtOD, S.), moved that the Bill be read that day three months. He said they must have been a lot of fools to have spent their money in the past on phantom ships and phantom men. (Laughter.) There must have been a lot of muddling and swindling going on. They had paid sufficient money to have is good army and navy, and what bad been done with it all? They wanted the best men in the ranks, and why did they not demand the best men at the top? The speaker made an earnest plea for the betterment of the oonditions of life of the working classes. "If you will give us something to defend "he exclaimed" we will defend it." He was opposed to the proposed committee as such bodies generally developed into cliques. The promoters of the Bill had not the courtesy to offer the working-classes representation on the committee. If they were going to uphold the destinies of the Empire they wanted a voice in its government. He appealed to the Government to do something to make the conditions in the nation worth fighting for. "You have tried to kill us with hard work" be declared "and now you are going to starve us to death by making our food dearer." He was not a "peace at any price "man; he believed in a religion that made him more manly than that. He opposed the Bill because it did not really touch the question. Mr. A. PERRIS (Central Bradford, L.), seconded the amendment. He had not much faith in imperial defence committees. If the Bill sought to consolidate the Empire by adopting Free Trade within the Empire he might have been in favour of it. Mr. G. H. WARBURTON STEEL (First Lord of the Admiralty) supported the Bill. He remarked that no member of the Liberal party had liscl the courage to move the amendment, and they had to go to their satellites, the Socialists, to do it. He was so greatly in favour of the Bill that he was prepared to forego his salary this year to assist in carrying out the scheme. (Laughter.) He urged the necessity for a strong navy, and said no Price was too great to pay for national independence. Mr. P. O'BRIF.N (St. Pancras, L.) in supporting the amendment, said be had always regarded the member for Normanton not as a satellite but as a whole con- stellation in himself. (Laughter.) Referring to the alliance between England and Japan, he stid the policy which gave Japan command of the Pacific Ocean was a false policy. There was always an Influence in the flag that was flying from vessels. Colonial opinion was that Japan was looking with hungry eyes on Australia as an outlet far its surplus population. With regard to the prospect of a German invasion, he did not think that there was any fear, so long as the present condition of things prevailed in Europe. He had a sympathetic feeling for the National Service League, because he believed young people world be none the worse for the training, and his experienbe had been that those who were least ansious to promote quarrels were the men who were best able to fight. Unfortunately, war to-day was not in the hands of the democracy and as long as they had in Europe an erratic individual who had the right to declare war just when he thought fit, it was absolutely necessary that our army and navy should be prepared to repel any onslaught. Mr. W. RIGBY (West Belfast, N.) said the fact that the Bill would allow the Colonies to declare war was sufficient to condemn it. He opposed the system of oompulsory military training as being tantamount to conscription. The Bill did not guarantee that the citizen who had to assume full responsibilities would have full citizen's rights. The speaker quoted French testimonies as to the evil moral effects of conscription and caintended that the same applied to Germany. He denied the right of any man to force him into a con- dition of things where good and had were herded together. How was the proposed four months' training to erredicate the physical effect of 18 years' life under the insanitary conditions which were the lot of great numbers of our people? Better housing, more open spaces, and reformed conditions of labour were necessary to improve the physique. Tee cost of the compulsory military scheme would be enormous and another evil was that the raising of such a force would encourage interference in European affairs. MR. MELT.on (Banbury, L) stud the Liberal Government in the Imperial Parliament had been making full provision for the defence of the Empire but the Tory party, who were loudest in clamouring for a strong navy, now refused to pay for it. The Conserva- tives talked a great deal of trusting the people now, but would they do so when they wanted to increase taxation for the benefit of their friends and parasites? CAPTAIN CROSFIFID (ROCbdalo, I.) moved the adjortrnment of the debate and he will consequently be the first speaker at next Monday, evening's sitting.

div.head: ST. HELENS ENGINEER CHAGES,
div.p: ST. HELENS ENGINEER CHAGES,

An interesting gathering of the officers of the West Dincashire Divisional Engineers took place on Satur- day evening, at the St. Helens headquarters, when the guests of honour were Captain Dobson, R.E., who has completed his term as adjutant to the corps, and Captain Painter, R.E., who has been appointed adjutant at St. Helens. Captain Dobson has been appointed divisional Royal Engineer at Lichfield.

div.head: EVANGELISTIC AIISSIGN AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: EVANGELISTIC AIISSIGN AT WARRINGTON.
VISIT OF MR. GEORGE CLARKE.

Mr. George Clarke, the world renowned evangelist, commenced a fortnight's mission in Parr Hall, Warrington, on Sunday. The town should proven fruitful field for the evangelist's labours if it is as the Rev. A. M. Mitchell has recently described it, viz. : "So brewery-ridden, so beer begripped, a town so befouled, begrimed and vitiated, whose slums, more slummy than the slums of our great cities, are death-traps and moral cesspools." The missioner has a striking personality and bears an unmistakable facial resemblance to Lord Rosebery- His manneris dignified and although his hair is grey he still posseses the fine p'usique which his athletic training gave him. Like Lord Rosebery again he has an eloquent and persuasive tongue which he uses not for playing on the emotions, but for getting at the heart through the brain. The mission is under the auspices of the Warring- ton and District Free Church Council and will be continued each day until December Cth, except Saturdays. The singing is led by a united choir- of about 150 voices and is under the con- ductorship of Ur. W. Hipkiss. Mr. Clarke held a service in the morning (Sunday) at 9 o'clock especially for Christians. In the afternoon the hall was crowded, the audience being composed mainly of children. Ur. Clarke gave his popular address for children entitled" From rags to paper." He held the atten- tion of the children throughout his speech, their eager flees showing their appreciatiou of his remarks. Mr. Clarke gave a detailed account of the conversion of rags to paper and drew the parallel re the conversion of sinners. The hall was packed in the evening and Mr. Clarke was supported on the platform by nearly all the Nonconformist ministers in the town. Mr. Clarke took for his subject "The raising of the widow's son" (St. Luke via.) He said that in the .11th verse it said that "He came into the city." They might have the best committee that had ever been organised, they might have all the ministers of the varieus churches, and they might have an evangelist mightily owned of God, but they would not make a mission. If they got; of people it would not make a mission. l'l.ere was only one thing that could make a mission and that wits" He (Jesus) came into the city:" If they did not meet with the Lord Jesus Christ in that hall it would never be a mission. They had been praying for a mighty revival in the town and that every Church would be blessed and if it were not that. it was a failure. He hoped that in every Church there were many people who were ripe unto the harvest and ready to be gathered in. Referring to the subject before him he asked the audience to let him paint the picture. In one road which led upwards to the city was a procession, with Christ at the head of it. Christ was facing the pro- cession and the ray cast by Him was alighting on His followers, the light of course, showing on the people nearest to Him in greater brilliance. Teat procession he called " Life." The other procession was headed by bearers carrying the widow's son, who were wending their way to the burial ground. The cortege he called "Death." The widow was weeping, but Christ went up to her and said" Weep not ! " and she was comforted. So it was that she was transferred to the procesaion of "Life," the same as Christ would trans- fer all those who were not Christians and were in the procession of " Death " to the one of "Life." Why was it that some were like Christ, and tbe people knew at once that they were Christians and others who called themselves Christians did not reflect anything of Christ about themselves ? It all depended whether they' were walking in the procession of which Christ was the head. Possibly some there that night would- not become Christians, because there were so many humbugs and hypocrites and therefore they said they would sooner be worldlings. They must not blame Christ for that, because it all depended upon the Christians themselves. The first thing C hrist did in a mission was to stand still and beckon to the people at the back of the procession to come up nearer. There would be no converts until the Christians got nearer to the Christ. In the procession of death, everybody seemed to despair and was hopeless or. joyless. Near to the back of the procession the people were less and less mournful and less and less sad until when they got at the back they walked with their heads up and their shoulders bacic. They were there out of sympathy for the widowed mother. At the head of the procession were the profligates, and drunkards, thieves and murderers, but everyone in that procession was going to death, just as everybody in the other procession was going to life. Continuing, the missioner said that Christ was not asking whether they were rich or poor, Episcopalian or Nonconformists. The question Christ was asking was: Which procession are you in? When those two processions met, the Spirit of Life—call Him the Spirit of God if they liked—bad his procession in His grip and the Spirit of Death—call him the Spirit of Deatti if they liked—had his followers in his power. As they met the two Spirits fought for the possession of the men's souls, and it chiefly depended upon those in the procession whom they followed. Continuing he said that many of them (the audience) had tried to be religious, but bad never met a living Christ. They were asked to come to Christ. He was sick to death of a religion that never brought him to a Christ, or a creed that did not bring him to a living Person. When he was in New York city 31 years ago —he was 21 then—Christ made the bearers stop and then he beheld tbe Christ and joined in His procession. There never had be3n a man or a woman yet who had gone down that road to death who had not shed bitter tears. When the two processions met and Jesus Christ stood in front of a soul that was in the procession, and that soul was crying out "Lord, save me," Christ made the bearers to stand still, and said unto the soul "Weep not," and "I say unto thee, arise." When that soul heard that it transferred itself to the procession of Life, and at the end of it was the City of Life. A short after-meeting was held and about twenty people were converted. 'During the week Mr. Clarke hns bad "Bible talks " during each afternoon excepting Monday, and has also held successful meetings i.n the evening. To-morrow (Sunday) afternoon Mr. Clarke will deliver an address to men only on" The Christian Athlete." Chairman, Mr. Jaknes Dodds.

div.head: KING MANUEL AT ETON COLLEGE.
div.p: KING MANUEL AT ETON COLLEGE.

The young Portuguese King foun I time from his haw round of State and social functions to pay a visit on Saturday to Eton College. King Manuel, who was accompanied by King Edward and Queen Alexandra, Qu.!en Maud, and little Prince Olaf, spent an enjoyable time at the histofc school. King Edward pointed out to him its many interesting features, the walls and pillars with their hundreds of names of dead and gone generations of schoolboys cut out in the woodwork, the memorial to the Etonians who fell in South Africa, and the playing-fields where, according to Wellington, was won the great battle of Waterloo. His Majesty saw a football game in full progress, and altogether was much delighted with his visit to the boys on whose shoulders rest so much of Britain's future gi eatness. _

div.head: NOBEL PRIZE-WINNER,
div.p: NOBEL PRIZE-WINNER,

MME. SELMA LAGERLOF. In spite of the secrecy maintained concern- ing the next Nobel prizes, it is now certain that the prize for literature will be given to the greatest woman writer of Sweden, Mme. Selma Lagerlof.

There is to be a great tussle for the Parliamentary representation of Portsmouth. The three candidates.—Mr. Lambert (Liberal), Lord Charles Beresford (Unionist), and Alderman Sanders (Labour)—are showing tremendous energy. During the week end there was a disturbance at the headquarters of the Budget Protest League, the windows being smashed by the crowd, who took exception to one of the League's election exhibits. Lord Charles Beresford's personality will count for a good deal in the fight. On Saturday he attended the football match between Portsmouth and Millwall, and at the finish oi the game presented the cup to the winners.
By Attoin MAKERS TO H.M.
