div.head: FORGOTTEN 114VENTOR.
div.p: A FORGOTTEN 114VENTOR.
Henry Cort.
THE ORIGINATOR OF PUDDLING'
In the parish 'Church of Lancaster there has recently been, placed a bronze memorial which reads:
In memory of Henry Cort Born at Lancaster 1740 Interred at Hampstead 1800
To whom the world is-indebted for the arts of refining iron by puddling with mineral coal and of rolling metals in grooved rolls.

Warrington people have an interest in puddling with mineral coal" and " rolling metals in grooved rolls," and may welcome a little:information concerning the Lancashire man to whom the world at large and our own town in particular owes these two discoveries.

It is a good and bracing thing to follow the careers of our pioneers. And it adds to the interest if not always to the happiness of life to know at which cost our comforts have been purchased. We all have some slight interest in Henry Cort, for do we not all ride in trams upon rails which are only possible through his invention of grooved rolls? And on the industrial side can we be indifferent concerning a man whose inventions have opened avenues of labour for six millions of

people. Yet in making enquiries concerning Henry Cort we are enquiring after a for- gotton hero, one of the greatest martyrs of industrial England whose very grave was unknown until an American ironworker after diligent search found it in Hampstead Churchyard. The disappearance of Cort from the public memory is due to the tragedy which wrecked his life, and it is in the hope of doing a little to give him the place he deserves that we attempt a brief account of his career.

div.head: CORTIS HISTORY.
div.p: CORTIS HISTORY.

Henry Cort was born in Lancaster in 1740 and as a young man of 25 went to London as a naval agent. At that time the iron used by the Admiralty for cables and anchors, and for gendral shipbuilding purposes was imported from Russia, Sweden and the Colonies, and as iron was constantly passing through his hands he would seem to have turned his attention to iron wbrking. At any rate we find him establishing an Iron Works at Fontley and entering upon the trade of iron working. On January 17th 1783, he took out his first patent for rolling metals in grooved rolls, and in the following year for refining iron by puddling with mineral coal. When we remember that Cort had no knowledge of chemistry we are impressed that he must have been a man of uncommon perception and genius, and the working out of the practice of puddling must have been a labour of unusual patience. The establishment of his works- at Fontley and the perfecting of his patents cost him £20,000. Unable to provide sufficient capital he turned for help to Adam Jellicoe, Chief Clerk to the Navy paymaster and entered into an agree- ment to share the profits with him. For three or four years all went well. The inventors were a perfect success and began at on3e to have a marked effect upon the iron trade. In illustration of influence upon English manufacture we may mention that while at that period the best iron was imported ninety years later we exported iron to the value of £38,000,000.

div.head: WEDDING OF COAL AND IRON.
div.p: THE WEDDING OF COAL AND IRON.

The extraordinary influence of his twin inventions lies in the fact that by them he wedded England's coal to England's iron. He showed how our coal could be used to refine our iron and in every coal or iron field the new industries leaped into robust life. Cort had imposed a Royalty of ten shillings per ton upon the iron made upon his patents, and his prospects of fortune and success were of the brightest. No sooner had his processes been perfected, then there came the great tragedy of his life. Adam Jellicoe died, probably by his own hand, and was found to have embezzled £39,000 from Navy Fund. His property was seized and with it the deeds of partnership. Finding that he had a joint interest in the iron works and patents they seized the property and both were sacrificed. Oth6rs were found to be implicated with the deceased Jellicoe and to shelter them, all papers were burned, and Cort was left without evidence gs to Patent Royalties and without security of any kind, With his property and patents snatched from him he became a ruined man.

div.head: CROWNING INJUSTICE.
div.p: THE CROWNING INJUSTICE.

His integrity remained to him and he faced the disaster with fine courage. After two years of uncertainty he appealed to the Navy Commissioners but he could obtain no redress. The licensees under his patents were relieved of all royalties due and indeed were encouraged to use Cort's methods with- out paying him anything. The Commis- sioners' reply to his appeal is brutal in the extreme and their action is a sad blot upon

the record of a public body which can never be effaced or forgotten. This crowning 'injustice seems to have crushed the talented iron-master. He dis- appears from view and it has only been by careful enquiry in recent years that the date of his death has been discovered. Of the heavy' yeArs that followed his ruin we know little or nothing. The nation gave him a small pension and on this he subsisted until he passed away a broken-hearted man on May 23rd, 1800. The ironmasters of the country were meanwhile making fortunes by the use of his inventions, but with an unfor- giveable greed were refusing to give bim what was legally and morally his due.

div.head: CORTS FAR-REACHING INVENTIONS.
div.p: CORTS FAR-REACHING INVENTIONS.

In 1786, two years after Henry Corts discovery Lora Sheffield made a strikingly suggestive statement which must at the time have seemed extravagant. England had recently lost the United States of America and Lord Sheffield said "If Mr. Corts very ingenious. and meritorious improvements in the art of making and working iron, the steam engine of Waft and Loira:Dundonalds discovery of making coke should all succeed, it is not asserting too much to say that the result will be more advantageous to Great Britain than the possession of the thirteen colonies of America." And this has been fully realized
The vast infltienes which have flowed from Cort's work have stirred a few thoughtful men to enquiry and tributes are

beginning to flow to him. Thus the "Times " has spoken of him as "The Tubal Cain of our I,country and the Father of the British iron trade." Chas. H. Morgan of Worcester U.S.A. said" By his labours your country —all countries—have been greatly enriched, and without them mine could not exist as a great unit," and showed his interest by pro- vidifig memorial tablets at Lancaster and Hampstead. Though the Encyclopedia Britannica has scarcely a word about him the Popular Encyclopedia attempting an estimate of his life stated that in seventy years "The amount added to the national wealth of his inventions was £600,000,000 while employment had been given to six million persons." But justice has yet to be done to his memory. His story reminds us strangely of that of Crompton the inventor of the Spinning Mule‘ and they may be classed together as men who deserved more from their generation and from posterity than they have yet received. A.M.

div.head: OUR fiIISCELL
div.p: OUR fiIISCELL

By the courtesy of 'Mr. John Naylor and in reference to our article of last week we are able to tell our readers that in the village of Loppington near Wem in Shropshire there may still be seen the ring to which the bull was tied during the village bull baits. It was usual to have a permanatit stake with a ring attached, or a ring imbedded in the pavemement as a firm anchorage for the bears and bulls that were baited, but few of them have survived. Mr. Naylor is not sure whether one other exists in the South of England; possibly some, of our readers can tell us. There are, of course, several places called "Bull Ring" which have taken their names from being the scene of bull baiting. One exists near Ludlow and another near Birmingham and there may be several more.

• Our elderly readers who were reared on the banks of the Bridgewater Canal have given us some interesting impr6ssions and remem- brances of the days when the canal was the waterway for travellers as well as for goods. There are still living those who can go back to the days of "Duchess Countess" the First and many who knew the second boat of that name. Both were very narrow and came to a knife edge at the bow the idea of the builders being to secure the minimum of fiction in the water. At the bow was a carved ornament resembling a swan's neck and head and the boat was pulled by two handsome trotting horses. The first horse was ridden by a jockey in coloured cap and with shining buttons, and at the rear of the boat another officer blew the boat's horn to give warning to intending passengers who were taken aboard at defined points on the route. •

To reach Liverpool passengers disembarked at Runcorn and committed themselves to a sailing boat—afterward replaced by a crude steamer—by which they were conveyed along the Mersey-. Manchester merchants travelled thus to Liverpool in preference to being conveyed by Stage Coach, and remembering the freedom from vibration and greater comfort we can understand their choice.' Horses were stabled at various points and rapidly changed as the " flying " packet arrived. The stables which sheltered them may still be seen at London Bridge,

div.head: FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
div.p: FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
By Philip Snowden, M.P.
LABOUR AND THE ELECTION.

My remarks made last week on the question of triangular contests appear to have been received with interest, judging by the comments upon them I have received. The prospect of an early general election in which there are risks that a minority vote may return a candidate who is directly opposed to the majority of the electors in a constituency on the great issue at stake has naturally brought this questioti of three- cornered contests into prominence. Every- body, I am sure, regrets that divisions should result in the return of a candidate ,who is objectionable to the majority of the electors. But the way to prevent that catastrophe at the coming election is not very clear and open.

div.head: WHIP'S MANIFESTO.
div.p: THE WHIP'S MANIFESTO.

The chief Liberal Whip has written a long letter to a meeting in Durham, which he evid‘ently intends to be a Manifesto on the question of Liberal and Labour opposition. His remarks do not carry the matter much farther, and in some respects they are calcu- lated to exasperate' existing differences. There is no recognition in his letter of the right of the Labout Party, as an independent political body to have direct representation in Parliament by virtue of its credentials from the whole force of organised- Trade Unionism. It is perfectly evident from Kr. Pease's Manifesto that he has no inten- tion of conceding any further representation to Labour, or of recognising that the Labour Party is entaled to more members than it at present possesses. Mr. Pease's position is that the status quo might be accepted, that Liberals should respect Labour seats and that the Labour Party should, keep away from constituencies where a Liberal now sits. AN IMPOSSIBLE BARGAIN.

That, of course, is a bargain which the Labour Party could not consider for one moment. The Labour Party does not con- sider that its present Parliamentary strength is an adequate or reasonable representation of Trade Unionism and Socialism. The Labour Party would refuse to look at a sug- gestion which confined them for the future to attacking only Tory seats, in return to security from Liberal attack in the seats the Labour Party now hold. The Labour Party could never agree to any bargain which restricted it freedom to put forward a can- didate in any constituency -where it thought Labour ought to be directly represented. The seats held by Tories are very often constitu- encies of a character where Labour would find it very difficult to obtain a foothold.

div.head: ONE-SIDED SACRIFICE.
div.p: A ONE-SIDED SACRIFICE.

Mr. Pease, in his Manifesto, betrays over and over again, his antipathy to an indepen- dent Labour Party. He justifies the attack of the Liberals on Mr. Johnson at Gateshead on the ground that Mr. Johnson has now joined the Labour Party: That is quite true; but at the last election Mr. Johnson was the miners' candidate, paid by the miners, res- ponsible to the miners, and only endorsed by the Liberal Association. And if it be justifi- able to oppose a miners' candidate at Gates- head because, lie has fallen into line with the decision of the vote of his own union, it would have been justifiable and consistent for the Liberals to oppose all the other dozen miners' men who were returned as Liberal-Labour at the last election, but who now have joined the Labour Party.

div.head: WITHOLDING CREDIT.
div.p: WITHOLDING CREDIT.

No, the fact is that Mr. Pease wants it to be all give and no take, the Labour Party to do the giving and Mr. Pease to do the taking. I am not for a moment suggesting that the Labour Party would listen to any suggestion of a bargain, but if they did I am sure Mr. Pease would have to offer enormously more generous terms than he has so far done. His unwarranted attempt to depreciate the value of the work done in Pariament by the Labour Party, by trying to magnify the value •of the Liberal-Labour group may deceive those who know nothing of the facts, but those who know the House of Commons, and who know the history of this Parliament will ,smile when Mr. Pease talks about the influence of the Liberal-Labour members. Mr. Pease knows quite differently; he knows that there has been in this Parliament no Labour group except the Labour party; that on all general questions the Liberal- Labour members have been an indistinguish- able part of Mr. Pease's well-drilled army, and that on Labour questions the Liberal- Labour members have acted with the Labour Party. • EXTRAORDINARY CIRCUMSTANCES. If the circumstances of the coming election were of an ordinary character it would be idle to talk of any understanding for the purpose of preventing the risk of returning the Tory by the intervention of a third candidate. But the circumstances are not ordinary, and even cast-iron constitutions may be made to bend when circumstances arise which were never contemplated, and which raise issues of transcendent import- ance. If the election comes as a result of the action of the House of Lords on the Budget, then there will be only one issue before the country. Old party divisions will , for the time be obliterated, and the only two parties will be those who believe in democratic governMent and those who prefer their necks to be in the feudal yoke. AN IMPROBABLE PROPOSAL.

I see that a 'journal, which is usually well-informed, has been hinting that the Government may pass a measure establish- ing the Second Ballot before the dissolution. That is impossible; such an innovation in our electoral system could not be introduced in such a hurry. There is a very general disapproval of the Second Ballot among men who are anxious for some amendment of our system which will prevent the minority can- didate securing the seat. The House of Lords would never consent to pass such a, measure on the eiie of an election in order to reduce the prospects of a Tory majority. No, if anything is done to get the issue at this election straight and clear on the question of the Lords, it will have to be by some commonsense understanding between those who are in agreement on this cfestion.

div.head: BOUNDEN DUTY.
div.p: A BOUNDEN DUTY.

I am expressing no opinion beyond saying that if the election comes now everything else should for the moment be put aside to let the Lords and the People fight out the question of who shall rule. So long as the Lords retain their present powers to mutilate and to reject legislation not even a Labour or Socialist Government would be able to get any thorough refotm measures through Parliament. Before the road can be clear for the democratic coach, the obstacle of the Lords' veto must be removed. If the Labour Party were returned to the House of Commons with a majority, their first job

would be to tackle the House of Lords. So that it seems to me that if an election comes now on the House of Lords question it will be the bounden duty of every section of the democratic forces to make common cause on that issue; for if the House of Lords win, the future work of the Labour party for generations to come will not be trying to advanco,--.reform, but will be resisting encroachments on the liberties we have already secured.

div.head: FIRST STEP.
div.p: THE FIRST STEP.

I am speaking only for myself. The Lab Our. Party has not considered this question in the light of the circumstances developed by the action of the House of Lords. Probably they will do so if the election comes, and though it would be an immensely difficult thing to recast the policy of the Party on the eve of a,n election, the special circumstances will no doubt receive the serious attention they deserve. If the Liberals are really anxious to join all democratic forces in opposition to the House of Lords, I would suggest that they might show their desire by works, and their works might take the form of withdrawing their opposition to certain sitting Labour members against whom they- have candidates in the field.

div.head: OUR SERIAL STORY.
div.p: OUR SERIAL STORY.
[ALL RIGIIT3 RESERVED.]
"I tell you you must go back,- exclaimeo Felix Goode, impatiently. "Every moment is precious. Every moment may mean a matter of life or death to him." _ _

" Life or death! I won't go back,", she exclaimed, taking John Baxendale's arm again and seeming to ct?ng to him. "What he can face I can face :leo. What has hap- pened? " John Baxendale said nothing. Some strange foreboding was in his mind that he had come, in a sense, to a great crisis in his life; the faces of the two men shewed him that at least. After • a pause Felix Goode, glancing for a moment over his shoulder, as though he would peer into the depths of the wood, spoke huskily. "There has been murder done, and you are accused," he said, simply. "A woman has been killed—" He said no more, for John Baxendale had snatched the lantern from his hand, so that it seemed in a moment that they were all pressing along together, with Felix Goode holding to the young man's arm and talking to him disjointedly, towards the place where the girl lay. When they came to it, Johanna Cridge was gone. They looked upon what was to be seen there—the dead girl and her ghastly epitaph—in a momentary silence. , "Is she dead?_!' whispered Evelyn, making a movement towards the silent figure at the foot of the tree. "Nee, past all help," said Dick Munby, holding her back. "Before Heaven, I didn't do it!" ex- claimed Baxendale, turning round upon then. and speaking in a shaking voice. I know this gtrl—at least, I've seen her—but I know nothing of it." "Why need you say that? asked Felix Goode. "In my own mind, I know that you are innocent. But you know," he added, in a lower tone, "whose work it is likely to be. Come away now; we've got to think." John Baxendale found himself walking away like a man in a dream, found also, in a moment or two, that Evelyn's hand had stolen down to his and was clasping his fingers. He shook her off half impatiently, and, with a great despair tugging at his heart, cried out: "Why do you touch me? Didn't you see what was written there?" "I don't believe it. I'll never believe it," she whispered. "No one that knows you will ever believe it. There is some trick in this, some conspiracy. Mr. Goode "—she ap- pealed to the lawyer, who was walking with bent head—" you don't believe it, do you?" "No, no, of course not," he exclaimed, sweeping the thing aside as impossible. "There is a plot and a conspiracy, but we can't tell you what it is. John will come out of this with flying colours somehow, believe me," he added, to comfort her.- "But we've got to decide what is best to be done at the moment. That's why I want you to go back to your aunt's house, you can do no gout. here." "I won't leave Jack," said the girl. "I'll ahew everyone if -only by my presence, that I believe in him. Besides, I may be of use after all," she urged. "I'm not so weak as you think." They had moved on to the edge of the wood, and so had come to the high road. And here Felix Goode stopped in the dark- ness and the silence, and held up a hand. In the distance could be heard, borne on the night wind, a faint noise like the giant hum of men corning in the distance, and crying and talking as they came. It grew nearer and nearer. It was as though all Deepington had flung wide its doors and poured out in the direction of the wood. Very quietly Felix Goode raised the lantern, opened it, and puffed out the flame. "The murder's out," he said, quietly. "The game is not in our hands any longer." It was evident that aw and sleepy Deep- ington was roused. A long, straggling line of men and women could be seen coming in the far distance along the road, their moving shadows dark against the sky. They mur- mured and talked, and called to each other as they ran, and the first of them carried lanterns that twinkled and bobbed about like stars as they were swung along. Silently John Baxendale and the others stepped from the high road, and gained the grounds of Baxendale Hall. There ,in the shelter of the trees they stopped, and for a moment the young man, realising what the crowd were to find, and what they were to read, and what they were to understand, stopped and covered his face with his hands, and shuddered. The next moment he raised his head and almost laughed. "I'm not afraid of them. I'm not going to sneak away," he said. "The truth has got to come out at some time or other. I'll go down there now "—he pointed towards the wood they had left, and towards which the crowd was now hurrying—" and face the men I know, and tell them I am innocent." "And let them read that writing, and so judge between your word and that of the dead?" broke in Felix Goode. "A young girl struck down in cold blood, what sort of tem- per do you think the crowd will be in, even towards John Baxendale? Come away, man ! "

"They'll come to the Hall," -exclaimed Evelyn, quickly. "You mustn't go there, Jack, it wouldn't be safe. It wouldn't be 6afe for anyone that belongs to John Baxen- dale to be seen to-night by that mob. Let us get away. Come on to aunt's place, until we decide what is best to be done." There was wisdom in those words, at least. The little party turned and hurried away in the direction of Miss Stubbs's cottage. And while they walked Felix Goode urged the necessity for flight, though he did that in the ear of John Baxendale alone, lest the girl should understand the secret.

"There is one great chance for you, and one only," said the old man, hurrying along beside the younger one. "I am convinced in my own mind that Rufus Cridge has killed this girl. You have already told me how she mistook you for him when she brought you out of that place in which you were im- prisoned. Dying, she has made that blunder again, and so put you in peril of your life. But if you can get away, with the help of friends and Money, this man, in his poverty- stricken condition, may be forced to give himself up—may confess—anything may hap- pen. It is imperative that the way, at least, shall be left clear for the finding of Rufus Cridge. It is not unlikely, indeed, that he may come back to the scene of the murder and so may be taken almost redhanded. If that happened, the seal is taken from my lips. I could no longer prevent the story be- coming known." "I don't like running away," said Baxen- dale. "It's a coward's game at the best, and a foolish one at the worst. But I quite see that it wouldn't do to face that mob in the temper they'll be in. None the less, I mean to give myself up, no matter what efforts you may use to hide me." If you like to be obstinate enough to put your neck in a noose on your own account, John Baxendale, that's your affair, and yours only," said the old man, a little sternly; "but for the moment I'm going to do the best I can for you. Those people have reached the wood by now, from the silence that seems to have fallen upon them. They'll .cry a different tune presently. Come along!" So they hurried along in the direction of the cottage, hearing behind them again the roar of voices, and seeing the flashing of lan- terns among the trees. Baxendale walked like a man in a dream. It did not seem pos- sible that to-night he was treading roads and paths he had walked in peace and security all these years. John Baxendale a hunted man, with those who knew him beet hungering to 'put a rope about his neck! The thing seemed impossible. They came to the cottage, and there burst unceremoniously upon Mies Dorcas Stubbs. From that point all the business had to be gone through again—of hurried explanations that were not explanations at all; while it had to be impressed upon the lady that John Baxendale, whom she had known all this time as a quiet and respectable citizen, lately betrothed to her niece, was accused of mur- der, and was a very-much-wanted man. But some explanation was given at last, and arrangements were hurriedly made for John Baxendale to stay there for that night

at least, until they could (Weide what was beat to be done. Dick Munby and the lawyer were for setting out at once for Baxendale Hall, but, on reflection, decided that it would be beet to remain where they were for the present. "The mob will have gone straight to the Hall," said Felix Goode, "and they will be in a queer temper. I'm not disposed, re a friend of John Baxendale, to meet them. Let them roar their wrath away and cool down." "I entirely agree with you," said Dick. "Jack's eafe for the time at least. We can afford to let matters alone." John Baxendale nothing, but he was thinking long thoughts. It occurred to him that in this matter he had some responsi- bility; that there were servants at the 4great heuts43 who must not be exposed to any dan- pr, and who must, • above all things, under- stand that their master, John Baxendale, was so coward, to skulk out of the light of day, or to shew a clean pair of heels when all men were crying out for him. He knew that strong oppcsition would be put in his why if he suggested returning to Baxendale Hall, 'Dut he was none the lcs6 determined to go here all the 'same. He only awaited an op- portunity to clip away. Meanwhile, that wretched, haunted crea- ture, his brother. had failed to adopt the sug- gestion made by Johanna Cridge, and to get away. In the trst place, he was drawn back to the scene of his crime by a dreadful fasci- nation—tortured by wondering what had be- come of the body, and whether it had been discovered, and whether the lie written above it had had any effect so far as covering him self was concerned. He feared to go back, and yet was drawn as by a magnet, and so compromised matters by stealing back to that little inn, wherein he knew that Amos Voles and Saul Tuttle were to be found. He found them with little difficulty, and discovered also that they regarded him somewhat shyly. However, he had much to tell them, and he plunged into the matter boldly enough. "'Well," he said, roughly, I suppose, my saintly ones, that you shudder at the mere sight of me, don't you?" He laughed, and clapped AlllO6 Voles on the back, for, after the fears that had shaken him, it was good to have some_man trembling before him. _ _ _

"Not exactly -that, dear boy," said Mr. Voles. "But you've put yourself in a tight place, you know." "I've done nothing of the kind," he re- torted. "I've put another man in a tight place, if you like, a man who's going to swing in place of me. John Baxendale is doomed, ii ever a man was doomed yet. Listen to me. I'll tell you the whole story." So he told them, all that had happened, told them also of that strange writing on the tree. And. greatly daring in the end, he made a proposition to them. "Now, look heie," he said, "you may be sure that Mother Cridge will see to it that the real John Baxendale knows what has hap- pened. You may safely leave the matter in her hands. Very well, then, what happens? John Baxendale, for the sake of his own skin, will fly, and the way is left open for me. Oh, I'm not going back to the Baxendale disguise, believe me, but I'm going to see what can be picked up at Baxendale Hall while the master is out. of the way. I know one snug corner where banknotes are locked away, and there are lots of things that one can slip into one's pockets quietly. More than that, boys "—he spoke genially, for he was in desperate need of friends and 'of support just then—"more than that, you shall share with me. Every- one will be flying after John Baxendale; this is our rare chance." _

"But what are you going to do, Rufus?" asked Saul Tuttle, with a shiver. "I don't 'alf like mixin' meself up with this Baxen- dale business." "Fool!'" exclaimed Rufus Cridge, roughly. "Who's asking you to mix yourself up in the business at all? I tell you they'll all be look- ing for Baxendale, and Baxendale flying for his life. I mean to get into the place and take whatever's to be found. You used to be spry enough at that game. Come on!" So that worthy trio set off across country for Baxendale Hall—Rufus Cridge, with the spirit of recklessness in him buoyed up a little by certain potations • he had taken at the inn, and the others following wonder- ingly, urged on by their natural cupidity, and yet dreading what the upshot might be. In due course they came, as Baxendale and his friend had done, to the edge of the wood, and saw, somewhat to their astonishment, the moving lights among the trees, and heard the

murmur of many voices. "Wot's up?" demanded Mr. Voles, peer- ing into the darkness. "Wot's the game?" "It means, my friends, that they have found what was left in the wood," replied Rufus, not too steadily. "It's a merry game this. Before we can say 'Jack Robinson' they'll be clamouring at the door of Baxen- ,lale Hall for the man who killed Bella Ogden. Ha! ha! it's a merry game! But we'll be before them!"

- He started to run to the house, calling to them to follow, for he saw in this something that should distract the attention of everyone from the place, for a time, at least. And of that time he meant to make the most.

But Mr. Voles was of a cautious nature, and Saul Tuttle timorous. So that, as a mat- ter of fact, Rufus Cridge ran on alone, and his followers, looking into each other's faces, decided that the game, with this changed aspect upon it, was scarcely worth the candle. In other words, they slunk away and started back for the inn they had left. Meanwhile, Rufus Cridge went on to the house, with his courage high for the game before him. Every lawless instinct the man possessed was roused. He had burnt his boats, and nothing worse could happen to him than that which threatened him if the truth were known. But he would not go empty-handed, if by good luck he could manage to escape. It was his to burn, and wreck, and destroy in this hour when every- thing had come to a crisis for him or for John Baxendale. -Above all, he told himself that with his cunning he might be able to escape and still not go empty-handed. Of a sudden he found, as he ran, that the mob was roaring at his heels. Some man had stood beside, the body of the dead girl, and had pointed to her epitaph, and so, naturally, to Baxendale Hall. And women who had daughters and men who had child- ren roared for John Baxendale, and did not mean to be denied. The years were swept away—wiped clean as a slate might be wiped. This man had spilt the blood of a young girl, and ordinary human nature rose up in arms against him; Urged by one or two, they set off for the Hall, crying for John Baxendale as they ran. _ _

The creature who ran -before them glanced back over his shoulder and scented sport, and ran harder yet. Outdistancing them, he came to the place, and entered as he had entered once before. He slipped through the shadows of the house, now and then al- most brushing against a frightened servant, who called out to know who he was in the darkness, and then ran on again to rouse others. So he came to the room he sought, and closed the door and sank down into a chair, exhausted but triumphant. "Ye gods, what a run!" he exclaimed. "Well, they'll bar the doors, and I'm safe Cor a time at least. When they've finished shouting, and have gone home to their beds, I can clear and get away. I'll have a drink first—and the money afterwards. Keys are hardly necessary on such an occasion as this; there's a shorter way." He seized the poker from the fireplace, and wrenched open a cupboard and got out spirits and glasses ; , went to the desk, and burst that open and crammed his. pockets with the banknotes and with the little gold that was there. Then, in a spirit of bravado, he poured out drink for himself and lit a cigar and listened to the uproar outside. It seemed that some of the servants were parleying with the mob from the windows, dethanding to know what .was wanted, or what the uproar was about. One stentorian voice outside roared for John Baxendale, and cried his crime to the stars; and the fright- ened servants said they &new nothing of him, and that the man was not there. And still the shouting and the clamour went on; and at last there came an ominous battering at the groat doors of Baxendale Hall. "It's as good as a play!" exclaimed Rufus Cridge, seated on the table in the smoking- room, with a glass in one hand and at cigar in the other. "John Baxendale's a dead'un, and I get away with something to line my pockets. Hammer away, you does! Ira a

nine ana merry wortu, alut the rogues come out on top!" He stopped suddenly and twisted round on the table as the door was flung open, and a man reelied in. The man was John Baxen- dale, who,* true to his promise to face the matter, had slipped aeiny from the cottage and come back to the hall. Coming thus as- toeufFnely face to face with his brother, he hesitated for a Moment while the noise went on outside, and then clapped to the door and faced the other man. "So here you are!" he exclaimed voice that was scarcely heard above the clamour. "You've put your head into the lien's den to-night! By heaven, I'll give you over to tilos?, wolves outside! There's the stain of blood upee -you, and they shall wipe it out with ,your death. Come out to them!" • Scarcely knowing what he did Baxendale flung himself upon the other man, and in a moment they were fighting desperately, now here and now there, about the room, with the table overturned, and with each striking blindly at each other, with scarce a word between them. The opportunity came for Cridge to strike a blow, and to dart past the other man and out of the room. He made a dash for the staircase, but John Baxenclale, crying madly .to those outside to break down the door, rushed after him, and grappled with him in a room above, 60 that they fought, desperately there, -until at last Rufus Cridge, getting away from him, seized a chair and stood at bay. "What are you going to do?" he de- manded, panting heavily and watching the )ther man.
m going to give you over to them. I'm going to tell them what I know, and who you are," exclaimed Baxendale. "You killed that girl, and left her lying in the woode there."

"Yee, I killed her, and you'll die for it!" cried ' the other. "Come, my brother, we meet face to face, let's see who's the better ->q an at the last!" The room was John Baxendale's bedcham- oer, and a tall, old-fashioned lamp had been set beside the bed, lighted in expectation of return. Before Buxendale could move Cridge dropped the chair . and seized the lamp, whirled it round his head, and flung it straight at .the other man. Baxendale sprang aside, and the thing crashed against the win- -inw, and in a moment it seemed that the T.....fut was ablaze. Once more Cridge darted nut of the room, and dashed across the cor- --r.or into another. In the blinding smoke mat. filled the place John Baxendale rushed after him.

In some fashion that was afterwards a mys- tery to him, Baxendale got out of the house. He had a dim notion that he swung himself out of a window at the back, and climbed down the thick growth of ivy, and so reached the ground. The crowd was round at the front, crying excitedly, now that they had seen John Baxendale at a window, and now that the place was ablaze, and that some- thing must be done to save it—this latter from those with cooler heads than their fel- lows. Baxenclale slipped round, under cover of the darkness, and watched from a distance.

And then suddenly at an upper window, round which the flames were licking, he ,saw himself, as it seemed, standing in the lurid light, while a great howl of execration went up from the mob. Rufus Cridge, standing there amid the very flames as it seemed, wrs shriekipg like a madman, and hurling any- thing on which he could lay his hands down on to the people below. "Baxendale! To the deuce with Baxen- dale!" he shouted above all the roar of voices below, and so seemed to fall back into the flames. John Baxendale, with his arm over his eyes to shut out the eight, ran on blindly through the. trees, going he knew not (To be continued.)

div.head: HIS FATHER'S SON.
div.p: HIS FATHER'S SON.
BY TOM GALLON
'Author of " Tatterley," "Dicky Monteith,q "Kiddy," "A Rogue in -Love," "Fate's Beg. gar Maid," Tho Charity Ghost," &o,
CHAPTER VIII.

For a moment or two that strange little group were gathered there, in the light of the Lantern, about the dead girl, and for that mo- ment or two, after the declaration as to who Johanna Cridge was, there fell a silence upon them. For the whole situation was BO extra- ordinary; and so much it seemed, indeed, that they had come to the end here of that strange business that had gone on for five- and-twenty years, that it was difficult to know who was to speak first. In all those years Felix Goode had seen nothing of this extra- ordinary woman, and he was puzzled now to know exactly in what position she stood to the dead girl, or, indeed, what new plot this might be for the undoing of John Baxendale. The fact that she was there seemed to indi- cate clearly that Rufus Cridge was at the bottom of this business; and, in any case, Felix Goode would have hesitated to con- demn .John Baxendale. Yet there was the writing upon the tree, and here was the dead girl at his feet. "Whose work is this?" he asked, in a hushed voice. "Read for yourself," she replied. "John Baxendale is the man." "I don't believe it—l won't believe it!" exclaimed the old man. "Come, there must be no bandying words between us," he went on, more sternly. "You know whose work this is. You know well that John Baxendale knows nothing about it." She got slowly to 'her feet and strode across to where the old man was standing. The servant, at a whispered command from Felix Goode, had set off for the house. He had been told to be silent for the present, but there was small prospect of his following that injunction. Johanna Cridge looked at the old man for a moment, and then spoke in a low tone. "I tell you I know that John Baxendale killed that girl," she said, pointing with her stick to the body. "Doubtless, with that clever, legal mind of yours, you'll invent something that shall enable him to slip tout of it. Perhaps you'll have something to say" —her voice had sunk to a whisper—', of another man." _

"Yes," he answered at once. "And you know the other man I mean. You've kept him out of the way for all these years, Johanna Cridge, but I see you have not trained him for nothing." "There never was another man," she re- plied, steadily. "John Baxendale and Rufus Cridge are one and the same." He uttered an exclamation as he realised to the full extent the meaning of her words. "What are you talking about?" he de- manded, harshly. "You know that Rufus Cridge, as you have called him all these years, killed this girl." "I don't deny it," she broke in, quietly. "Rufus Cridge did kill the girl, but his other name is John Baxendale. The girl knew him as John Baxendale, that's why she wrote that." She pointed again to the tree. "But whether he calls himself John Baxendale or Rufus Cridge matters to no one, he's got to answer for his crime." _ _

The old man looked helplessly at Dick Munby, and at the dead girl, and back again to .the old woman, then he answered quickly, and yet with almost a frightened gasp to ac- company the words: "But you know that there were two men. You know you took the one, and kept him, according to your threat, to train for your own vile purposes." "la deny it," she replied. "I have known the one man for years past, and I have known that he was John Baxendale. To me and to others about me he has called himself Rufus Cridge. That's the whole matter." The old man paced about for a moment or two with the lantern swinging from his hand. At last he faced the woman again. "And do you really mean to tell that story?" he asked. "I do," she replied. "More thip that, there are others I can call, .who will /be wit- ness to the fact that John Baxendale and Rufus Cridge are one and the same person. My man of law, you have matched your wits against those of a woman," she added, in a lower tone, t` and the woman wine. You'd better go away, and leave that poor thing lying there. She'll be found in due course. Unless "—she added, • tauntingly—" you'd like to summon assistance yourself and let that writing be seen ? " The old man looked at her helplessly. He realised that that vvri Ling had already been seen by those who would • spread the news. He understood that nothing he could do would prevent the catastrophe. Unless by a miracle, John Baxendale was doomed. Some other way of escape must be found, and that way would probably be, in the end, in the hands of Felix Goode. After all, he knew the otory and the secret, and in the proper time and place he could declare them. But in that her wit outmatched him; she seemed almost to read his thoughts. "You have no scrap of evidence that the other boy ever existed," she said, coming close to him and laying a hand on his arm. "One son of John Baxendale was registered, there is no record of any other. John Baxendale, in hie pride, did that. You needn't think I haven't Aearched the records, to be certain where I stood. The monster I brought up, and bred and taught, is a thing without a name or without a place in the world, save such name and such place as I gave him. There is only one John Baxendale, remember, and his re- cord is written by the dead girl." Felix Goode turned away. There was (nothing left for him to do. Dick came after him and whispered agitatedly in his ear: "You won't leave the dead girl there, sir ? " he pleaded. "It seems scarcely human to do it."

"She's past all help," said the old man. "Besides, if anyone connected with John Baxendale touches her it will only be another point against him. She will be found, and that, too, in a very short time, if I'm not mis- taken. Leave the dead, it's the living we have to think of. John Baxendale stands in peril of his life, he and we must decide what is best to be done."

"You're a lawyer • you should know," said Dick, walking on beside him. "I'm a lawyer, and I don't know," re- torted the other. "This is beyond me. At one moment I am for urging him to give himself up at once, and let those whose business it is find out the meaning of that damning ac- cusation written by the dead girl; at another, I am for urging that he shall fly the country and let them find the other man—if they.can. Don't talk to me, I -want to think."

But there was to be small time even for thought. Horribly and incongruously enough they heard, before they had gone twenty yards from the dead girl, a peal of light, happy laughter from the living, and towards them through the trees came Evelyn and John Baxendale, laughing and chatting like boy and girl together. They cried out, and waved their hands when they saw the two men. But Felix Goode _put up a hand to stop them, and, above all, to hold them back from that towards which they were ad- vancing. "For heaven's sake, be silent!" ex- claimed the old man. "This is no time nor place for laughter." "Why, what do you mean?" asked John Baxendale, his mirth gone in a moment. "What's wrong?" "Miss Baylor," said Felix Goode, taking the girl's hand and speaking with infinite gentleness, "I want you to let Mr. Munby take you back to your aunt's house. There is something I have to say to John, something of vital importance." • "Bad news!" she exclaimed, glancing quickly at her lover. "If there's bad news, Mr. Goode, I want to know what it is. You would not have me desert him. would You?"

div.head: PLAN FOR THE LITTLE ONES.
div.p: A PLAN FOR THE LITTLE ONES.

Acorns have been shed in great numbers all. over the country and the litte ones may have a pretty little ornament for their windows by trying this plan, says "Farm and Home." Get a well-ripened acorn, and suspend it by means of a string over a bottle containing a little water (or there are glasser, like very small hyacinth glasses, that can be obtained for the purpose). Let the pointed end, not the broad, be towards the water. Then wrap it up by in a dark place for a month or six weeks, by which time roots will have begun to form. Add a little more water, and bring the plant gradually to the light. Soon a tiny shoot will start upwards, and later you will have ieaves, so that there is a miniature oak growing in the bottle. It is really very pretty, and its growth is interesting to watch.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

Censuelo Duchess of Manchester.—The death of Consuelo Duchess of Manchester at the early age of fifty-one, removes a lady who was a popular member of Society, and a personal friend of the King and Queen. The daughter of a wealthy Cuban gentleman she was one of the first of the many American ladies who have married into the British aristocracy. As a girl she figured among the most beautiful debutantes in Society in New York, and when little more than eighteen married Lord Mandeville, oldest son of the seventh Duke of Manchester and his Duchess, who is still living. and is now the twice-widowed Louise Duchess of -Devonshire. Lord Mandeville succeeded to the Dukedom of *Manchester in 1890, and died in 1892 leaving a son and twin daughters, but unhappily the late Duchess suffered a great bereavement by the deaths of her two daughters in their early teens. Her son the present Duke of Manchester, married an American lady —Miss Helena' Zimmerman—in 1900, and has three young children. The late Duchess was a brilliant pianist,the Queen being a great admirer of her playing. She was also a gifted linguist, and was always in request at Court, and at country house parties, especially when distinguished foreign guests were being enter- tained. _ _

An 111-Omened Jewel.—That an inanimate object may bring misfortune on its owner, is one of the oldest of superstitutions, and it would certainly seen that the famous coloured gem known as the" Hope" or "Blue" diamond has brought a curse on its owners. It was first sold to Louis XIV. of France by Tavernier, who afterwards became completely ruined and died of yellow fever. It passed successively into the bands of carious people, of whom it is said that at least fifteen died violent deaths, and that five or six more suffered imprisonment or ruin after possessing it. Its penulti- mate owner was Abdul Hamid, ex-Sultan of Turkey,who , has since fallen on evil days. while his Court favourite, ho had charge of his jewels was one of those banged by the Reformers in the ;trees of Constantinople. This, however, is not the end of the sinister history of this jewel. It was bought in June last for £BO,OOO by Habib Effendi, a Persian dealer in precious stoves, who put it up to auction. It fetched only £16,000, and was bought back by Habib who, it is now confirmed, was among those who perished to the French mail steamer La Seyne lost in a collision off Singapore. There is some doubt as to whether he had the " Hope " diamond on board with him, but, if it has another owner, the next one will want some courage to defy the ill- omened record of this seemingly fatal jewel. The General Election.—Many people are pulling long faces over the dislocation of Christmas trade and social engagements, by the impending General Election. It will probably be found that there is less reason than is supposed for this apprehension. Certain interests will suffer, and it will be bad for theatrical managers and pantomime productions. There are, however, only two pantomimes in the West End of London this year, and not to many as usual in the suburban houses; so that it looks as if this form of entertainment were becoming less in demand in the Metropolis. But there is no reason to suppose that the sborkeepers will suffer from an unsatisfactory Christmas trade. After all, people must. eat, feast, and dress, all the same, end parents will not allow politics to spoil their children's Christmas. On the other band, the general election will keep many people at home, who usually go to the Alps or the Riviera for Christmas and the early winter, and there is no particular need for us to abed tears over the fact that there will be fewer visitors to foreign winter resorts this season.

More Suffragism.—There will be some compensation for the Unionists, their leaders in particular, if they are defeated at the general election. Mrs. Pettrick Lawrence assured the Liberals the other day, that their experiences of the past four years would he as nothing in comparison with what the Conservatives would have to undergo if they came into power. This would be particularly hard upon Mr. Balfour who, with several members of his family, is a believer in Woman Suffrage. The Liberals have been chastised with whips, but it seems the Tories will be scourged with scorpions. Hard Winter Foretold.—The early touch of winter this year, has not only set people thinking of Christmas but has encouraged the exports to predict a season of unusual severity. There are people who, every autumn see signs of a severe winter, but this year, we are told that one is duo according to the law of averages, and that the existing conditions are the same as thcse that have generally preceded such visitations. These, it is raid, have mostly supervened on a wet and chilly summer, and them are other conditions which strengthen the expectation of a hard winter. Apparently our only hope lies in the fact that there is much that is doubt- lid and uncertain in tho history and science of meteorology. Dress for Winter Weddings.—lt has frequently been remarked of late that many more guests appear at the reception than the Church, and the explanation given is as follows :—One can never be sure whether the toilette selected for a winter wedding will be worn in Church by natural or artificial light, and considerable difficulties therefore attend the sblection of colours. For instance it is an easy matter in these days of an artificially-lighted apartment in all large emporiums, to choose a pink, a green, or a blue, that looks well by day, and another that looks well by night, but such colours rarely look well on both occasions. Therefore, when wearing a shade more suitable for natural light, guests very frequently avoid the Church, and proceed straight to the reception where they are more sure of looking their best. Jewellery in the Daytime.—With regard to the wear- ing of jewellery by day, we have completely changed i our views of late. It sno uncommon thing to note the wearer of a simple morning tailor-made costume, exhibiting earrings, brooches, chains. bracelets, and rings, in considerable profusion, a state of affairs that would have been deemed impossible a year or so ago. Smart dressers too think nothing of adding a chain of diamonds, or a rope of pearls, to an afternoon toilette, and a fashionable reception is a very glittering affair indeed. It cannot be said that this move is one in the right direction. In the morning, much jewellery strikes a jarring note, while ropes of pearls, chains of diamonds and masses of other ornaments in the after- noon afford the impression of vulgarity. We can only hope that our ideas upon the point will change again, and that we shall speedily return to more simple, and refined ways. Gifts for Christmas.—Tho seeker after home-made Christmas gifts should not overlook the new handker- chief sachet, whicir is this year much larger than formerly—quite square, and divided into four pockets. The notion is undoubtedly of tho time-saving persuasion, for instead of searching through a whole, heap of handkerchiefs it is possible, by means of the , divisions described, to light upon the class required in a moment. There is for instance the morning hand- kerchief, quite simple and plain, the afternoon ' specimen more ornamental, the evening one very dainty and delicate; and those exquisite creations only drawn from their perfumed nest upon very special °cessions. A little scented wool should be inserted in every sachet, and of course the covering can be as ornate or simple as may be desired. Pretty Paper Goods.—ln many ways paper now replaces linen, and the daintiest possible tray cloths and cake d'oleys are being offered, bearing borders in imitation of Teneriffe work, or insets of simulated lace. Then there are the most charming little d'oyleys for dessert, made of soft, silky paper, hand-painted with flowers add delicate foliage. But the newest invention of all is the paper window blind, with its insets and edgings of laco. These blinds are said to clean per- fectly, and last but by no means least, they are marked already at extraordinarily low figures. MADGIC.

div.head: WHAT IS GOD?
div.p: WHAT IS GOD?

This is a question of vital importance tl the Churches, one thai goes to the foundations upon which the fabric of our religious belief is built. .Now that the forces of materialism are hammering at the very root of the Christian Church it is time that we should have some definite and authoritative statement as to our position. Therefore the book which is about to be issued by the National Free Chnrch Council under the title of " The Christian Conception of God" will make a timely and welcome appearance. There are few men who have the Mental and spiritual equipment necessary for the production of such a treatise, but none will deny that Principal Adeney of Lancashire College, Manchester, is fitted in ovary way to be the author of this book. It was a happy inspiration that induced Rev, F. B. Meyer, the editor of the series of which "The Christian Conception of God" is to form a unit to place the writing of the book into such capable , hands.

• -PLACING or LAMPS.—At the meeting of the Runcorn Rural District Council on Tuesday the Clerk said that at a meeting of the Private Street Works Committee they had considered the justification of placing lamps in Victoria-road and the planting of trees before the road was made under the Private Stree-t Works Act. They had recommended the placing of 42 lamps before the road was commenced. Mr. Pilling proposed the adoption of the report Mr. Mynekyme seconded and it was agreed to.

div.head: Penketh.
div.p: Penketh.

LANTERN LECTURE.—On Sunday evening a lantern lecture was given in the Wesleyan Sunday School after service was over in the chapel. The lecture which cemmenced at eight o'clock was the first of its kind and was held under the auspices of the Wesley Guild Mission band) and through the energetic work of Mr. Wolfencroft the Secretary, the room Cr4S well filled. The meeting was opened with a hymn after which the Rev. H. W. Kernick. M.A., offered prayer. Mi. J. G Withenshaw pre..iided and in a few remarks said the object of the meeting was to get those people to come that were not in the habit of attending any place of worship. He gave all such a hearty invitation to become members of the chapel. A quartette from the Penketh Tannery Baud then pland a selection the following being the players: Messrs. b, Dobson, G -Carman, A. Bowyer, and D. Massey. The Rev. F. W. Kernick then lectured on "The Life of the Apostle Paul " this being the first set of pictures.—The quartette then played- another selection after which pictures were thrown on the screen illustrating" Tbe Life of Christ." Mr. Kernick proved himself. to be not only a good preacher but a most able lecturer. Mrs. Keraiok also sang a solo in a very tasteful manner The hymn" Abide with Me was then sung while a collection was being taken to defray the expenses of the slide. Mr. James Woodward had kindly given his ,ervices in working the lanter n.

LANTERN 1./WTI:UM-1n connection with the Wesley Guild on Wednesday evening a very interesting lectute was given in the Sunday School by Mr. Congreve of Moore. The subject was "A voyage through the Nogolk Broads." The lecturer, who is thoroughly acquainted with the history of places thrown on the screen, gave a most interesting account of the same and through the excellent slides provided a very entertain- ing evening for all who had the good fortune to be present. The Rev. F. W. Kernick, M.A. presided and was supported by Mrs. Robert Garnett. A very hearty vote of thanks was proposed to the lecturer also to Mr. James Woodward who was in charge of the lantern by Mr. J. G. Withinshaw seconded by Mr. Midwood.

Throughout the United Kingdom and also the British Colonies it would be difficult to find a village, or even a street of over twenty houses, in which there do not reside persons who frankly state that they owe their present good health to the old and world-famous remedy, Mother Seigel's Syrup. The extent to which this well-known remedy is used s the regular family medicine, for all those troublesome ailments which arise from stomach or liver disorder, would be surprising were it not for the fact that this root and herb extract has established itself as a popular favourite, by reason of the remarkable cures it has effected all over the world. Here are two cases in point :
A young Irish soldier named David Murray, who lives at Todd's Row, Com- ber, County Down, Ireland, writing to the Proprietors of Mother Seigel's Syrup, on May sth, 1909, says:—

down the food I did eat. When I had taken the medicine for about a week, I was quite well again, and have remained so from that day to this. I took less than one bottle of the Syrup and still have the remainder of it by' me. I feel very grateful for the good I got from your medicine."

"I have thought that you might like to know about a very remarkable cure of Indigestion due to Mother Seigel's Syrup. It was my own case. In the Autumn of 1907 I fell ill and could not make out what was the matter with me. My appetite, which had always been good, became very poor; sometimes for several days at a time I would eat a mere nothing. 'When I did eat a little food, it nearly always caused me dreadful pains in the chest and stomach. So .1 had to choose between pain and starvation. " After a while I became so weak that I was fit for nothing but lying about and dozing. Then a new trouble came upon me, and my stomach would not keep down the food for more than a few minutes. No matter what I ate, it caused me to vomit almost at once. While in this condition, acting on medical advice, I took a mixture which relieved me a good deal. I thought I was all right then, but, bless you! in a day or two I was as bad again as ever.

An equally striking case is that of Mrs. Douch, of 45, Middle Street, Hastings. In a letter dated April 20th, 1909, she says, amongst other things : "About thirteen years ago I began to suffer from Indigestion. Shortly after every meal I would be taken by an awful pain at the chest, as if I were being suffocated, and this would go on, becoming more violent every minute, until I vomited. Then relief would come; but it would last only until I had eaten again, and then the misery would be repeated. I became wretchedly ill and weak, and had careful medical attendance, but nothing seemed to help me. "That was the condition I was in when I tried Mother Seigel's Syrup, and its efiect upon me was wonderful. After taking a few. doses of the Syrup I could eat with no dread of pain to follow, and by the time I had taken two bottles I was entirely cured.

_ "It was through reading the newspaper that I came to know about Mother Seigel's Syrup. According to what I read, some of the people that medicine has cured, suf- fered very much the same as I did. So I made up my mind to try it, and bought a bottle. I had not taken more than three doses when I began to feel better, and the appetite for food returned. I could keep

_ "During the thirteen years which have passed since my cure, I have several times taken Mother Seigel's Syrup, not for quit.: the same purpose but as a sort of 'pick- me-up,' as I regard it as a grand tonic. It braces one up in a marvellous way. I wouldn't be without it."

These letters are typical of tens of thousands received by the Pro- prietors of.. Mother Seigel's Syrup, and their genuineness can easily be proved by anyone who will take the trouble to do so. To any fair-minded person they cannot fail to establish the merit of this old family medicine. Indeed. the very fact that Mother Seigel's Syrup with its record of over forty years unbroken success, has stood the severest of all tests—the test of time— should convince the most sceptical that there is some great merit or quality in this root and herb extract which is not found in any other medicine known to the public, and which accounts for its world-wide popularity and success in curing disorders of the stomach and liver.

GRAND OPERA AT THE ASYLITM.--WallaCe'S famous opera " Maritana" was performed at the County Asylum lust Friday evening by the Mendelssohn Grand Opera Company of Salford. The following was the cast : Don Ctesar, Mr. Philip Howard ; Don Jose, Mr. Owen Grant; Marquis de Montellori, Mr, Fred Morgan, jun. ; King of Spain, Mr. W. Barton-Berwick • Alcade,Mr. T. Bennett -, Captain of Guard, Mr. MI Fortesque ; Lazarillo and Ma rchioness de Montefiori, Miss Mary Jones ; Maritana, Miss Edith Mostyn. Miss Mostyn scored a great success in the title part, her rendering of ." Scenes that are brightest "or evoking rounds of applause. Miss Mary Jones as Lazarillp, the poor boy, sang with great expession " Alas ! thoge chimes." Mr. Philip Howard was a dashing Don Cesar.

div.head: Orford.
div.p: Orford.

OLD Boys' ASBOCIATIOS.—The seventh annual dinner in connection with this association was held in the schools 'last evening week, about forty members attending. The catering of Atkinsons' Cafe, Ltd., gave every satisfaction. After dinner the election of officers took place. Mr. Cann, the schoolmaster, was again unanimously appointed president: Councillor Steel, hon. treasurer; and Mr. T. Reddish, hon. secretary. The following were appointed the cornmittees : Messrs. R. Andrews, W. J. Woods, T. Attwell, G. ILW. Steel, G. Higham, W. Povey, G. Ball, S. J. Antrobus, J. Willett., T. Williams, and W. Attwell. Councillor Steel presented the secretary with a smokers' cabinet in recognition of his valuable services. The following toasts were honoured :—" The Past and Present Managers." by Councillor Steel ; 'The Old Boys," hz the Rev. G. Vale Owen.; and" The President" by Mr. W. Attwell. Mr. Steel said it had come to his notice within the last few days that the newly-appointed headmaster of Rugby had been taught mathematics as a boy by Mr. Cann (Aoplause). Daring the evening songs were rendered by Mr. T. Attwell, Mr. Reddish and Mr. H. Clare, while Mr. Sutton contributed some capital humorous selections. Mr. R. Hatublett was the accompanist.

div.head: Stockton Heath.
div.p: Stockton Heath.

CHILD'S SUDDEN DEATH.—An inquest was held by Mr. T. Ridgway on Monday, touching the death of Hugh Sharpe Ashton, the ten=montbs-old son of Hugh Ashton, lanndry engineer, residing at 15, Leonaid- street, Stockton Heath.—The lather said his son was perfectly well last week. About 8 a.m. on Sunday Mrs. Ashton and witness were dressing when they heard their son make a noise as though gasping for breath. His face went a eark purple colour. The face was not covered. Witness told his wife to go to INlrs.Brereton's opposite, to see if she could do any thing for the child. She did so but it was found that life was extinct.—Dr. George Binns, Stockton Heath, said that death was due to natural causes and the jury returned a verdict to that effect.

WESLEY GUILD.—The annual weekly meeting of the Wesley Guild was held on Tuesday last when a lantern lecture was given by Dr. Bennett on "Ireland and tne Irish," Some very picturesque views of the Emerald Isle were thrown on to the screen aud the vivid description of the land and the people given by the lecturer were much appreciated. The Rev. T. Gladding occupied the chair and Mr. F. Appleton was the lanternist.

div.head: Moore.
div.p: Moore.

"THE QUAKERS."—On Wednesday evening in con- nection with the Wesley Guild, the Rev. Thomas Gladding gave a very interesting account of the history of Quakerism" and its many excentricities, also a character sketch of George Fox the founder of the movement. Many amusing stories were told of the early days of" Quakerism," but in spite of the many eccentricities there are many characteristics of the Quaker which we should do well to copy to-day. There was a very good attendance and Mr. R. H. INleldrum presided. At the close a very hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Gladding for his highly interesting and profitable paper was proposed by Mr. 1. Lawton, and seconded by Mr. Davies, and carried unanimously. DILAPIDATED FOOTPATH.—At the meeting of the Runcorn Rural District Council on Tuesday, Mr. Broome drew attention to the footpath across the fields from Moore to Daresbury, which he said was in a very dilapidated condition.—Mr. Jones said that if it were allowed to remain in such a state there would be accidents, especially in foggy weather.—The Clerk said that if the Parish Council were willing to spend the money of the parish on an improvement they could do so.—Mr.Broome : It is really for the benefit of the Moore people? (Laughter).—Mr. Jones to Mr. Broome: It is for your liabilities though.—Mr. Jones (to the clerk) what about the landowner ?—The Clerk said that if the landowner, on being informed, did not put the footpath right the public had the authority to walk alongside the path on the field*—Vir. Pilling : They will get drowned. (Laughter.)—The part of the footpath which is alleged to be in the worst condition is near a. brook.

Lyaun. CONGREGATIONAL GuILD.—On Thursday evening the Congregational Guild held a devotional n,eating. The Speaker for the evening was Mr. J. D. B. Smith, his subject being " Music" Mr. J. H. !Joh engaged in prayer. Mrs. C. Lewis rendered a solo "Count your many blessings," the accompanist for the evening beihg Mr. P. N. Leather. About 35 members assembled and a very interesting and helpful evening was spent. MISSIgNARY SERVICES.—The annual missionary ser- vi,ces were held in the Congregational Church on Sunday last. The preacher in the morning was the Rev. G. Parker' who went out to Travencore, Southern India, a few years ago. He gave a very good 'address an the work that was going on out there, mhich was much appreciated by the congregation.—ln the evening the Rev. C. E. Watson, the former raster of the church, preached to a full congregation. rin visit was quite a surprise, and afforded much pleasure. Collections in aid of the Missionary Funds were taken both in church and Sunday school, the school collections realizing over

LTMM CRICKET CLUB.—An excellent concert took place in the Drill Hall on Wednesday evening, in aid of the above club. A very good audience attended and thoroughly enjoyed the items tendered. The star of the evening was Miss A. Backsbeen Wood, who played on her violin in a most masterful manner the following two pieces: fantasie "Faust " and "Tarantelle." Mr. John McCabe (tenor) rendered "I seek for thee in every flower" r.nd "For all eternity," and was warmly applauded. Madame Gwladys Williams recited, 'The old maid," "The progress of madness" and "Wilfred Denver's dream" from the "Silver King:" This was rendered with much feeling and was enjoyed immensely. Miss Florence E. Browne tastefully sang "April morn," Scent of the " "Orange blossom," "The rose garden." Mr. G. W. Nicholson greey amused the audience with his "Laughing song," and his character sketch "The old folks polka" and other humorous items which he gave with much zest, Mr. Herbert Morris was the accompanist. The members of the cricket club are to be congratulated on the way in which the concert was carried out. it was a success in every way. LYMM COUNCIL. _

The monthly meeting of the Lyram Urban District Council was held on Thursday evening. Mr. 0. G. Smith presided and there were present :—Rev. G. B. Thurston, Messrs. S. Davies, IL H. Gotobed, T. H. Warburton, F. 0. Moston, W. Ewart, W. G. Groves, W. Mullard (clerk), W. L. Donaldson (gas manager), D. Mort (surveyor), Dr. De Jonge (medical officer).

Mr. Warburton said that two lamps bad been put up at Lymm-lane Crossings. Everyone, so tar as he could hear, seemed to he satisfied with the Railway Company for the way they had treated them.

ROADS COMMITFER. At a meeting held on November 18th the Surveyor prodnced his estimate for the maintenance of the mnin roads for the year from the Ist April, 1910, to 31st March, 1911, amounting to £692 les. 2d. The Council were recommended to approve of the estimate and that same be sent to the County Surveyor. At the same commiteee the Surveyor was directed to write and ask for an appointment with the L. N.-W. Railway Company Engineer on the ground to consider the proposed alterations to Railways, Curb and level of road.

div.head: SANITARY CONIMITTEF.
div.p: SANITARY CONIMITTEF.

At this Committee's meeting on the 18th November it was recommended that a guinea be paid to Mrs. Reid as an honorarium for extia services in connectiou with nursing patients at the Isolation Hospital. The minutes were agreed to. The Clerk read letters from " Lizzie Mostyn " "Wilfred Phillips " Mr, and Mrs. Cheetham,Ed% in arid Ellen Gilberts and Mary A. Kinsey and John Kinsey testifying to the excellent nulling and attendance at, the Hospital. The Chairman said it was very gratifying to see those notes. They were all ready for thanks when conscien- tiously bestowed. It. was desirable that their institu- tion should stand well in public opinion and he hoped it would do. The Rev.G.B. Thurston observed that the effect on the children was marvellous.

div.head: Culcheth.
div.p: Culcheth.

INDEPENDENT METHODIST CHAPEL.—A meeting of the Twiss Green Band of Hope was held in the school- room on Tuesday evening last, when a lantern enter- tainment was given by Mr. George Fenton, Miss Kenyon assisting with a reading. A small charge was made for admission, the proceeds being in aid of the Band of Hope expenses. CONCERT.—A grand concert under the auspices of the Leigh Friendly Co-operative Society was given in the Newchurch School on Thursday evening last.. The room was crowded and a capital. programme was gone through. Miss Miriam Charnock of Leigh, sang with exquisite taste "Three green Bonnets," and "Madam Dormette," being rewarded with an encore for the latter item. "Needles and pies" and "Flight of ages" were excellently sung by Mrs. H. Jackson, the latter receiving a well deserved encore. Mr. Brirratt Calvert gave excellent renderings of "Flight of ages" and "The' sailor's grave," but the star of the evening was Mr. R. Tyldesley, the celebrated Lancashire humorist of Leigh. is a great favourite in the village and hisk quaint patter and mannerisms along with his singing created roars of laughter and applause. His singing of' Me Me, Me" ens deservedly rewarded with an encore for which he gave "My word if I catch you bending." His song entitled " Bury Lane Band "was received with great enthusiasm and after repeated calls for an encore he gave "No, No, No." An address on" Co-operation" was given by Councillor Charles Aubrey of Leigh. He said be was pleased to be at Culcheth knowing what a successful branch shop they had there. It was in 1897 that a branch was first opened in the village and since then the cause had been one continued run of successes. They had a turnover of over £5,000 during the last six months in Culchoth shop alone. The society was in such a position to-day that was never dreamt of in the days of the pioneers of tho Co-operative movement. He said it was our duty as co-operators to do all we can to help thosa who sire in poorer circum- stances than we are. Until we recogn:se this we are failing in our duty not only as co-operators but as citizens of a great Empire. He wotld like to see more interest taken in the meetings by the Culchoth people. This is necessary to see that the affairs of the society are being carried on in a proper manner. In con- clusion he appealed to all preseht to unite in one brotherhood and establish a compound common- wealth to strive and further a better condition of things throughout the whole universe. A vote of thanks to the Chairman, speaker and artistes wit.; moved by Mr. Prescott and seconded by Mr. Peter Rirnmer. Mr. Prescott said that before Christmas the Leigh Society hoped to have a petrol waggon by which means they would be able to deliver to the outlying districts fresh goods which were necessary for the workingman's dinner. Mr. Luke Hunter of Leigh was the chairmen. and Mr. Hurdus of Leigh very ably officiated at the piano. A very en'oyable evening was brought to a close by the singing of the National Anthem.
