div.p: WARRINGTON.
Penny Popular Concert

Bold-street Schoolroom was again crowded on Saturday evening when a highly entertaining pro- gramme was submitted, Many of the items were of a humorous character, the sketch "In School," by the Bros. Crosse proving especially popular. A humorous duet. "the spider and the fly,' by Madame Edith Hopkinson and Bert Crosse, was well received and the song "Dear Homeland" was pleasingly given by Madame Edith Hopkinson. A quartette by the Excelsior Quartette, "Good-night, beloved," was sung in a very creditable manner and earned a hearty encore.
MOSELEYS FOOD.—" Made in a minute." Strongly recommended by the Medical Press and Medical men. Ask your doctor.—Advt.
Rev. E. G. E. Carleton and Welsh Dls- establishment.

In the course of a discussion on Welsh Disestablish- ment at the Liverpool Diocesan Conference on Tuesday, the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton thought it was rather a curious proposal that while property given for religious purposes since Nonconformity sprang into existence was not to be touched, the property given rrevious to that . time was going to be con- fiscated. The Christian spirit of the Christian religion was the raw material out of which all the charities were created, but Mr. Asquith wished to blot out these records, to make a great blank in history and to begin afresh. PEVERIL " FIRE GRATES still unsurpassed, Inspection invited.—J. S. GARLAND, Kitchen Range and stove Warehouse, 51 to 55, Bridge et, Warring. ton.—Advt. Warrington Man Drowned.

John Jackson, (67) of 259, Liverpool-road Warring- ton was drowned at Liverpool last Friday night. It appears that two hands of the steam flat Florida, lying in the Prince's Dock were in the cabin of the flat when they heard someone walking along the deck, followed immediately by a splash. They hurried on the deck and found that Jackson who was the master of the flat was in the water, having evi- dently fallen from the deck of the vessel. Sarkey obtained a boat-book and held up the man until his mate Tilby reached him in a small boat, When be was lifted on to the deck agatn he was in an unconscious condition, and although artificial respira- tion was resorted to he did not recover. He was afterwards removed to the Northern 11(vital, where life was found to be extinct.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.

RAILWAY MYSTERY.—ECHO OF A TRAGEDY. Mr. Brighouse resumed the inquest at Burtonwood on Wednesday on Edith Cooke, of Station-road, Haydock, whose mutilated body was found on the Liverpool and Manchester rain line, near Collins Green Station on Sunday the 7th inst. The body was only identified a few minutes before the inquest was opened a fortnight ago. Dr. Unsworth had singe made a post-mortem examination. He skid that both ankles were dislocated, and there was a large wound in the middle of the back, which had evidently been caused by a very severe blow by a large blunt instrument. The skull was smsshed the neck WAS broken, and there were other injuries. The Coroner asked if witness had ever seen a cue like this, of a body being smashed up. Dr. Unsworth : No, nothing like it. The Coroner asked if death was clearly caused by the injuries. Witness said the conditions were consistent with being knocked down and run over by a train. He did not think she had been run over in the sense that the wheels passed over her. He rather fancied that the woman was lying down and that she was struck in'the back by the guard in front of the wheels and pushed violently along the line. The Coroner: The train must have been going at a great speed? Witness said the speed must have been high to cause such injuries. Inspector Burton said he thought it was simply a case of suicide.

Constable Iltu3sett said that when he was preparing the body for the post-mortetn he found stitched in the chemise a newspaper report of the proceedlugs at Newton-le-Willows, where the deceased was tined for cruelty to her son, Elijah Perkins. Herbert Cooke, the husband, said that on Saturday, the 6th of 'November, be went to his father's at Burtonwood, and at night his wife followed. When they left the house she said that she would go shopping and was undecided whether to go to Earlestown or Si. Helens. She then left him, and he went home to Haydock. He waited up until one o'clock, but his wile never dame back. He was her second husband. When the constable came to inquire about his wife he cou'd not believe that she was the woman who had been found .on the line. His wife was very much upset by the police court proceedings which followed the inquest on her son, who was found drowned in the canal at Earlestown.

The Coroner pointed out that there was no absolute evidence that the woman bad committed suicide, and the jury returned an open verdict. They expressed the opinion that there slas no blame attaching to the bushand. The Coroner called Cooke into the room and told him what the jury had said, and said that be concurred in the verdict. It sr ould be a satisfacti(m to him to know that that inquiry arid the police incpiries had been held.

div.head: PIT FIRE AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: PIT FIRE AT ST. HELENS.

About eight o'clock on Monday night an outbreak of fire was discovered in the Itavenhead mine of the Bold Colliery, St. Helens. The lite was rituated in the work. ings, about 500 van's from the pit shaft, and not far from the coal race. The workmen endeavoured to extinguish the flames, but eventually the St. helms Fire Brigade had to descend the pit and tackle the fire by it ears of their or emical apparatus. After nearly four hours' work, attended with considerable danger, the outbreak was greatly subdued. As the fire burnt away the props and timber th. roof began to fall, ind the smoke and fumes ,%hich filled the roadway were a great handicap to tte firemen and the colliers assisting them. By two o'clock on Tuesday morning the fire was almost got under, and part of the brigade men were , able to return to their headquarters.

div.head: Baden-Powell Boy Scouts.
div.p: Baden-Powell Boy Scouts.

Sir,—l notice a grand display is to be giren by various troops of the above resident in Warrington and district, including Corporal Francklin,of Leicester, holder of the Silver Wolf, on Thursday next, in the dining hall of Messrs. Crosfield's Ltd., Bank Quay. I understand the object in view is re-organization, also to provide .if possible a central club and drill room for the various troops. The scout laws embody every rule which actuates the advancement of the moral side. of a youth's life, viz., no bad language is tolerated, smoking and drinking of intoxicating liquors are also forbidden until a certain age. The boys are tamht such useful work as ambulance, signalling, life-saving from drowning, knotting and splicing ropes ; then they have (bills, walking exercis( s. &c., which hOp materially in their physical development. These advantages should, I am sure, be enough to create a sound impression on all parents, and induce them to do all in their power to help their sons who are desirous of joining the movement. Many who have previously ridiculed this very worthy cause will now realize that the object d( serves appt eciation frcm at least two points of view viz. : "Moral and Physical Welfare." May -I appeal to all who are interested to attend on Thursday next and so make the boys first ventures thorongh success. Any boys who desire to join the scouts should also come, aria they can inter- view the various Scout Masters, who will only be too happy to furnish them with any ,information they would lequire.—Yout s truly, CHARLES J.. NEWTON. 1.57, Orford-lane, Warrington.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. ROBERT BOLTON.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. ROBERT BOLTON.

We regret to announce the death of Mr. Robert Bolton, who pass* d away at his residence, 88, Man; chester-road, on Saturday, after a short illness from bronchitis pneumonia, and heart disease. Mr. Bolton, who was 01 years of age, had for twenty-five years been an agent for the Prudential Assurance Company. Since April, 1904, he bad represented the Fairfield. Ward on the Board of Guardians. He aas the vice-chairman of the Cottage Homes Committee, and a member of the Assessment and Houses Committees; being very regular in his attendance at the meetings. He was a member of the "Samuel Wakefield" Lodge of the Ro3al Antede- luvian Order of Buffaloes, a Conservative, and a Church- man. He leaves a widow and an adopted daughter.
[Parkin s c n. THE LATE MR. ROBERT BOLTON.
THE FUNERAL.

The funeral took place at the Cemetery on Wednesday afternoon, the Rev. J. H. Bankes officiating. There was a large gathering of relatives • and friends. The Warrington Board of Guardians was represented by the Rev. T. R: Matthews (chairman), Mr. E. L. Bent (chairman of Abe Padgate Cottage Homes Committee), Messrs. W. H ' Zfughton W. C. Brooks, NV. Flennagan, R. Forshaw, W. Furness, A Bottomley (clerk), B. Shearer, (inquiry officer), A. Wright (superintendent of Cottage Homes), F. H. Mariam! (relieving officer) and John Fairhurst. The fdllowing members of the local lodge of the R.A.0.11. acted as bearers :—Bros. R. Burrows W. Marshall, J. Welsh, T. Conroy. G. Atkinson and F. Scott. At the close ot the Church burial service, the special rites of tn.) R.A.0.8. were conducted by Primo A.H. Walker, C.P. Amongst other members of the Order in attend- ance were: Primos J. W. Taylor and A. Roberts, Bros. F. Ward, J. Payton, H. Teece, NV. Davies and R. Young. Others present at the graveside ircluded Mr. It. Pierpoint, Councillor Steel, Mr. G. H. W. Steel and Mr. Herbert Hayes. Amongst those who rent floral tributes were: Mr. Wright and staff of the Padgate Cottage Homes, the Cottagg Homes Committee, the Cemetery .Hotel Bowling Club. tile Junior Conservative Club, the Prudential agents, and the Samuel Wakefield Lodge, R.A.0.8. VOTE OF CONDOLENCE.
. _ At the meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians on Wednesday a vote of condolence with Mrs. Bolton was passed on the motion of Mr. W. Houghton seconded by Mr. W. C. Brooks. ,

div.head: ROLLER SKATING.
div.p: ROLLER SKATING.
THE EMPIRE RINK,

Skating under ideal conditions is the first thought of the managers of this most popular link and on Thursday night they presented a new departure in the shape of a " Moonlight" carnival, which proved a brilliant success. The skaters Lumbered about 700 and there was a large assembly of spectators. The rink, alive with skaters in their gay and novel costumes, presented a pretty spectacle. The sole illumination came from two electric arc lights fixed to the band-stand and manipulated by Mr. H. Bibby. A comedy band added to the gaiety. The prize winners were :—Neatest costume (lady), prize, electro flower stand, lliss Mona Williams (lady jester); highly commetnded, Miss Urmsley (pielette) ; Miss Williamson (night). Gents' neatest costume, Mr. C. Plinstori (Admiral), prize, silver mounted oak biscuit barrel; highly commended, Mr. Aldred (Toreador) ; Mr. Bibby (Indian chief) ; A. Finlayscn (Mephistopheles). Most decorative (lady), Miss Brough (winter), prize, silver brush and comb in case; highly commended, Miss Chalmers (Bohemian girl) ; Miss Finlayson (harvest queen). Gents' humorous, Mr. B. Brown (French clown), prize, gents' dressing case ; 121-hly cnmmended, Mr. Pritchard (Mac Nab); Mr. T. Wihliam....ranny Welker) ; Mr. G, J. Basketter (suffragette). • There will be •special attractkns next week. On Monday Crosfield a Band will be in attenVance and will play special skating music. On Tuesday a grand hockey match between Chorlton B.C. and the Empire H.C. will be played. Thursday night will be a social night, when thtre will be a grand march and also -.musical chairs.

div.head: Primitive Methodist Centenary _Concert
div.p: Primitive Methodist Centenary _Concert

A high-class concert was held on-ThurSday evening in Legh-street schoolroom, the chairman being the Rev. J. B. Buglass. The Excelsior Glee Party treated the company to two,pieces rendered in perfect style. Mr. E. Bate was heard to advantage in the songs "My mountain rose" and "Sound of the drum," and for an encore sang "Peg away." Tenor horn solos were given by Mr. Moore. Miss Elsie Hewitt sang sweetly " Dear Heart" and "May Morn." Miss Peake sang " Come back to me" and "Summer showers" in a pleasing style. Oboe solos were contributed by Mr. Percy Whitfield in his usual capable manner. A pianoforte duet by Miss Foden and Miss Annie Titchett was ably rendered.. Mr. Alf Smith,lightning caricature artist, was well applauded. The humorists were Messrs. Bert Spruce and Herbert Wilkes, and the accompanist Miss Annie Titchett.: Tbe proceeds were in aid of the coming bazaar.

div.p: LOCAL WEDDING.
Rirtles.

div.head: Roberts—llissold.
div.p: Roberts—llissold.

A pretty wedding of considerable local interest took place at St. John's Church, Gainsborough, on Thursday. when Mr. William Edwin Roberts, eldest son of Mr. William Roberts, J.P., and Mrs. Roberts, " Harleydene," Latchford, was married to Miss Emmeline Constance Clissold, youngest daughter of Mr. William Leonard and Mrs. Clissold, "Ashcroft," Gainsborough. A large congregation witnessed the ceremony. The Rev. F. W. Hutchinson, M.A., vicar of Gainsborough, officiated and gave an eloquent address to the newly married couple at the close of the service. The hymns " The Voice that breathed o'er Eden " and "How welcome was the call " were sung. Mr. Councillor R, Judson wasat the organ and played choice selections, including Mendelssohn's "Wedding March." The bride who was given away by her father, was charm- ingly attired in an Empire gown of white cloth with picture hat to match and carried a shower bouquet of white lilies and roses, the gift of the bride- groom> Her ornament was a pearl pendant, the gift of the bridegroom's mother. The bridesmaids were Miss Frederica Clissold. sister of the bride, and Miss Irene Roberts, sister of the bridegroom, who wore pretty Princess gowns of pastel blue cloth, and black picture hats. Their bouquets were composed of gold chrysanthemums which, together with gold brooches, were the gifts or the bridegroom. Mr.A. Rathbone, of Grappenhall, discharged the duties of best man. After the ceremony the weddinc, breakfast was served at the Yarboro' Hotel. The health of the bride and bridegroom was "proposed in a very neat and appro- priate speech by the Vicar and supported by Mr. Councillor Judson, the bridegroom responding: Later the happy couple left for London where the honey- moon is being spent. The bride's travelling dress was a mole cloth costume withhat to match. div.head: DEATH OF MR. J. B. CALDWELL.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. J. B. CALDWELL.

It is with deep regret that we announce the death of Mr. John Bernard Caldwell, one of our best known local musicians, .who passed Away at his residence, 110, Bewsey-road, on Wednesday morning. Mr. Caldwell, who had been suffering from a bronchial complaint for about a fortnight, was exactly forty-nine years of age on the day of his death.He was the third son of the late Mr. Peter Caldwell, of Stockton Heath, and from boyhood displayed exceptional musical talent. He received instruction from Dr. Bridge, of Chester, and Dr. Kendrick Pyne, of Manchester, and became a very capable performer on the organ. For thirty years he held the post of organist at St. Alban's (R.C.) Church and was most regular and devoted in his attention to the duties. Mr. Caldwell was organist to the Warrington Musical Society for between ten and eleven years and on resigning in 1901 he was the recipient of a token of esteem which took the form of a handsome rose

bowl. The present was on view at the annual meet- ing in July of that year but Mr. Caldwell had inti- mated that he was " too shy" to attend to be formally presented with it. The hon. secretary (Mr. W. E. Atkin) in his report said: "By Mr. Caldwell's resignation the Society has lost an accompanist and organist who for the past ten to eleven years has been most faithful in his regular attendance at the rehearsals and concerts, and we cannot let this opportunity pass withont expressing our gratitude to him for his great help" The President (Mr. J. C. Parr) also paid a tribute to Mr. Caldwell's faithful services. Mr. Caldwell was of a retiring disposition and took no part in public or political work. Much sympathy is felt with the widow and two sons in their sudden bereavement. _ _
This (Saturday) morning a requiem ta-s will be offered at St. Alban's Church at ten o'clock and after- wards the funeral will take place at the Cemetery.
THE LATE MR. J. B. CALDWELL (From an early photograph).

div.head: CROSS COUNTRY RUNNING.
div.p: CROSS COUNTRY RUNNING.

WARRINGTON UNITED' HARRIERS. A club run should have taken place last Saturday from beadquarters.the Black Horse Inn,Sankey Bridges, with Farnworth Harriers but owing to the foggy weather the visiting team did not turn up. This, how- ever, did not spoil the home club's sport. An ordinary run round the lanes for about five miles was indulged in at a brisk pace. .1. Litherland, the winner of last weeks novice medal still improves, while F. Sha.,dsvell, runner up to novice medal winner, ran very well and will improve a lot yet. Warrington United's novices are a grand lot this season and with a little more experience will do themselves justice cn the treck.

div.head: TO-DAY'S MEET.
div.p: TO-DAY'S MEET.

In view of the gathering of the clans at Rylands' Ground Gorsey-lane this afternoon the local clubs were taking things easy on Saturday last. Although the fog prevented other games the devotees of this sport mustered well at their various headquarters and short slow inns were indulged in, but what racing did take place suggests that to-day's contests will be sternly fought out.

, The five mile race has closed with 101 entries. This rumber includes many athletes who hitherto have con- fined their efforts to shorter disthnces, some with a good measure of success, since the definite flx;ng of the date many of these have applied themselves to prepare for to-day's contest and perhaps the results will be surprising. The six mile vice has ".'0 entries which represent the hest class locally and many have earned fame in hard fought races.

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
" The March Hare."

Mr. Harold Smith, brother of that political and legal luminary, Mr. F. E. Smith, K.C., M.P., has blossomed forth as a playwright, and his farcical comedy "The March Hare "is produced at the Royal Court Theatre this -week by Mr. Chas. Pell's Company. The story is of the flimsiest, the situations from the start being frankly ridiculous, and smart stagecraft is a Very strong element in the success of the production. All the same, the farce achieves its object as a mirth- provoker, hilarity reigning supreme throughout the evening. The fun arises through the misreading of a letter, the outcome of feminine ingenuity, which causes poor Uncle John, eminently respectable but testy in temper, to be regarded as a danger- ous lunatic—as "mad as a Mai ch hare " and Dr. Dart, the promising young locum, to be shunned as a professional poisoner. The fearsome, haunting " smile " of a butler and a grand smash-up of crockery—which, repeated nightly, should prove fairly expensive—are quite indispensable adjuncts of the performance. We cannot speak took highly of the company, which enters ipto the farce with the utmost spirit, the boisterous merriment not being allowed to flag for a moment. Miss Aida Jenoure is a very talented aerkess and presents a finished portrayal of Mrs. Tiverton. Mr. Alfred Ibberson is superb as Uncle John Croker, his grotesque mano3uvres on learning that he is fated to be a victim of the poisoner convulsing the audience. Mr. Horace Sinclair does well as the Rev. Joshua Flewitt, and Mr. J. H.Roberts, in the role of James, the butler, is a host in himself. Miss Babs Stuart proves a favourite as the irrepress- ible Kate, Miss Wanda 3Jeryll is a winsome Lucy,and Miss Elizabeth Rosslyn is especially praiseworthy as Mary. The orchestral selections, under Mr. Norman Latham's conductorship, are well varied and tastefully played..
NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME. "
Next week Mr. Douglas Bruce's company will present Walter Melville 's exciting drama "The girl who lost her character."
DRAMATIC SOCIETY'S PERFORMANCES,

The Warrington Dramatic Society will give its annual performances at the theatre during the week commencing December 6th, when the repertoire will be :—Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday, Mr. Sydney Grundy's successful comedy*" A pair of spectacles, preceded each evening by the comedietta "Mrs. Hilary regrets." Thursday, Friday and Saturday, Mr. Haddon Chambers' original modern play "The Idler." The Society, which has already raised the hundsome sum of £2,000 for local charities, ;s making a special effort this year, as the Infirmary is urgently in need of funds. The plays have been exceedingly well rehearsed and finished performances are assured on the opening nights. The cast will be an exceptionally strong one. The box office opens to-day (Saturday) at 11 am. at the theatre, where seats may be booked daily.

div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

div.head: Billiards at Ryland's Pavilion.
div.p: Billiards at Ryland's Pavilion.

At the invitation of Messrs. Rylands' Bros. a visit was made by the members of the staff of Pearson and Knowles to the Recreation Pavilion when a game of billiards was played, ending in a victory for Pearson and Knowles by 121 points. After refreshments had been partaken of a musical evening was spent, the following artistes taking part :—Songs were rendered by Messrs. J. Rabbitt, T. Humphreys, A. Fieldhouse, T. Reddish and Higham. Messrs: W. Moores and W. Whittle gained much applause by their humorous selections. Mr. Taylor was the accompanist. Mr. T. Truslove, who occupied the chair thanked Messrs. Rylaiads Bros. on behalf of Pearson and Knowles for their kind invita- tion and was ably supported by Mr. A. Crowe. Mr. Jeffrey and Mr. Knott responded on behalf of Messrs. Rylands' Bros.

div.head: NIMROD AT LA.TCHFORD LOCKS,
div.p: THE NIMROD AT LA.TCHFORD LOCKS,

There was much excitement in Latchford on Tuesday when Sir E. Shackleton's:sturdy little ship, the Nimrod, fresh from her South Polar expedition passed up the Ship Canal and through the Locks en route for Manchester. She reached Latchford just before noon, and the news of her coming had spread sufficiently for the scholars of the schools to assemble and give her a lusty cheer. Captain Waring and a number of ladies and gentlemen were present- at the Locks, and boarded the vessel during her brief stay.

The Isfimrod has been making a few weeks 'stay at Liverpool, but has not attracted great attention in the city of ships, and it is hoped Manchester people will appreciate her more generously. She is only a small vessel of some 226 tons, and is essentially a sailing ship notwithstanding the sere wand the masts and the long heavy spars stretching over the water dwarf the yellow funnel that tells of the engines below. In akw days the ship will be open to public inspection. It is probable that after leaving Manchester the Nimrod will be sold, the British Antarctic Association having no further use for her. She may make a short stay at Latchford on her return journey.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. W. BOOTHROYD.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. W. BOOTHROYD.

A. painful sensation was Created in Warrington .when it became known • that .Mr, Walter Boothroyd, managing director of the Empire Skating Rink, had passed away at his residence, Ellesmere-road, Stockton Heath on Sunday afternoon. Mr. Boothroyd had enjoyed robust health and up •to the previous Monday had taken a very active part in the manage- ment of the rink. On that day he attended a meet- ing of directors al Mr. Olive's office. He complained of feeling unwell' and later in the week seriou's symptoms developed, and Dr. Binns was Called in. Despite every attention death ensued on Sunday, the cause being Bright's disease. Mr, Boothroyd came
Photo] [Parkinson. THE LATE MR. W. BOOTHROYD.

to Warrington from Stalybridge about twenty-five years ago, and started business as a pianoforte and music dealer in Sankey-street. Later he removed to premises in Bridge-street. He was a good bu sness man and his work was attended with such success that he was able to retire into private life a few years ago. Som.what s;ngular to state, Mr. Boothroyd was not musically inclined and was unable to play any instrument He leaves a widow and a son and daughter with whom much sympathy is felt in their bereavement.
THE FUNERAL.

The funeral took place on Wednesday afternoon at St. Thomas' Church, Stockton Heath. The Revs. James Collins and H. A. Lester performed the last rites. Many relatives and friends gathered round the grave to pay their tribute of respect to the deceased. The chief mourners were :—Mr. Tom Bonthroyd (son), Master T. B. Parkinson of Blackley (nephew), Mr. Wright Boothroyd of Stalybridge (cousin). Others present were Dr. Ilinns ; Messrs. J. W. Greenhalgh, R. H. Meldrum (executors), Edwin Bradshaw, H. J. West- brook, James Atkinson. Messrs. W. Chalmers, John Finlayson. John Cooper, J. T. Barton. A. H. Clive, R. E. Garnett. S. J. I3eamon and Thortas Cooper represented the Skating Rink Co. Floral tributes were placed on the grave from Mrs. Boothroyd, Mr. Tom Boothrovd, Mrs. Briers (daughter), Mr. James Atkinson, Mr. Robinson, Mr. Thomas Cooper, Mr. D. Cooper, Dr. Binns, Directors of the Empire Skating Rink, Employees of the Empire Skating Rink, Orchestra of the Empire Skating Rink, Mrs. Briggs, Mr. Mather and Mr. French.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF
GUARDIANS.
Christmas Beer.

The fortnightly meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday the Rev. T. R. Mathews presiding. There were also present :—Mrs. Collingwood, Mrs. Simnson, Messrs. A. J. Jolley, W. Gill, W. Houghton, W. C. Brooks, W. Furness, R. Lee, J. A. Rusbworth, M. W. Seton, A. Brooks. R. Forshaw, A. Bottomley, (clerk), R. W. Peacock, (assistant clerk) J. F. Awbery, (master) aud A. Wright (superintendent of Cottige Homes).
CHRISTMAS BEER.

The House Committee recommended that the inmates and officers be provided with extra rations on Christmas Day. The supplies to he purchased included 40 dozen one pint bottles and 15 dozen half pint bottles of dinner beer, the order for which was placel with Messrs. W. Hall and Son, Warrington. Mrs. SIMPSON moved an amendment that the minute relating to Christmas beer be not approved. It seemed to be a "double extra "that they were giving this Christmas time. As they had to deal with such sad cases that came into the House, she thought a good sub- stantial dinner, without the !Her, would be a greater charity to the inmates. "I won't say much this time " concluded Mrs. Simpson " You know what I would like to say."

COLLINGWoOD in seconding said that at this particular season there was likely to be heavy expense. There was great depression in trade and they should dispense with the luxury of beer on this occasion. If the inmates had apples and oranges and other good things provided for them, they could do without beer. At the request of the Board, the Clerk read the list of extras which were to be ordered for Christmas. They included, in 'Addition to 550 pounds of beef, eight turkeys, the usual plum pudding ingredients, nuts, sweets, apples and oranges, tobacco and snuff, and toys or the children.'

Mr. JOLLEY said he wls sorry the amendment had Feet' moved, because it seemed to him that the argu- sments of Mrs. Collingwood cut both ways. If circum fiances were going to be so very depressing during the approaching festive season, it was a reason for taking a little more stimulant to keep their spirits up.(Laughter). Mrs. Simpson characterked the beer as a "double extra." Personally he hoped it would be a "treble extra," for they should give the inmates decent beer while they were at it. Mrs. COLLINOWOOD asked if the quantities bad been thoroughly gone into. It seemed incredible that any institution could require 5501b5. of beef. The inmates could not possibly eat it on Christmas Day and she would like to know in what length of time it was supposed to be consumed? Was it to last a month or a week ?
Mr. GILL: What numbers are there in the House? The CLERK: About 400 in the Workhouse and 250 in the hospital.
Mrs. COLLINGWOOD : There will be many more in the hospital afterwards.
Mr. RUSH WORM stated that Mr. Mather, ho carved at the CottagA Homes, said there would not be above 4 or slbs. of beef left there.

Mr. GILL said the qnantity of beef did not work out at one pound each, and it was not too much. Mrs. COLLINGWOOD : To a new COMM', it seems absolutely incredible that it is possible to get through that amount.
Mr. RUSH WORTH : There is the bone and the loss in cookinr.
On Mrs. Simpson's amendment being put to the vote, it was defeated by 8 votes to 4.

A PLEASING REPORT. The CLERK reported that a boy who was chargeable to the Union for some considerable time was, on arriving at working age, apprenticed with a prominent local tradesmen. The other day that gentleman met him (Hr. Bottomley) and asked him to inform the Guardians that the boy bad turned out an excellent tradesman, that he was still working for him and earn- ing good wages, and that if he would stay there he could have a situation for life.

div.head: TENNYSON AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS. What he thought of the House of Lords.
div.p: TENNYSON AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS. What he thought of the House of Lords.

The Rev. W. L. Schroeder delivered the fifth of the course of University Extension lectures on,' Tennyson: his art and personality" in the Conservative Club Assembly Room on Wednesday evening. The special subject for consideration was "Tennyson's attitude to the social problems of the time." The lecturer dealt with poetry as expressive of the soul of the people and said that from the great poet the demand must be made of something of a divine lead, something that would keep us in the way that led to life and the Kingdom of God. Social progress was only possible because some men thought in advance of their day. . When they realized that every reform started probably with a minority of one, they looked to the reforming element in society as distinctly that which was less than the general body of opinion or of aspiration. If the poet was to embody anything of that feeling of the soul of God in life, he would always stand out against the rest of the nation. He would not merely embody something which people knew, but he would tell them something which they did not know or had not yet seen. The poet could not separate himself from the multitude and sing sweet little ditties alone. If he wanted to move the people strongly, to utter a sound which would reverberate through the generations, he must live with the people and realise their needs. Even with the utmost charity, they had to say that Tennyson's experience of life was strictly limited. He moved about among the educated and cultured classes ; be was exclusive in his manners and habits. In one word, he bad mothing of that. great, rough humanity which would have made him one with the people, despite his aristocratic sympathies and his position. When he (the lecturer) thought of Walt Whitman, with his great heart and his great voice, singing the song of the people, he was almost obliged to think there was something not quite so great in the nature of Tennyson, which drove him only to the society of those with whom he could feel perfectly comfortable. Tennyson was distinctly Conservative— probably that was a virtue in those days of frighful reform. (Laughter). But when they considreed Tennyson as a young man and Tennyson in his later days, they found there was a change. As a young man he was certainly more Radical than in later life. Probably most of us were. In 1830 he said "I am of the same politics as Shakespeare, Bacon and every sane man." We were justified in saying that Tennyson's nature and habit made him somewhat averse to anything like real democracy. He always liked to hug the idea that although there was much that was really bad, things were not so bad as some social reformers made out. He had a profound distrust of anything like disorder and did not care for revolutionary ideas. Theoretically he believed in the pro- gressive evolution of humanity; practically he was always one of those who abode by convention. Tennyson did not realise that it was because of the education of the men and women that there came the increased demand for liberty and better social con- ditions. And yet he was a great lover of freedom, although he was noV willing to trust certain sections of society with it. TE might be of interest to console themselves with the idea that Tennyson was an Imperialist. All who believed in that great world-wide Empire, with England as the nucleus and the heart, would go to Tennyson with great hopes that would not be disappointed. He believed that the best guarantee of peace was preparation for war—the kind of thing which had been very much exploded by peace exponents, judging by the literature he (the lecturer) had had the privilege of reading. Referring to Tennyson's advocacy of the training of all the manhood of the nation to I ear arms,the lecturer said"l feel rather out of court, because I don't mind telling you I am a peace man through and through, and I don't believe in that sort of rubbish.' With regard to the British Constitution, Tennyson thought the fault of the Englishman was that he thought, he and his ways were always right everywhere. Tenny- son did not approve of the British Constitution for all countries. In 1881—and this was prime in view of what was going on now in the House of Lords and throughout the country—Tennyson looked upon the House of Lords as "foremost in bebating power," as "a stable, wise and moderating influence in these changeful democratic days." Foremost in debating power! He regarded the House of Lords as the greatest upper Chamber in the world—some people wanted it to be very much upper—and esteemed it a high honour that he should belong to it and have a voice among "many men of mark and among the descendents of those who have made England what she is." Then why in the world, didn't he use his voice in the House of Lords and help to make it a debating Chamber of the highest worth? Tennyson regtrded the House of Lords as a safeguard against the destruction of the Constitution and the disruption of the whole Empire. It might he wise for i some of them who were so nclined,te send Tennyson's opinion to certain people who were mightily concerned at the moment. (Laughter.) Tennyson's political creed was summed up in a letter written to Mr. Glad- stone in 1884 : "The nation is one and includes all ranks of people. I take it for granted that both Houses are equally anxious to do justice to all. Certainly the House of Peers has the prior claim to confidence, being the older of the two, and it would be a base abnegation if it forewent its right and its duty to reconsider an all-important question." He (lecturer) did not want to point out the logic of that. Age was to he the criterion of worth—"it has the prior claim to confidence, because it was the older of the two." His (the lecturer's) only exclamation was " Great Scott ! " The lecturer also dealt with Tennyson's attitude on such questions as the franchise, Home Rule, and Disesteblishment. Tennyson was a "safe" man and to many he commended himself as truly admirable, but to those who wanted some kind of guidance in social reform he was of very little use. They turned to men like Browning, Shelley and William Morris and they found much more definitely the kind of thing which ultimately would mean the salvation of the nation.
